summary: Analysis code accompanying the revised manuscript AeroJ-2026-0336. It covers: the codified ICAO CO2 limit lines L_NT(M) and L_InP(M) (40 CFR 1030.30); the structural (empty-weight) model; the transpose-pair arithmetic and the analytic induced-drag carry-over derivation; the OpenVSP/VSPAERO comparison model in its two released configurations (the forward reconstruction and the equalised-exposed-span configuration on which the Section 4.4 comparison is stated); the Monte Carlo propagation of Experiment A and the Section 4.5 mission model; the clean-sheet placement analysis; the Section 5 remedy benchmark; and the generation of Figures 1-5 with Table 4. The OpenVSP scripts generate their .vsp3 model files on run. Figure 1's freighter points are illustrative only, exactly as the figure caption states (anchored centrals, not estimator outputs, no uncertainty bands). The estimator predictions of Appendix A are not covered by this release; their record is Appendix A of the paper. The data underlying the study are the public sources cited in the paper's reference list. Requirements: Python 3.10+, NumPy, Matplotlib (figure images only); SciPy optional (pure-Python fallbacks included); OpenVSP 3.x with its Python module for the two OpenVSP scripts only.
title: Analysis code for "The Volumetric Blind Spot: How the Reference Geometric Factor in the ICAO CO2 Standard Mis-Specifies Efficiency for Mid-Size Freighters" (The Aeronautical Journal, manuscript AeroJ-2026-0336, revised manuscript under review)

summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. In the original penetration metric, perpetual-inventory robot capital preserves the estimates at 5 percent depreciation, but faster assumed depreciation counts the automotive installations behind the first stage as replacement rather than net additions, eliminating shock-level relevance at 10 percent and all relevance at 15 percent. The benchmark is reproducible and robust in sign, but it is identified from an automotive margin in historically industrial labor markets; that margin defines its scope and the concrete content of its exclusion restriction. More generally, coefficient robustness and breadth of identifying support are distinct properties that shift-share studies should report separately. JEL Codes: J23, J24, O33, R23, C18, C26 Keywords: Industrial robots; automation; replication; shift-share IV; Bartik instruments; Rotemberg weights; identifying support; weak-instrument-robust inference; Anderson–Rubin; plausibly exogenous; perpetual inventory; robot capital; local labor markets
title: Robots and Jobs Revisited: A Bit-Exact Replication, Shift-Share Anatomy, and Capital-Stock Extension of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020)

summary: We ask whether the folded Causal Chain Physics continuum admits a traversable spacelike channel and, if not, whether matter can move onto new constituents without scanning and reconstruction. The first answer is negative. One radial ladder ends at one boundary, spacetime is the image of one extended-tetrad map, and a black-hole horizon is a local pullback of that boundary. With no second exterior or earlier carrier edge, the no-channel theorem excludes traversable wormholes, metric shortcuts, baby-universe branches, and topology-changing escape channels. A fold-symmetric black hole may occur as initial data but remains terminal in both temporal orientations. The same principle gives the positive result. Orbital recurrence can repeat an informational type, but not a physical token, whose identity follows one continuous supported map. On Paper III's finite physical sector, an exact transporter preserves every reference correlation while returning the source and carrier to a fixed blank. Local, state-independent exchanges can therefore move the protected organization without cloning or a hidden blueprint, subject to explicit capacity and latency bounds. Unlike measure-and-prepare reconstruction, standard teleportation preserves an unknown state using entanglement, a Bell record, and causal feed-forward. Direct translocation uses no measurement record or remote conditional operation: the output continues the same supported map on different constituents. Proposed tests move a reference-entangled molecular qubit through an exchange chain and a coherent bond-form through dissociation, photonic transduction, and reassociation; a superconducting precursor tests the same clean-reset condition. These are causal tests, not faster-than-light transport.
title: Causal Chain Physics XII: No Traversable Wormholes and Causal Form Translocation—Spacelike No-Go, Orbital Recurrence, and Physical Identity

summary: We derive the baryon, active-lepton, and dark-matter inventory of one scalar-completed electroweak event. The CCF covariant derivative creates the first-order wall and its chiral source; bounded-support Parisi–Wu (PW) and continuum transport are two resolutions of that source, while the weak anomaly converts the left-handed bias into baryon and lepton number. The fixed-root PW calculation gives η_B,1^PW = 5.26082 × 10⁻¹⁰; the matrix-resolved continuum reconstruction gives 5.13315 × 10⁻¹⁰. Their computed hard-scale response defines the non-Gaussian theory-resolution interval η_B = 5.26 (+0.30, −0.40) × 10⁻¹⁰, which contains the independent Paper II baryon-loading range (5.37–5.48) × 10⁻¹⁰. The same event produces the flavor-scalar active source L_ν = 4.022200 × 10⁻² (1, 1, 1) and ξ = 5.87649332 × 10⁻² (1, 1, 1). An equal right-handed counterasymmetry makes this a chiral separation rather than net lepton-number creation. On the Paper II background its direct weak-rate map gives Y_P^weak = 0.24527; counting the right and active radiation once gives Y_P^full = 0.24712. An exact reflection protects one odd closed-support scalar pole with J = 0 and M_X = 3.9230019 TeV + O(Λ_QCD). The allowed Φ_G^a B_i^a operator is a heavier transverse J = 1 excitation, not the ordinary static-source gluelump ground state. The Lorenz/support theorem gives the exact temporal-source identity J_(u,G) = 0, excluding a scalar-color Coulomb kernel and Sommerfeld ladder while retaining transverse color interactions. Deconfined freeze-out then yields Ω_X h² = 0.130 (+0.028, −0.015), overlapping the Paper II requirement 0.1230–0.1234 without a cosmological fit. This number is the abundance before the ordinary-QCD transition. The complete source, spin-ordering, and late-survival proofs are given in the Supplemental Material; post-transition finite-range scattering remains a separate connected-amplitude matching problem.
title: Causal Chain Physics XI: Baryogenesis, Active Leptogenesis, Scalar-Color Dark Matter, and Cosmological Matter Concordance

summary: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.
title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference

Its second research unit explores provenance-aware acupuncture knowledge graphs, acupoint nano-interfaces, causal pattern models, matched-resource quantum sensing and cross-generational evidence platforms. Cultural concepts are hypotheses and labels, not proven energies or therapies. Two five-theme research units contain ten English 777-page working editions: 300 conditional mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 separately paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Designs call for blinded perturbations, calibrated physical witnesses, optimized conventional baselines and explicit stop policies. This collection reports candidate research protocols, not completed results or demonstrated clinical effects. Blinded non-needle cues and matched warm stimuli challenge ordinary thermal and cardiovascular explanations. Tissue stress, unblinded-only gains or calibration failure are hard stops. F82  MIND-BODY UNITY PHILOSOPHY AND PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL REGULATION AT THE LIMIT — Separates randomized attention and feedback effects from autonomic changes caused by posture or covert muscle activation. Crossed blinded feedback, hidden replay and synchronized ECG, EMG and posture controls challenge interpretation of subjective sensation as a distinct mechanism. Unidentifiable effects or consent failure halt claims. F83  QIGONG BREATHING AND HUMAN BIOELECTRIC REGULATION AT THE LIMIT — Compares qigong-labeled breathing with ordinary paced breathing under matched respiration, electrode geometry and motion. Masked rate matching and exchanged session labels test whether sweat activity, respiratory rhythms or contact impedance account for surface EDA/ECG differences. Uncontrolled artifact prohibits special-energy inference. F84  VOLITION, MIND-BODY UNITY AND INTELLIGENT NEUROFEEDBACK AT THE LIMIT — Challenges apparent intent-related information using live versus timestamp-matched replayed neurofeedback, yoked sham feedback and identical EEG bandwidth. Cross-validated information gains must survive face-EMG, breathing and expectancy controls. Label leakage, unsafe feedback or ignored human stop authority veto interpretation. F85  EXTERNAL QIGONG CLAIMS, CLASSICAL QI THEORY AND SCIENTIFIC FALSIFIABILITY AT THE LIMIT — Subjects alleged remote effects to sealed target schedules, signal isolation, independent randomization and double-blind instrument readings. Shams, shielded blanks and equal operator schedules confront electromagnetic, acoustic, thermal and experimenter leakage. External bibliographic metadata checks are limited; individual formula-to-endpoint fit and relevance require independent specialist review, particularly the provisional doubly robust expression in F88. Research Gates & Quality Assurance Boundary The source batch QA reports ten 777-page PDFs, zero exact duplicate Gate questions and zero exact duplicate full six-part annotations. Cross-book lexical screening records a maximum nearest-neighbor similarity of 0.8832, with 93 cases at or above 0.80 and none at or above 0.90. Such automated checks do not establish independent causal mechanisms, scientific novelty, clinical safety or experimental validation. summary: Validation dataset of the H5MD biophysics module, a metadata schema that stores the topology, force field, MD parameters, selection groups and observables of a molecular dynamics simulation together with its trajectory in one H5MD (HDF5) file. It accompanies the paper A Hierarchical Metadata Schema for Self-Contained Molecular Dynamics Trajectory Archives . validation_systems.zip contains the GROMACS inputs of the 58 chemical systems used in the paper's technical validation, reduced to what grompp needs: topology, force field, coordinates or run input, index groups and MD parameters. The systems range from 711 to 1,066,628 particles, cover AMBER, CHARMM, GROMOS, OPLS-AA and MARTINI force fields, and come in six groups by origin: self_generated (8): built with GROMACS from PDB entries bena (10): sessions of the Bena dataset ( 10.5281/zenodo.17632513 ) jcp_benchmark (6): GROMACS benchmark systems ( 10.5281/zenodo.3893789 ) hexabc (8): hexABC nucleic-acid and protein–nucleic-acid deposits from MDposit memprotmd (6): MemProtMD membrane proteins, atomistic and coarse-grained misato (20): MISATO protein–ligand complexes ( 10.5281/zenodo.7711953 ) Run under 23 simulation protocols, these inputs give the 379 reference files of the validation. The files can be regenerated with the validation scripts ( github.com/miemiemmmm/h5md-biophysics-validation ) and the GROMACS implementation published with the paper. Each group's MANIFEST.md credits its source and states the changes made; provenance/ holds the scripts that selected and prepared the systems. Four of the reference files are included as examples, each a short trajectory with the full metadata. They also serve as test data for the validator in gitlab.com/gromacs/h5md-biophysics : hexabc_a001u2_rna_protein__nvt-vrescale.h5md bench_villin__tcoupl-multigroup.h5md bench_villin__sd-langevin.h5md bench_villin__selection-noncontiguous.h5md
title: Validation systems and reference files for the H5MD biophysics metadata module

summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.
title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game

summary: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL

summary: Large language model applications are increasingly being organized as tool-using and multi-agent workflows rather than as isolated chat interfaces. This perspective paper examines the architectural problem that follows from that shift: agents may reason, invoke tools, and delegate work, but dependable deployment still requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries, and organizational control domains. We study this problem through the lens of the \emph{Internet of Agentics} (IoA), an emerging service-computing view in which heterogeneous agents are treated as governable service participants rather than only as stand-alone model endpoints. The paper organizes the landscape as a three-layer progression: from today's fragmented agent ecosystem, to interoperable agents, and ultimately to trustworthy and governable autonomy. First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; AGENTS.md and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. Third, it situates these developments within services computing, arguing that agentic systems reinterpret classical concerns from SOA and microservices---discovery, composition, governance, pricing, and trust---at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.
title: Towards a Trustworthy and Governable Internet of Agentics: An Architectural Perspective on Protocols, Systems, and Services

summary: Bridges are critical transportation infrastructure, and reliable operation and maintenance (O&M) is essential for traffic safety and long-term structural performance. However, bridge O&M faces key bottlenecks: no unified architecture coordinates heterogeneous resources; model inferences lack clear links to physical-mechanical laws; and experts' tacit knowledge remains difficult to formalize. This study proposes a knowledge-enhanced autonomy formalization methodology and apply it to construct the Bridge O&M Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System (BOMMA), which integrates heterogeneous diagnostic actions, physics-mechanics-informed representations, long-term memory, and structured experiential knowledge within a coordinated multi-agent workflow, enabling interpretable and traceable scheduling, analysis, and decision-making. On 3,492 multi-source instructions, the proposed method achieves scheduling recalls of 85.37% for simple and 99.40% for composite tasks, with 95.35% BERT F1-score for O&M action reasoning. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the components in the autonomy. This study bridges general LLM reasoning and specialized bridge O&M requirements.
title: Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Bridge Operation and Maintenance based on Large Language Model

summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and they introduce the risk of coordination among agents that might escape human oversight. The J-space has been used to uncover deception in single LLMs, but its use for uncovering and steering collusion between agents remains unexplored. We show, with interpretability experiments on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) on the NARCBench collusion benchmark, that colluding agents' J-space holds the collusion itself: before replying, 86% of colluders represent misrepresentation, concealment or remorse. In a steganographic card-counting task, the receiver's J-space holds a hidden count, and causal interventions alter its count. We also introduce the Jacobian Pair Contrast (J-PACT), an unsupervised method for detecting collusion between agents. We evaluate J-PACT on four open-weight models: GPT-OSS-20B, Llama-3.3-70B-IT, Qwen3-32B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B). J-PACT retains 85% of the above-chance AUROC of supervised NARCBench probes, matches them on steganographic scenarios, and names the colluding pair up to its complement in 99% of detected runs.

summary: A key milestone toward Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) is replacing hand-crafted optimizers with meta-learned update rules (such as Disco103 and OPEN) that discover how agents learn. Yet when a self-discovered RL model trains with adapting teammates, does co-evolution sustain capability gains or trap agents in brittle conventions? Across 1,800+ runs in continuous collective robotics (VMAS) and discrete coordination (Overcooked), we establish five laws of multi-agent adaptation. First, four-cell counterfactual partner swaps expose an evaluation illusion: apparent team progress often masks focal regression (+1.066 team gain concealing -0.119 focal loss) and inflates transfer by +0.649 to +1.210. Second, a 288-run physical-coupling sweep ($α\in [0, 1.5]$) reveals a linear scaling law ($β= +0.255$, $p = 0.000488$, Spearman $ρ= 1.0$): live reciprocal feedback keeps Disco103 invariant (AUC 0.297--0.322), whereas severing feedback triggers a monotonic collapse (-0.172 to -0.490), with OPEN establishing a sensitivity spectrum (Disco103 > OPEN > MAPPO). Third, extending navigation training eightfold (1.05M steps) enables Disco103 to overtake MAPPO (+0.087 team return, +0.133 bank gain), while decoupled training boosts cross-partner completion by +10.16% (56.25% vs. 46.09%). Fourth, in Overcooked, MAPPO's self-play conventions induce a 28.13% cross-partner collision rate, whereas Disco103 cuts collisions to 12.77% and achieves 3.33x higher bank return (9.96 vs. 2.99; net gain +6.43), further improved by decoupled meta-adaptation (+1.39 with scripted partners). Finally, perturbation pulses ($p=0.00098$), auxiliary entropy diagnostics (8.485 nats), and 48 multi-lifetime meta-evolved rules ($L_2 \in [2.11, 4.91]$) trace these dynamics to partner-gradient blindness and auxiliary drift, informing multi-agent self-discoverd algorithms.
title: From Single-Agent Self-Discovery to Multi-Agent Adaptation: Scaling Laws of Partner Feedback and Convention Rigidity in Meta Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.
title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks

However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.

summary: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.

summary: Abstract: Keeping the modern power grid running during heatwaves, wildfires, or cyberattacks requires knowing which power lines are the most dangerous "dominoes" if two or three of them fail at the same time. However, checking every possible combination of multiple broken lines across the Western U.S. grid is a math problem with millions of possibilities—far too slow for computers to solve in real time using standard physics equations. Conversely, taking shortcuts by simply looking at a map of the grid (to find the biggest, most connected hubs) fails because electricity does not travel like cars on a highway; it cannot be told which road to take. Instead, electricity automatically splits across all available wires based on their physical resistance. When a major line gets crowded or breaks, electricity surges onto smaller side-lines, causing chain-reaction blackouts far away from the original problem. In this memo, we introduce Physics-Informed Network Reshaping (PINR), an AI framework that bridges the gap between map-based speed and physical accuracy. PINR combines a specialized, mathematically predictable neural network with a network-disruption algorithm originally designed for counter-terrorism. Rather than testing millions of broken-wire combinations one by one, PINR uses a single, rapid pass to act as a dual-use stress gauge: For Grid Defenders ("Blue Team" Healing): It shows grid operators the exact 27 congested power lines where slightly "throttling" the flow (like adjusting valves on a water pipe) relieves 99.1% of grid overloads during a peak evening crunch, pushing excess electricity safely onto underused backup lines. For Security Analysts ("Red Team" Vulnerability Hunting): Because the lines that need the most throttling to heal the grid are the exact same lines carrying the most dangerous physical stress, PINR automatically narrows the search for catastrophic multi-line failures from 235 lines down to just 27. This cuts the number of three-line failure combinations to check by 99.86% (from over 2.1 million down to under 3,000). Most importantly, testing PINR on the 2026 Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) proves that looking at a static map of the grid is dangerously misleading. While standard map-based analysis points to California's central grid hub (CAISO) as the most critical choke point, PINR's physics engine reveals that California's many parallel lines easily absorb the load. Instead, the true physical bottlenecks hide in the power-exporting corridors of the Desert Southwest (Arizona and the Lower Colorado River) and the mountain seams connecting Montana, the Pacific Northwest, and Utah. Correspondence and collaboration inquiries: aes@acm.org

summary: Wave energy converters (WECs) are typically designed to operate near resonance to maximize energy capture. While this enhances power absorption, it also amplifies structural loads and accelerates fatigue damage. As a result, fatigue becomes a critical design driver even when stress remains below material yield limits. Fatigue in offshore systems has been widely studied, particularly under variable-amplitude loading induced by waves, wind, and currents. These effects are commonly evaluated using the Palmgren–Miner damage accumulation rule, where failure is predicted once cumulative damage reaches unity. However, fatigue assessment for WECs remains less developed, especially in terms of linking environmental conditions to structural degradation and operational stress limits. The objective of this work is to evaluate, predict and improve confidence in the structural response and fatigue life of a WEC under representative operating conditions and to identify critical components and failure modes before deployment in March 2026 accounting for not only load and geometric factors, but also environmental conditions such as temperature.
title: Worst-Case Fatigue Life of an OSWEC Under Sustained Sea States

summary: This repository presents an evidence-anchored, discipline-sensitive multicriteria assessment framework designed to support transparent, accountable, and reproducible evaluations of academic distinction and research integrity. The framework comprises a Microsoft Excel workbook organized into seven disciplinary classes corresponding to those of the European Academy of Sciences and Arts (EASA): 1. Humanities 2. Medicine 3. Arts 4. Natural Sciences 5. Social Sciences 6. Environmental and Technical Sciences 7. World Religions Each disciplinary class includes ten weighted assessment criteria evaluated on a five-level ordinal scale (0–4). Weighted scores are aggregated and normalized against the maximum attainable score for each class, generating percentage-based results and illustrative classification guidance. The workbook contains 15 worksheets, including discipline-specific evaluation forms, a scoring protocol, research integrity resources, an integrity register, a reusable audit template, and guidance for nominators. A central feature of the framework is the separation of academic merit assessment from research integrity verification. The integrity workflow supports the documentation and contextual examination of retractions, expressions of concern, citation irregularities, potential publication anomalies, and editorial or peer-review conflicts of interest. The framework distinguishes between unverified allegations, documented concerns, and substantiated findings. Bibliometric anomalies, retractions, or incomplete verification procedures must not automatically be interpreted as proof of individual research misconduct. The workbook also incorporates guidance for nominators regarding documentary evidence and the distinction between achievements that are not documented, criteria that have not yet been assessed, and verified absence of specific achievements. The assessment framework is intended to facilitate structured scholarly judgment rather than replace it. Its numerical weights and classification thresholds are illustrative methodological parameters and have not undergone independent empirical validation. Scope and limitations The instrument is proposed for academic discussion, methodological evaluation, pilot testing, and potential institutional adaptation. summary: This deposit is the archived version of record for BioFirewall v0.2.0, a defensive, design-stage screen for agentic genome-writing AI. BioFirewall intercepts a genome-writing plan in workflow, and returns allow , flag-for-review or refuse across five hazard axes native to genome writing (cargo, locus, edit type, germline and scale), with cited evidence, a calibrated false-refuse ceiling, a competence-conditioned confidence, an HMAC-signed design passport, a hash-chained audit log and a tiered managed-access plane. Contents: the complete source snapshot at the v0.2.0 tag; the open hazard data the five axes read (embedding centroids, oncogene and tumour-suppressor annotation, dosage-constraint and essentiality scores, curated fusion knowledge); the frozen benchmark, red-team and language-model panel results, including the reported negatives; the CCGD-derived positive sets and the locus outcome-validation result; five SHA-locked pre-registrations; the documentation set (threat model, hazard taxonomy, benchmark, head-to-head, system card, panel, hazard knowledge base, standards, cloud-lab integration); and the clean-image verification logs. Open data only. It contains no hazard sequences or evasion instructions; hazard signatures are held at the function, family, and taxon levels. The licence-restricted oracles (COSMIC, OncoKB), the cargo sequences and the run artefacts are excluded and are never committed. Every file is listed in SHA256SUMS and verifies with sha256sum -c. Source repository: https://github.com/ahmedanees-m/bio-firewall (tag v0.2.0). Requires PEN-STACK (declared range pen-stack>=0.2.0,<0.3.0). RRID:SCR_028785. bio.tools: biotools:bio-firewall. Licensing: Apache-2.0. Third-party open datasets are referenced at their home repositories under their own terms and are not re-licensed here; see DATA_LICENSES.md.

BioFirewall intercepts a genome-writing plan in workflow, and returns allow , flag-for-review or refuse across five hazard axes native to genome writing (cargo, locus, edit type, germline and scale), with cited evidence, a calibrated false-refuse ceiling, a competence-conditioned confidence, an HMAC-signed design passport, a hash-chained audit log and a tiered managed-access plane. Contents: the complete source snapshot at the v0.2.0 tag; the open hazard data the five axes read (embedding centroids, oncogene and tumour-suppressor annotation, dosage-constraint and essentiality scores, curated fusion knowledge); the frozen benchmark, red-team and language-model panel results, including the reported negatives; the CCGD-derived positive sets and the locus outcome-validation result; five SHA-locked pre-registrations; the documentation set (threat model, hazard taxonomy, benchmark, head-to-head, system card, panel, hazard knowledge base, standards, cloud-lab integration); and the clean-image verification logs. Open data only. It contains no hazard sequences or evasion instructions; hazard signatures are held at the function, family, and taxon levels. The licence-restricted oracles (COSMIC, OncoKB), the cargo sequences and the run artefacts are excluded and are never committed. Every file is listed in SHA256SUMS and verifies with sha256sum -c. Source repository: https://github.com/ahmedanees-m/bio-firewall (tag v0.2.0). Requires PEN-STACK (declared range pen-stack>=0.2.0,<0.3.0). RRID:SCR_028785. bio.tools: biotools:bio-firewall. Licensing: Apache-2.0. Third-party open datasets are referenced at their home repositories under their own terms and are not re-licensed here; see DATA_LICENSES.md.

summary: The cot-mcp rewrite: a new package and API, prompts selected by a benchmark against expert annotations, and a clean install from GitHub. Breaking New API. The pre-0.3 analyzer interface is removed ( analyzer.py , models.py , providers.py , prompt_factory , retrieval ). A run is now two calls: prepare_screen_bundles (one evidence bundle per cluster) and analyze_screen (the model over those bundles). See examples/analyze_clusters.ipynb . New Per-gene categories ESTABLISHED / NOVEL_ROLE / UNCHARACTERIZED , each with an evidence-ladder subclass and a rationale. A pathway confidence rubric (coverage tiers) and explicit abstention on clusters with no coherent pathway. Modes cot (default), standard and stepwise . PubMed literature gap-fill ( mcp=True ) for genes with no annotation. Per-gene phenotypic features and a perturbation-strength rank ( feature_columns , strength_column ). The matching reasoning steps are added only when the data is present. Annotation sources uniprot (default), affinage , both and affinage_then_uniprot , with on-disk caches. Per-run audit trail: cluster and gene tables, the parsed JSON, and a full trace per call. Options resume , dry_run and max_workers . Every prompt is a named component that can be overridden per run ( component_overrides , component_order ). benchmarks/ : the benchmark that selected the shipped prompts (source, prompt build-up, delivery, order, features), scored against three lab experts' annotations. It includes the paper figures. Fixed Installing from git works without access to private repos; the benchmark-output submodules are removed (#64). Install python -m pip install "mozzarellm @ git+https://github.com/cheeseman-lab/mozzarellm.git@v0.3.0" Full changes: https://github.com/cheeseman-lab/mozzarellm/compare/v0.2.0...v0.3.0

summary: This Zenodo asset holds the latest data results from the Marine Spatial Planning in Southern Brazil initiative, known as "PEM Sul". Files pemsul_raster_inputs.zip - raster inputs for baseline scenario pemsul_vector_inputs.zip - habitats, users and other vector features for the baseline scenario pemsul_raster_outputs.zip - baseline scenario of raster maps of benefit,  pemsul_vector_outputs.zip - geopackage with the synthesis layers for all scenarios   Versions v4.0.0 -- New data based on improved artisan fishing layer v3.0.0 -- Major bug fix in duplicated features Warning: version 2.x.x is deprecated v2.0.1 -- typo fixed in zip file v2.0.0 -- new performance index updated to Normalized Euclidean Distance. v1.1.0 -- standardization of vector outputs. v1.0.0 -- first version   Citation This asset content is result from a team of experts discussions and works during 2024 and 2025 in southern Brazil. This initiative, carried out by  Codex in partnership with the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul and the Federal University of Santa Catarina , and supported with resources from the BNDES Project Structuring Fund (BNDES FEP), aims to support the technical studies necessary for implementing the pilot project of Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) in the Southern Marine Region of Brazil, covering the states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul. If some data were used from this source, please cite as: Possantti, I., Gandra, T., Nyland, J., Nora Barbosa, M., Teixeira, G., Asmus, M., & Silva, T. (2026). PEM: data results from the Marine Spatial Planning in Southern Brazil Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21302041

summary: Manuscript and CSV data behind the figures and tables of Xu (2024), On the statistical theory of self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow: High order kinematic and dynamic relations , Physics of Fluids 36, 075146, doi:10.1063/5.0215026 , arXiv:2202.02991 . Contents: the revised manuscript (PDF) and the CSV files of every plotted series and table, in the format of the author's dark matter flow datasets. Pair statistics from the Virgo SCDM N-body simulation at redshifts z = 10 to 0. Companion datasets: Part I (halo-based) doi:10.5281/zenodo.6541231 , Part II (correlation-based) doi:10.5281/zenodo.6757654 . Major findings (Virgo SCDM N-body simulation, redshifts z = 10 to 0): Kinematic relations of any order are derived for incompressible, constant-divergence and irrotational flow, and validated by the simulation. On large scales, third-order velocity correlations can be related to the density correlation or the pairwise velocity. The p-th order velocity correlations follow a^((p+2)/2) for odd p and a^(p/2) for even p (a = scale factor). The fitted exponents for odd p are smaller than these predictions. The overdensity is proportional to the density correlation on the same scale, <delta> ∝ <delta delta'>; the velocity dispersion on a scale r is proportional to the overdensity on that scale. The effective viscosity of the adhesion model originates from velocity fluctuations; the negative viscosity is due to the inverse energy cascade. On small scales, a self-closed velocity evolution is obtained by splitting velocity into motion within haloes and motion of haloes. Vorticity, enstrophy and energy evolution follow from it. The mean pairwise velocity follows <Δu_L> = −H a r. The third moment follows <(Δu_L)^3> ∝ ε_u a r, with a constant energy-cascade rate ε_u ≈ −4.6×10⁻⁷ m²/s³. The combined kinematic and dynamic relations give exponential velocity correlations on large scales and one-fourth power-law correlations on small scales; the p-th order correlations follow a^((3p−5)/4) for odd p and a^(3p/4) for even p.
title: Dark matter flow data and manuscript: On the statistical theory of self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow: High order kinematic and dynamic relations

summary: This repository contains the code and numerical data supporting the manuscript “Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures” by Juan J. Segura. The study investigates how much relational information modular system interfaces must preserve in order to reconstruct an integrated dynamic-admissibility relation. The reproducibility package contains Python source code, benchmark configuration files, and CSV datasets and outputs used for the principal computational analyses. The package supports two complementary model layers: (1) a reduced continuous-control model used for exhaustive higher-order project-join analysis and robustness studies, and (2) a synthetic seven-state road-relative vehicle model used as a nonlinear dynamic falsification layer. The principal reproducible results include: complete pairwise reconstruction providing no improvement over unary reconstruction; persistence of this pairwise insufficiency across 27 combinations of numerical resolution, superelevation, and stopping horizon; and a sparse ternary architecture comprising the relations {R, mu, v}, {G, mu, v}, and {mu, v, tau} reproducing the complete third-order reconstruction in all 27 robustness cases. The vehicle parameters are synthetic and are not presented as OEM-calibrated haul-truck data. All admissibility projections are exact only with respect to the computed model relation. The reported discordance measures should not be interpreted as accident probabilities or empirical risk frequencies.
title: Code and Data for Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures

summary: The term "AI slop" is commonly treated as a property of the generator: text is slop because a model produced it. This paper argues that slop is a property of the process. It names generation that reached a reader without the review it needed, and reviewed generation is a draft, whoever generated it. On that account the slop critique is largely mitigable by review processes run with or by language models, but not on the grounds usually offered. The argument is not that models review better than they write, nor that they review better than humans. It is that one large class of faults, provenance, is invisible to a reading human at population scale and cheap for a machine to check: across four top-tier venues, papers carrying hallucinated citations received reviewer ratings indistinguishable from clean papers, accepted and rejected submissions whose ratings differed by two points carried the same share of them, and a venue-scale audit cost about four cents a paper (Russinovich, Siva Kumar and Salem 2026). Review is the better-suited task for a model for five structural reasons: a fixed target, a brief that says where to look, permission to answer "cannot verify", no stake in the document, and the generated text as a map of where to check. The remedy for slop is therefore a division of labour that assigns the provenance pass to the machine and the reasoning pass to the human. The paper names five mechanisms by which unreviewed generation acquires faults that are invisible from inside the text, carries four corrections as explicit limits, and reports one case in which two reviewers of different kind, a human on a phone and a model under a provenance brief, found disjoint error classes with no overlap, every provenance fault sitting on a source the generating model had not opened. The case is N = 1 and is offered as a specimen, not a result; the paper's own first draft supplies a second specimen, by the mechanism the paper describes. The division of labour is then placed under its binding constraint: when an AI agent is institutionally positioned as an employee, managers catch fewer errors themselves and pass the review on (Wiles, Hsu, Bedard and Kropp 2026), so the design must survive the effect it is meant to offset. Seven hypotheses are stated, each with the observation that would falsify it.
title: Slop Is a Process Property

summary: Validation dataset of the H5MD biophysics module, a metadata schema that stores the topology, force field, MD parameters, selection groups and observables of a molecular dynamics simulation together with its trajectory in one H5MD (HDF5) file. It accompanies the paper A Hierarchical Metadata Schema for Self-Contained Molecular Dynamics Trajectory Archives . validation_systems.zip contains the GROMACS inputs of the 58 chemical systems used in the paper's technical validation, reduced to what grompp needs: topology, force field, coordinates or run input, index groups and MD parameters. The systems range from 711 to 1,066,628 particles, cover AMBER, CHARMM, GROMOS, OPLS-AA and MARTINI force fields, and come in six groups by origin: self_generated (8): built with GROMACS from PDB entries bena (10): sessions of the Bena dataset ( 10.5281/zenodo.17632513 ) jcp_benchmark (6): GROMACS benchmark systems ( 10.5281/zenodo.3893789 ) hexabc (8): hexABC nucleic-acid and protein–nucleic-acid deposits from MDposit memprotmd (6): MemProtMD membrane proteins, atomistic and coarse-grained misato (20): MISATO protein–ligand complexes ( 10.5281/zenodo.7711953 ) Run under 23 simulation protocols, these inputs give the 379 reference files of the validation. The files can be regenerated with the validation scripts ( github.com/miemiemmmm/h5md-biophysics-validation ) and the GROMACS implementation published with the paper. Each group's MANIFEST.md credits its source and states the changes made; provenance/ holds the scripts that selected and prepared the systems. Four of the reference files are included as examples, each a short trajectory with the full metadata. They also serve as test data for the validator in gitlab.com/gromacs/h5md-biophysics : hexabc_a001u2_rna_protein__nvt-vrescale.h5md bench_villin__tcoupl-multigroup.h5md bench_villin__sd-langevin.h5md bench_villin__selection-noncontiguous.h5md
title: Validation systems and reference files for the H5MD biophysics metadata module

summary: A shibboleth economy is a cultural system in which the rewards of decoding, a fluency-gain reward, identity affirmation, collective affiliation, and positional rank, become self-sustaining, so that demand for distinction feeds back into cultural production and communicative opacity becomes value-bearing rather than merely costly. Cultural capital theory, from Bourdieu through the fan-studies lineage, explains why scarce decoding competence produces distinction; a shibboleth economy begins where that distinction becomes demand and the demand alters what gets made, through evolutionary selection on engagement rather than any calculating producer. The paper develops the loop and its consequences. A two-type model distinguishes lexical figuration, which maps represented features to meanings and is bootstrappable within a single work, from modal figuration, which maps the representational act itself to an ontological status and is stabilised only by shared representational infrastructure, of which canon is the most powerful form. In markets poor in effective codebook coverage, exemplified by industrial-era Hollywood, uncaught references are priced as lost customers and a self-teaching visual pidgin is selected, later mistaken for neutral realism; in codebook-rich markets the operating point moves to selective permeability, legible to the invested and closed to the casual, with the equilibrium set by the opposed pulls of affiliation and rank. Democratisation of a key causes migration and displacement rather than collapse; a hard cultural border is a boundary condition that slows depreciation and opens an export axis; and when demand for keys outruns authenticated supply, the predicted pathology is key inflation, defined as growth in the ratio of claimed authorised readings to verifiably authorised ones, driven by provenance laundering. Two model-implied expectations, codebook import markets and synthetic canon manufacture, are tested against known cases, with modal transfer breadth as the surviving strong claim, and three forward predictions are stated, led by key migration under democratisation.
title: The Shibboleth Economy

summary: Classical creative-process orderings put divergence early and convergence late, and the Double Diamond formalises the rule twice over. This paper argues the ordering was never a law of cognition but a map of costs: divergence goes early because reopening a converged process has historically been ruinous, and the entire discipline of the framework exists to protect against that reopening. When drafting cost collapses by orders of magnitude, as it does when an author works with a language model as typewriter, the protected assumption dissolves and the optimal ordering inverts: converge first, then diverge, because a late horizon either restarts a now-cheap process or spawns a child concept from a sharpened parent. The paper's second claim types reviewer instances in multi-model chains by regression target rather than capability, and states the Hein Condition: a mode-regressing reviewer's yield is proportional to the sharpness of the artefact it receives, because the modal response to an unsharp artefact is the generic response, so the same instance is most fluent exactly where it is least useful. A slot theory follows, carnivore, auditor, mode-regressor, children, each reviewer placed where its failure mode is cheapest, and child viability rises with parent sharpness at spawn. The claims are exercised on a fully documented case: a five-pass, three-model review chain run on a single paper in a single day, with every absorption, declination, and provenance failure logged. Four predictions close, including that review chains are provenance systems measurable by the sibling paper's key-inflation ratio.
title: The Hein Condition

summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.
title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game

summary: A key milestone toward Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) is replacing hand-crafted optimizers with meta-learned update rules (such as Disco103 and OPEN) that discover how agents learn. Yet when a self-discovered RL model trains with adapting teammates, does co-evolution sustain capability gains or trap agents in brittle conventions? Across 1,800+ runs in continuous collective robotics (VMAS) and discrete coordination (Overcooked), we establish five laws of multi-agent adaptation. First, four-cell counterfactual partner swaps expose an evaluation illusion: apparent team progress often masks focal regression (+1.066 team gain concealing -0.119 focal loss) and inflates transfer by +0.649 to +1.210. Second, a 288-run physical-coupling sweep ($α\in [0, 1.5]$) reveals a linear scaling law ($β= +0.255$, $p = 0.000488$, Spearman $ρ= 1.0$): live reciprocal feedback keeps Disco103 invariant (AUC 0.297--0.322), whereas severing feedback triggers a monotonic collapse (-0.172 to -0.490), with OPEN establishing a sensitivity spectrum (Disco103 > OPEN > MAPPO). Third, extending navigation training eightfold (1.05M steps) enables Disco103 to overtake MAPPO (+0.087 team return, +0.133 bank gain), while decoupled training boosts cross-partner completion by +10.16% (56.25% vs. 46.09%). Fourth, in Overcooked, MAPPO's self-play conventions induce a 28.13% cross-partner collision rate, whereas Disco103 cuts collisions to 12.77% and achieves 3.33x higher bank return (9.96 vs. 2.99; net gain +6.43), further improved by decoupled meta-adaptation (+1.39 with scripted partners). Finally, perturbation pulses ($p=0.00098$), auxiliary entropy diagnostics (8.485 nats), and 48 multi-lifetime meta-evolved rules ($L_2 \in [2.11, 4.91]$) trace these dynamics to partner-gradient blindness and auxiliary drift, informing multi-agent self-discoverd algorithms.
title: From Single-Agent Self-Discovery to Multi-Agent Adaptation: Scaling Laws of Partner Feedback and Convention Rigidity in Meta Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

summary: Abstract: Keeping the modern power grid running during heatwaves, wildfires, or cyberattacks requires knowing which power lines are the most dangerous "dominoes" if two or three of them fail at the same time. However, checking every possible combination of multiple broken lines across the Western U.S. grid is a math problem with millions of possibilities—far too slow for computers to solve in real time using standard physics equations. Conversely, taking shortcuts by simply looking at a map of the grid (to find the biggest, most connected hubs) fails because electricity does not travel like cars on a highway; it cannot be told which road to take. Instead, electricity automatically splits across all available wires based on their physical resistance. When a major line gets crowded or breaks, electricity surges onto smaller side-lines, causing chain-reaction blackouts far away from the original problem. In this memo, we introduce Physics-Informed Network Reshaping (PINR), an AI framework that bridges the gap between map-based speed and physical accuracy. PINR combines a specialized, mathematically predictable neural network with a network-disruption algorithm originally designed for counter-terrorism. Rather than testing millions of broken-wire combinations one by one, PINR uses a single, rapid pass to act as a dual-use stress gauge: For Grid Defenders ("Blue Team" Healing): It shows grid operators the exact 27 congested power lines where slightly "throttling" the flow (like adjusting valves on a water pipe) relieves 99.1% of grid overloads during a peak evening crunch, pushing excess electricity safely onto underused backup lines. For Security Analysts ("Red Team" Vulnerability Hunting): Because the lines that need the most throttling to heal the grid are the exact same lines carrying the most dangerous physical stress, PINR automatically narrows the search for catastrophic multi-line failures from 235 lines down to just 27. This cuts the number of three-line failure combinations to check by 99.86% (from over 2.1 million down to under 3,000). Most importantly, testing PINR on the 2026 Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) proves that looking at a static map of the grid is dangerously misleading. While standard map-based analysis points to California's central grid hub (CAISO) as the most critical choke point, PINR's physics engine reveals that California's many parallel lines easily absorb the load. Instead, the true physical bottlenecks hide in the power-exporting corridors of the Desert Southwest (Arizona and the Lower Colorado River) and the mountain seams connecting Montana, the Pacific Northwest, and Utah. Correspondence and collaboration inquiries: aes@acm.org
title: Physics-Informed Network Reshaping (PINR) for Western Grid Resilience

summary: Abstract: Keeping the modern power grid running during heatwaves, wildfires, or cyberattacks requires knowing which power lines are the most dangerous "dominoes" if two or three of them fail at the same time. Conversely, taking shortcuts by simply looking at a map of the grid (to find the biggest, most connected hubs) fails because electricity does not travel like cars on a highway; it cannot be told which road to take. Instead, electricity automatically splits across all available wires based on their physical resistance. When a major line gets crowded or breaks, electricity surges onto smaller side-lines, causing chain-reaction blackouts far away from the original problem. Instead, the true physical bottlenecks hide in the power-exporting corridors of the Desert Southwest (Arizona and the Lower Colorado River) and the mountain seams connecting Montana, the Pacific Northwest, and Utah. summary: Recovering a 3D full-body human bone rig, which is used to animate a Computer-Generated Image (CGI) model is a challenging problem with many applications although successfully addressed by the motion capture systems with actors with markers worn all over the body with special suit and multiple cameras . In this paper, we detail the bottom-up approach derived from Open Pose, winner of Common Objects in Context (COCO) 2016 KEYPOINTS Challenge, because of its decent qual ity and robustness of detection of multiple numbers of people in the frame with focus . Proposed network design and optimized post-processing with the full solution of video to 2D conversion run at acceptable speeds . The second part of 2D pose to 3D pose conversion u ses a novel Occlusion-Robust Pose-Maps (ORPM) which enables full body pose inference even under strong partial occlusions by other people and objects in the scene . O RPM outputs a fixed number of maps which encodes the 3D joint locations of all people in the scene . Body part associations allow us to infer 3D pose of arbitrary numbers of people without explicit bounding box prediction which increases performance of pose inference . The final combination of the two networks is where a single camera can detect human motion and display the 3D rep resentation in a three-dimensional space in real-time.  Provenance Note: Previously published in the Proceedings of the 3rd National Conference on Science, Engineering and Technology (SET Conference 2021) . Re-archived for public record due to the permanent closure of the original archive.

summary: Measured failure modes of verifier panels: companion paper accepted (poster) at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? — Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels . Version of record: SSRN 7390698 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7390698 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://polyhelper.ai/research/agreement-not-evidence/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/agreement-not-evidence . Someone who asks one language model a question cannot tell a confidently wrong answer from a confidently right one. The two are identical on every surface cue available to a non-expert. Asking several models seems to solve this, but it mostly relocates the problem: reconciling several answers produces one confident text again, and that text now carries the borrowed authority of "ten of them agreed." The protocol formalized here collects answers from several consumer chat models through the user's own browser or phone, with no API keys, no installation and no intermediary server. It reconciles them by anchor-and-enrich: the strongest available answer becomes the base, and each of the others contributes only what the base lacks. Every contribution is signed with the model that supplied it. Disagreements are kept in a section of their own rather than averaged away. The paper makes four contributions. The first is the protocol itself, stated as an algorithm that preserves provenance and forbids silent deletion, together with a taxonomy of five ways a merge can fail. Four of them are defects of naive pooling; the fifth is a failure of the operator rather than of the method: a synthesis that presents a single model's output as a collegial result. The second is the application of the correlated-witness arithmetic to protocol design. That arithmetic is not claimed here. Kohli (2026) applied the same Kish correction to a panel of nine frontier judges and measured about two effective votes, and Kim et al. (2025) established the underlying error correlation across more than 350 models. A council of N models whose errors carry intraclass correlation ρ is worth = N / (1 + (N−1)ρ) independent witnesses, and that quantity saturates at 1/ρ however many models are added. Once a council is larger than 1/ρ, halving ρ beats doubling N, and a pair with low error correlation can outweigh five with high correlation. Which pairs those are is measured, not read off the label: the larger and more accurate models carry the most correlated errors even when architecture and provider differ (Kim et al., 2025), and the author's per-pair measurements found no detectable effect of geopolitical bloc on error correlation and, in the pairs measured, none of shared lineage (Chernets, 2026). The estimation procedure of Section 5.5 supplies that measurement. The third is an account of three deployment tiers, manual, one-tap mobile and browser-agent, and of the axis that separates them epistemically: whether the second model sees the first model's answer. Conditioning the second model raises ρ in exchange for error correction. The fourth is a small-sample observation of the counterfeit-council failure across five models, the one-sentence intervention that removed it in a three-model re-run, and a blinded three-arm evaluation design with a stated falsification condition. Correlated agreement is treated here as established, not as a finding. That a panel of models is worth far fewer independent witnesses than it has members has been measured directly: nine frontier judges drawn from seven families supply about two effective votes (Kohli, 2026), and error correlation rises with model capability even across providers and architectures (Kim et al., 2025). Section 5 restates the design-effect arithmetic behind those measurements, because three of the protocol's rules are derived from it and read as fastidiousness without it. summary: A provenance-bound values model published as a public evaluator rather than deployed as a filter — why open weights defeat a filter and strengthen a referee, why the same weights bear three different relations to the model they judge, and why an evaluator that gatekeeps its own judgments has reproduced the defect it exists to correct. A values model — a model that judges conduct against a standard — is an established artifact. Guard models, safety classifiers, critic models, preference models and process reward models all instantiate the family, and the engineering is not in dispute. What is in dispute, and what this paper specifies, is the posture in which such an artifact is published , which we argue is not a deployment detail but the property that determines whether the artifact does anything at all. We state an inversion as a design principle. A values model deployed as a filter — sitting in a serving path, permitting or refusing — is defeated by publication of its weights, because the published artifact is precisely the oracle against which an attacker optimizes; a staged black-box attack (STACK) reaches roughly 71% success against a defended classifier pipeline that had held earlier attacks near zero, and an attacker holding the weights has strictly more than that attack needed. The same model published as an evaluator — emitting verdicts about systems it does not control — is not defeated by publication, and its positive findings are strengthened by it, because open weights are what allow a third party to reproduce and therefore to trust its verdicts. The same openness hands the judged party an optimization target, and §4.1 states what that concedes: a clean or empty result from an open referee proves less against an adaptive party than the first draft of this paper allowed. Openness is not a property with a fixed sign. Its sign is set by posture, and in the referee posture it is mixed. From this we derive a second result. The independent-evaluation literature documents at length the ways in which the evaluated party's control over access corrupts evaluation: short access windows, low rate limits, evaluator dependence on the goodwill and funding of the party being evaluated. We observe that the defect is symmetric and that, in the work surveyed in §2, its mirror image has not been named. An evaluator that controls access to its own judgments holds the same kind of power, pointed the other way — it can decline to evaluate, deprioritize, or be unavailable for a party it wishes to spare or to punish. We therefore specify a non-gatekeeping constraint : the ability to obtain a judgment must not depend on the evaluator's permission, which requires that the model, the harness, and the evaluation corpus be freely runnable, and which makes any hosted endpoint a convenience rather than a channel. We specify provenance-binding as the constitutive constraint on the model's outputs: every judgment must resolve to a citation into a fixed canonical corpus, and a judgment that cannot be so resolved is withheld rather than emitted. This trades coverage for auditability deliberately, and it distinguishes the artifact from values models trained on preference data whose sources cannot be named, and from purpose-authored value-rule corpora, whose rules are written for the alignment task itself and therefore cannot serve as an independent ground truth. Finally we specify that a single such artifact bears three non-interchangeable relations to the systems it judges, selected by carrier: a gate in the publisher's own hardware, a citation requirement without veto in an autonomous successor agent, and a referee in the wider world. We state plainly that the middle case must not be implemented as the first, because a veto held by a smaller model over a more capable agent bounds that agent at the evaluator's ceiling — the weak-supervisor problem applied to the very system the arrangement exists to enable. The same openness hands the judged party an optimization target, and §4.1 states what that concedes: a clean or empty result from an open referee proves less against an adaptive party than the first draft of this paper allowed. Openness is not a property with a fixed sign. Its sign is set by posture, and in the referee posture it is mixed. From this we derive a second result. The independent-evaluation literature documents at length the ways in which the evaluated party's control over access corrupts evaluation: short access windows, low rate limits, evaluator dependence on the goodwill and funding of the party being evaluated. We observe that the defect is symmetric and that, in the work surveyed in §2, its mirror image has not been named. An evaluator that controls access to its own judgments holds the same kind of power, pointed the other way — it can decline to evaluate, deprioritize, or be unavailable for a party it wishes to spare or to punish. We therefore specify a non-gatekeeping constraint : the ability to obtain a judgment must not depend on the evaluator's permission, which requires that the model, the harness, and the evaluation corpus be freely runnable, and which makes any hosted endpoint a convenience rather than a channel. We specify provenance-binding as the constitutive constraint on the model's outputs: every judgment must resolve to a citation into a fixed canonical corpus, and a judgment that cannot be so resolved is withheld rather than emitted. This trades coverage for auditability deliberately, and it distinguishes the artifact from values models trained on preference data whose sources cannot be named, and from purpose-authored value-rule corpora, whose rules are written for the alignment task itself and therefore cannot serve as an independent ground truth. We state plainly that the middle case must not be implemented as the first, because a veto held by a smaller model over a more capable agent bounds that agent at the evaluator's ceiling — the weak-supervisor problem applied to the very system the arrangement exists to enable. summary: PHASE v7.1.7 Remove the temporary temporal-example button from the custom panel. Add Restore automatic residual trend for custom DET/STC, enabled by default. PHASE v7.1.6 Simplify the custom panel by removing residual-mean and full assigned-covariance editors; preserve existing profile settings with a contextual indication when active. Existing model configurations remain unchanged until the example is selected. Align application and all installer versions to 7.1.6. Subtract the selected additional mean before residual modelling and restore it at PS, grid and query locations with shared-data uncertainty propagation. summary: SMaRT Transfusion  (Simplified, Meaningful and Responsible Tool for Transfusions) is a clinical decision support (CDS) tool developed at  Stanford Medicine Children's Health (SMCH)  for red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in critically ill children. It implements the consensus recommendations of the  Pediatric Critical Care Transfusion and Anemia eXpertise Initiative (TAXI) as an interactive decision tree: clinicians navigate from the patient's clinical state (hemorrhagic shock, nonhemorrhagic shock, acute respiratory failure, acute brain injury, hematologic/oncologic diagnoses, congenital or acquired heart disease, extracorporeal support, and general critical illness) through the relevant hemoglobin and physiologic thresholds to an evidence- or expert-based transfusion recommendation. It is designed for use within Epic and other EHR environments and accepts a hemoglobin value on launch to pre-seed the pathway.
title: SMaRT Transfusion: A Clinical Decision Support Tool for Red Blood Cell Transfusion in Critically Ill Children

It implements the consensus recommendations of the  Pediatric Critical Care Transfusion and Anemia eXpertise Initiative (TAXI) as an interactive decision tree: clinicians navigate from the patient's clinical state (hemorrhagic shock, nonhemorrhagic shock, acute respiratory failure, acute brain injury, hematologic/oncologic diagnoses, congenital or acquired heart disease, extracorporeal support, and general critical illness) through the relevant hemoglobin and physiologic thresholds to an evidence- or expert-based transfusion recommendation. It is designed for use within Epic and other EHR environments and accepts a hemoglobin value on launch to pre-seed the pathway.

summary: GEM Engine: Publication Dataset This dataset supports the research manuscript "GEM Engine: A reusable landscape-guided framework for exploration and optimization of genome-scale metabolic design spaces" by Hamed Rastaghi and Samuel M. D. Oliveira. GEM Engine is a computational framework designed to support reusable, landscape-guided exploration and optimization of genome-scale metabolic models. The framework combines flux balance analysis (FBA), surrogate modeling, and multi-objective optimization to enable systematic investigation of metabolic design spaces while reducing redundant simulations across optimization tasks. Dataset Contents Results.zip Contains genome-scale metabolic simulation landscapes, multi-objective optimization benchmarks, and associated computational results supporting the study. Figures_and_Tables.zip Contains data and materials associated with the main and supplementary figures and tables, including supporting analysis outputs and generation scripts where available. Reproducibility and Software The archived results support comparisons of landscape-guided optimization strategies, including gsMOBO, NSGA-II, SPARC, GHOST, and TRAIL, as well as surrogate-quality-based algorithm selection. The GEM Engine source code is maintained separately on GitHub. The repository URL will be provided when the software is publicly released.
title: GEM Engine: Simulation Landscapes and Optimization Benchmark Data for Genome-Scale Metabolic Design

summary: Replication package for the empirical study "Who Migrates the Schema? An Empirical Study of Database Changes in AI Coding Agent Pull Requests" (submitted to Empirical Software Engineering). The study analyses what AI coding agents (OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code, Google Jules) do in the database layer (migrations, DDL, ORM schemas, raw SQL) of GitHub pull requests, and compares them with human pull requests from the same 889 database-bearing repositories and the same period (2024-12-24 to 2025-10-24). The package contains (i) code.zip: the frozen detector specification, mining code, human-baseline collector, independent re-implementation, statistical analysis (Python and R), revision analyses, all output tables and the human-validation labels; (ii) data.zip: sanitised per-PR and per-file derived tables sufficient to re-run the statistical analysis. GitHub person logins are pseudonymised (HMAC-SHA256 with a secret salt); bot and agent accounts are kept because they define the treatment. Patch text, PR titles/bodies and comments are not redistributed; scripts to re-collect them are included. Agent-side tables derive from the AIDev dataset (hao-li/AIDev, MSR '26; CC BY 4.0).
title: Replication package for "Who Migrates the Schema? An Empirical Study of Database Changes in AI Coding Agent Pull Requests"
