summary: A staged, reproducible pipeline for VLT/MUSE narrow-field-mode integral-field data: raw-cube reduction, spectral extraction of a faint companion next to a much brighter primary star with six independent extraction schemes, and hydrogen-line accretion analysis with detection limits calibrated against empirical nulls from control positions processed identically to the object. Every stage emits a machine-readable quality-control document, and later stages read those documents rather than trusting assumptions; provenance (input cube, SHA-256 hashes, specification version, wavelength frame, flux unit) travels with the products. Research code under active development. This is the version used in Ramírez Reyes & Cáceres (in preparation).
title: MUSE accretion pipeline

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Two results on complementary (mutually unbiased) measurements and the complementary quantum correlation (CQC) inequality of Schneeloch, Broadbent and Howell (2014), which proposed that the classical correlations in two complementary measurement tables never exceed the quantum mutual information. 1. Sharp qutrit discrimination. For every pair of complementary bases of a qutrit and every two orthogonal states, the triangular discrimination summed over the two bases is at most 8/3 (the trivial ceiling is 4), answering Qian, arXiv:2608.14806v2, Section 11(4). Every equality case is classified; for the computational and Fourier bases they are tied to the nine Hesse SIC rays. Consequences: choosing one of the two measurements at random recovers at most two thirds of the quantum Fisher information in a two-state estimation task, and Qian's two-ray qubit-qutrit family obeys CQC with margin at least 0.1005 nats. The proof is computer-assisted: an exact rational sum-of-squares certificate (scout_qutrit/exact_sos_certificate.json, 660,609 bytes, SHA-256 825bb8108096d38a44f63f1bc91964405d189ad57b5f568530b5d8e27d598c2f) checked by a standalone exact verifier; this deposit is the certificate's citable locator. 2. Every prescribed pair fails for a qubit and a qudit of dimension n ≥ 4. For every prescribed pair of complementary measurements on each side there is a separable state violating CQC, with a uniform certified margin below −9/20,000,000 nats (previously the every-pair statement was known only for n ≥ 164). A phase-averaging extension of the known shared-label mechanism covers every prescribed pair when both dimensions are at least three; an earlier, unchecked every-pair statement for equal dimensions by E. O'Connor is credited. Open: the full qubit-qutrit CQC question and the sharp constant in dimension 5 (numerics only). The margins are tiny and structural, not experimental. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), the exact certificate and verifier, negative controls, an exact rational margin checker, numerical cross-checks, working proof notes, novelty audits, the bibliography with registry records, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: computer-assisted exact rational arithmetic, not a formal proof; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review or independent reproduction). Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Sharp qutrit discrimination and unavoidable correlation overcounting for complementary measurements

summary: BarrierMap is a computational framework for comparing molecular permeability across the blood–brain barrier (BBB), skin, and intestinal Caco-2 systems. This record contains processed results, model summaries, cross-barrier analyses, and reproducibility materials supporting the associated manuscript. A common physicochemical descriptor baseline was combined with barrier-specific information, including ionization-derived descriptors for BBB and Caco-2 and anatomical/experimental context for skin. Predictive performance was evaluated using 20 repeated Bemis–Murcko scaffold-based train/test splits. Cross-barrier analyses were performed after molecular standardization using within-barrier percentile ranks to enable comparison among experimentally distinct permeability endpoints.
title: BarrierMap: Barrier-Specific Determinants of Molecular Permeability across Biological Interfaces

summary: This resource contains Python and Wolfram Mathematica variants of the simulation code accompanying the article Effect of Electoral Seat Bias on Political Polarization: A Computational Perspective by Daria Boratyn and Dariusz Stolicki ( International Journal of Public Opinion Research ). The code implements an agent-based Monte Carlo model designed to investigate how electoral seat bias in favor of larger parties affects the evolution of mass ideological polarization over repeated electoral cycles. The model represents voters and parties as ideal points in a two-dimensional policy space. Voter choice combines ideological proximity with preferences for larger parties, capturing strategic and bandwagon motives, and retrospective evaluations of government performance. Voter positions evolve through random preference perturbations, affective shifts associated with party attachment, and thermostatic responses to the incumbent. Electoral systems are represented by aggregate seats–votes functions: the pot-and-ladle approximation for Jefferson--D’Hondt and a power-law approximation for first-past-the-post plurality. The degree of seat bias is varied through mean district magnitude and the power-law exponent, respectively. Mass ideological polarization is measured using a modified Mehlhaff index with a degrees-of-freedom correction, with voter clusters identified through adaptive mean-shift clustering. The code is provided to facilitate inspection of the model’s assumptions and mechanisms, replication of the simulation experiments, and further computational research on the relationship between electoral institutions and political polarization.
title: Simulation Code for "Effect of Electoral Seat Bias on Political Polarization: A Computational Perspective"

summary: Operator Compounds: A Compositional Theory of Human Cognition and Behavior proposes a structural framework for understanding how elementary cognitive capacities combine to produce higher-order human capabilities. The theory introduces operators as functional cognitive capacities, operator compounds as stable organizations of interacting operators, and compound networks as higher-order organizations responsible for complex capacities such as deliberation, responsibility, self-regulation, resilience, and identity. The framework argues that development is fundamentally a process of organizational construction rather than information accumulation. Human capabilities emerge through the progressive formation, stabilization, and integration of operators, compounds, and networks. The paper develops a model of compound formation, degradation, collapse, and reconstruction, applies the framework to childhood development, proposes the Network Absorption Hypothesis, and outlines a research program with testable developmental predictions.
tags: operator theory; operator compounds; cognitive architecture; developmental psychology; child development; cognitive development; organizational complexity; self-organization; developmental systems; dynamic systems theory;
title: Operator Compounds: A Compositional Theory of Human Cognition and Behavior

summary: Revised manuscript with errata, and the CSV data behind the figures and tables of Xu (2024), On the statistical theory of self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow: Scale and redshift variation of velocity and density distributions , Physics of Fluids 36, 117158, doi: 10.1063/5.0236964 , arXiv: 2202.06515 . Contents: the manuscript (P13_revised.pdf); statistics/ (53 CSV files, halo-based and correlation-based statistics); figures/ (32 CSV files, one per figure); tables.zip (19 CSV files); particles_velocity_pdfs.zip (13 particle and 15 velocity PDF CSV files). Companion datasets: Dataset Part I (halo-based), 10.5281/zenodo.6541231 ; Dataset Part II (correlation-based), 10.5281/zenodo.6757654 ; the 2022 preprint 10.5281/zenodo.6640676 ; and the slides 10.5281/zenodo.6569901 . Major findings (Virgo SCDM N-body simulation, ten redshifts): Delaunay tessellation reconstructs the comoving density field; the density correlation, spectrum and dispersion functions are obtained, modelled and compared with the N-body simulation. Velocity distributions are symmetric on small and large scales and non-symmetric with a negative skewness on intermediate scales, due to the inverse energy cascade at a constant rate ε u on small scales. On small scales, the even-order moments of the pairwise velocity Δu L follow a two-thirds law, ∝ (−ε u r) 2/3 , while the odd-order moments scale linearly, ⟨(Δu L ) 2n+1 ⟩ = (2n+1)⟨(Δu L ) 2n ⟩⟨Δu L ⟩ ∝ r. Fully developed velocity fields are never Gaussian on any scale, even when they start from a Gaussian initial condition. On small scales, u L and Σu L are modelled by an X distribution that maximises entropy; the distribution of Δu L can differ. On large scales, Δu L and Σu L are modelled by a logistic or an X distribution, while u L has a different distribution. The redshift variation of the velocity distributions follows the evolution of the X distribution, whose shape parameter α(z) decreases with time.
title: Dark matter flow data and manuscript: scale and redshift variation of velocity and density distributions

summary: VERSION 2 1. 𝓧 𝒇 sampling V2.0 covers a wider range of faradaic contributions, with faradaic up to 35%, distributed as follows: 𝓧 𝒇 = 0% (25% of CV curves) • 𝓧 𝒇 = 0–10% (50% of CV curves) • 𝓧 𝒇 = 10–35% (25% of CV curves) V1 was limited to 𝒳 𝑓 values between 0 and 10%, with very few purely capacitive CV curves (Xf = 0%). Predictions are valid for 𝒳 𝑓 ranging from 0% to 25%. Beyond 25%, the tool displays “Out of valid range”. 2. ESR and leakage messages When ESR or leakage contributions are negligible, the tool displays a message instead of a value: - “ESR contribution negligible” if 𝑹 𝒆𝒔𝒓 · 𝑰 𝒄 < 0.02 · ΔE (2% threshold vs. 1% in V1) - “Leakage contribution negligible” if 𝑰 𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒌 < 0.01 · 𝑰 𝒄 (1% of the capacitive current). 3. Capacitive–faradaic coupling V1. Only the capacitive current flowed through the ESR. The faradaic and leakage currents were computed at the applied potential E, so they caused no ohmic drop. V2. All currents flow through a common ESR, in series with three parallel branches: C, R leak , and the faradaic branch. The total current produces an ohmic drop, resulting in an interfacial potential E int given by: E int = E − R ESR (I c + I leak + p · I f ) The three currents are computed at E int : I c = C · dE int /dt I leak = E int / R leak The faradaic current I f uses the same Butler–Volmer and diffusion model as in V1, evaluated at E int , with p scaling its contribution. Since E int depends on the currents and the currents depend on E int , these equations are solved self-consistently at each time step. The measured current is their sum: I = I c + I leak + p · I f . In V1, the faradaic charge scaled linearly with p, allowing p to be calculated directly from the target 𝒳 𝑓 . In V2, p also changes the ohmic drop, and therefore the shape of the faradaic peak. The faradaic charge is no longer proportional to p, so p is adjusted iteratively until the target 𝒳 𝑓 is reached. 4. 95% confidence intervals V1. Each parameter was shown with a fixed ±, equal to the median error on the test set. It was the same for every curve and contained the true value for only half of the curves. V2. Each value comes with a 95 % confidence interval computed for the analysed curve: value (low – high). A second neural network estimates the expected error for each curve and each parameter. A calibration step on 25,000 curves set aside from training (split conformal prediction) then sets the interval width so that it contains the true value for 95 % of the curves. On 50,000 test curves, coverage is 95.0 % (C), 95.1 % (R leak ), 94.9 % (ESR) and 95.2 % (𝒳 f ).
title: Physics-driven deep learning for inverse extraction of faradaic and capacitive parameters in supercapacitors: code, trained model and synthetic database

summary: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection

summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

summary: Standard spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks need a fixed-size adjacency matrix, coupling model weights to a specific sensor count N; they cannot produce any output at a sensor absent from training. We present OmniST, a topology-invariant forecaster whose computation has zero structural dependency on the number of nodes, and which, composed with inductive split-conformal calibration, gives distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at arbitrary (including never-seen) sensor locations, preserving that guarantee as sensors are added or removed. Topology invariance follows from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing via a bidirectional GRU. On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019-2023), OmniST attains a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and degrades at most 1.1 percent when 40 percent of stations are removed. Its inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation (about 12 percent) and a learned kriging GNN (IGNNK, about 21 percent), and, unlike either, carry a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The guarantee holds at 90 percent or above under 30-50 percent node dropout across four real datasets over three domains (Delhi and Beijing air quality, NOAA GHCN weather, Caltrans PeMSD7-M traffic), and still holds at 325 real sensors (full PeMS-BAY). We also fix a temporal-drift failure: static conformal under-covers over time (about 0.50 late), but a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator restores target coverage (0.89 overall, 0.96 late) at the cost of wider intervals.
title: OmniST: Topology-Invariant Spatiotemporal Forecasting with Guaranteed-Coverage Uncertainty at Unseen Sensor Locations

summary: This paper investigates whether low-order packet-loss statistics suffice to assess survival-time risk under bursty packet losses, i.e., the probability that no update succeeds for a prescribed number of consecutive slots. Conventional models, such as the Gilbert model, characterize packet losses using the loss rate and mean burst length, but channels sharing these statistics may exhibit substantially different failure risks. We characterize the Markov channels one order above a given low-order fit that share its statistics and analyze their risks under acknowledgment-based scheduling with transmission budgets. We show that, with dense transmission attempts, risk is primarily governed by loss persistence beyond the modeled memory, and the worst-case channel need not be the most persistent one. Under limited budgets, retry spacing makes loss relapse probabilities important and can reverse the risk ordering of compatible channels. Numerical and measurement results show that low-order models can substantially underestimate the risk, highlighting the need for scheduling-dependent channel statistics.
title: Survival-Time Risk Beyond Low-Order Channel Models: Identifiability and Scheduling

summary: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
title: Dr. No: Feature Steering for Abstention in Vision-Language Models

summary: This record contains the rights-safe reproducibility package supporting the manuscript “Observed agreement is not decision portability: A typed evidence-authority audit of national renewable-energy priorities.” The study distinguishes retrospective cross-country recurrence from source-to-target decision authority. Stage I freezes a retrospective calibration corpus of 14 reports and 15 study units. Stage II contains three sequential outcome-blinded validation blocks with 25 exact technology relations. Context-blind transfer issued 11 certificates: four correct and seven incorrect (coverage 0.440; conditional agreement 0.364; false-portability rate 0.636). The criterion-resolved bounded rule issued no positive certificate across 13 applicable opportunities; this is reported as zero coverage and disciplined abstention, not predictive superiority. The package includes derived evidence registries, full-domain RASS representation records, frozen criterion-dependency and authority configurations, prediction and result locks, source-native replay records, relation-level validation outputs, Scopus title/abstract and purpose-driven acquisition audit records, protocols, analysis scripts, tests and file-level SHA-256 manifests. The Scopus component contains a frozen 1,363-record title/abstract universe. Of 251 full-text candidates, 110 received full-text-stage decisions across 13 dated batches; 49 were map eligible, 61 were excluded and 141 remained unassessed because exhaustive full-text census completion was not an objective. Acquisition ordering and stopping were documented but not preregistered. Later map-eligible records were not retroactively added to the already frozen Stage I calibration corpus. Copyrighted article PDFs, extracted article text, licensed Scopus exports, browser sessions, credentials and institutional-access artifacts are excluded. Original code and tests are licensed under MIT. Original derived data and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0, subject to the World Bank, IRENA/IRENASTAT and other third-party exceptions recorded in the package. The package is related to, but does not replace or revise, the prior Stage I reproducibility record at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23145110.
title: Reproducibility data and code for Observed agreement is not decision portability: a typed evidence-authority audit of national renewable-energy priorities

summary: Social support is an essential protective factor against the risk of talent development failure, especially in the catastrophic situation. This study aimed to test the validity and reliability of social support instruments specifically for talented sports students in Malaysia. Content validity index (CVI), exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and internal consistency are the methods used to ensure that measurement instruments are appropriate for use in local contexts and cultures. A total of 268 from four talented sports students aged 16 years were selected by proportionate stratified random sampling in this study. The study found that the instrument had good content validity, with the items reaching the minimum level of CVI value and exceeding the recommended cut-off point of 0.78. Factor analysis found that the final measurement model has three factors, namely i) family support, ii) friends' support, and iii) coach support, with factor loading ranging between 0.49 and 0.89. The correlation matrix was also measured through the KMO and Bartlett test of sphericity. All three factors had internal consistency values of 0.83 for coach support and 0.85 for family and friend support, which was defined as good. Future research is warranted to explore the instrument with different samples and measurements in various scenarios.
title: Valid and reliable instrument for measuring Malaysian talented students' social support

summary: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis

summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.
title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting

summary: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.
title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation

summary: Can an LLM directly edit the weights of a diffusion-based image-restoration model to \emph{improve} restoration quality---without gradients, paired data, or fine-tuning? Recent experiments show frontier LLMs can fix structural bugs by modifying as little as \(0.016\%\) of parameters, but cannot instill new capabilities. We ask whether weight-space programming (WSP) can move from \emph{debugging} to \emph{improvement} in the precise-regression setting of image restoration (deblurring, super-resolution, denoising, inpainting). Restoration diffusion UNets present a middle ground: low-level signal-processing layers are concentrated enough for targeted weight-direction edits, while high-level semantic layers remain distributed and resistant to sparse modification. We propose three technical conjectures: (C1) an LLM can localize the layer behind a quality gap (over-smoothing, color shift, hallucinated texture) within a 200 forward-pass budget; (C2) editing a small set of identified weight directions (e.g., scaling high-frequency filter norms, correcting output-bias channels) can measurably improve PSNR and perceptual quality; (C3) a recursive loop---diagnose \(\rightarrow\) edit \(\rightarrow\) evaluate \(\rightarrow\) re-diagnose---can compound gains across rounds, forming a minimal recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop for vision. We analyze the required AI capability (arguing targeted edits need not superintelligence, while general capability generation does) and detail the challenges of precise pixel-level regression. We provide a PyTorch-style deployment pipeline and outline a benchmark. This manuscript is conjectural, intended to open a new subtopic for image restoration.
title: Weight-Space Programming for Improving Image-Restoration Diffusion Models: Technical Conjectures and a Recursive Improvement Loop

summary: Inoculation prompting is a method to reduce undesired behaviours such as reward hacking in frontier models. It works by training a model on harmful examples under a prompt that specifies the undesired behaviour, which reduces the model's tendency to exhibit it unless prompted. However, the inoculation prompt is written in plain English, so any user can re-elicit the behaviour easily. We introduce neologism inoculation prompting (NIP), which replaces the English prompt with a new token that is trained on the frozen model and removed at deployment. NIP outperforms other inoculation methods, and performs competitively with gradient routing despite being simpler. It also works on reward hacking, but fails on sycophancy and harassment. Using control tokens and analyses of activations, we identify the mechanism for this as NIP hiding the harmful behaviour behind an unreachable region of model inputs, rather than deleting it. More broadly, our work suggests that neologisms can be a powerful way to carve out and shape access to behaviours that are undesired or harmful.
title: Neologism Inoculation Prompting

summary: Understanding what kind of prompts users typically ask and how well an LLM performs on these prompt categories is crucial for LLM practitioners. The existing methods satisfy the demand by hierarchically clustering the user prompts and synthesizing the cluster names using an LLM to build a taxonomy. However, the cluster names from these methods are usually too general for humans to understand the detailed prompt distributions and identify the exact strengths and weaknesses of LLMs. In this study, we propose COMPREHEND, which automatically constructs an ultra-fine-grained entailment hierarchy for the prompts. The entailment hierarchy replaces the cluster names in the taxonomy with sentences to provide more precise cluster descriptions for more fine-grained categorization. Compared with EvalTree, a state-of-the-art taxonomy construction method, COMPREHEND improves an entailment/faithfulness metric from 22.6 to 41.7 and an informative metric from 16.3 to 39.1 in WildBench. Our experiments also show that the weakness report generated based on our entailment hierarchy is much more informative than EvalTree in terms of predicting the response scores in the benchmark. All the code is released in https://github.com/JackNapier20/COMPREHEND_public.
title: COMPREHEND: Ultra-Fine-Grained Benchmark Understanding by Entailment Hierarchy

summary: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.
title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds

summary: Graph databases are often used to manage relationship-rich data, whose graph structure and attributes may be sensitive. In many applications, a database owner or a service provider evaluates queries over a private graph for a client. Because the graph cannot be fully disclosed and independently re-executing the query may be impractical, the client cannot directly verify the returned result. This creates a need for verifiable graph query evaluation that preserves data confidentiality. We present VerfGraph, a zero-knowledge system for verifiable graph query evaluation, which enables a client to verify that the query result was correctly computed over a committed graph data, without revealing private graph records or intermediate query values beyond the public inputs and what is implied by the query result. Building on the expansion-centric model introduced by the state-of-the-art zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation system ZKGraph (ICDE'26), VerfGraph achieves more efficient and expressive zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation by advancing design in two key ways. First, we propose novel operator-proof methods for core expansion and shortest-path operations that reduce costly sorting and comparison checks and eliminate edge canonicalization for bidirectional expansion. Furthermore, we introduce correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators, broadening the class of graph queries that can be verified. We evaluate VerfGraph using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark. Compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves $33.9\times$-$59.7\times$ speedups in proof generation and reduces peak prover memory by factors of $4.5\times$-$6.6\times$, while maintaining millisecond-level verification and producing sub-MB proofs.
title: VerfGraph: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Graph Query Evaluation System

summary: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.
title: DualWorldBench: Can Agents Plan Deliveries across Symbolic and Grounded Worlds?

summary: Satellite dwarf galaxies are reshaped by the tidal field of their host, a process that may account for part of the structural diversity of the observed dwarf population. We study how the stellar component of a satellite responds to tidal stripping using a suite of 480 controlled $N$-body simulations of satellite galaxies consisting of both dark matter (DM) and stars orbiting a Milky-Way-mass host. The simulated dwarfs span a broad range of DM halo structural and stellar-distribution parameters, including halo concentration, inner density slope, stellar-to-halo mass ratio, compactness of the stellar distribution with respect to the halo, as well as the Sérsic index of the stellar profiles. We present a comprehensive library of tidal tracks, namely, the evolution of the stellar mass, half-mass radius, mean surface density, and line-of-sight velocity dispersion, as functions of the bound mass fraction of the hosting DM subhalo, and provide simple and accurate fitting functions. We also identify the dependence of tidal tracks on key factors in the initial structural conditions. Notably, stellar compactness determines the duration over which the stellar mass remains relatively intact while the surrounding DM is being stripped. The Sérsic index and inner DM slope, in turn, govern the late-stage stellar mass-loss slope and the contraction or expansion of the remnant. Our simulations and empirical models provide a framework for modelling the stellar evolution of satellites across a broad range of progenitor structures, useful for semi-analytical models of satellite galaxy evolution.
title: Tidal Evolution of Satellite Dwarf Galaxies. I. Tidal Tracks of Stellar Mass and Structure

summary: Frontier LLM agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits, but are costly and often access-restricted due to their potential for malicious use. Open-weight models offer a more accessible alternative, but struggle to maintain progress across long exploitation chains. They also often fail to apply relevant security knowledge at the appropriate stage and in the right context to identify and evaluate promising attack directions. To address these limitations, we propose DoGNAVY-Exploit, a multi-agent harness built around two complementary designs: stage-aware decomposition with progressive expert knowledge disclosure, and hierarchical orchestration with parallel exploration. Specifically, DoGNAVY-Exploit uses configurable milestones to recast long-horizon exploitation as short, verifiable capability transitions and provides only the knowledge relevant to each stage. Within each milestone, a hierarchical architecture separates strategic planning from parallel execution: a planner proposes diverse attack routes, executors test them concurrently, and a controller accepts progress only when supported by runtime evidence. A shared structured memory consolidates verified facts, artifacts, replay steps, and failed routes across branches, allowing agents to build on collective progress and carry validated knowledge into subsequent milestones. In controlled benchmark environments, DoGNAVY-Exploit with GLM-5.2 achieves 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench, and 97.5% zero-day and 100% one-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench. On ExploitGym, it solves 79 tasks with GLM-5.2 and 157 with GLM-5.3, while the corresponding public Claude Code baselines solve 39 and 130 tasks, respectively. Ablation results further demonstrate that the stage-aware orchestration, expert knowledge, parallel exploration, and memory designs can substantially improve the exploitation capabilities of open-weight agents.
title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation
