summary: Generative AI tools have become part of how students study physics, yet unstructured use may reduce students' opportunities to work through problems independently. The Physics AI-Replication (P-A.I.R.) framework structures AI use as a four-step cycle: students identify a challenging problem, obtain an AI-generated explanation and solution, request similar practice problems, and solve them independently before reviewing the AI's solutions. We evaluated P-A.I.R. in 11 algebra- and calculus-based introductory physics sections at four U.S. institutions using a common end-of-semester survey. Most students reported improved conceptual understanding (90.9\%) and found the replicated practice problems helpful (97.7\%), and these two ratings were strongly associated ($r_s = 0.58$). Perceptions of both components, as well as post-engagement confidence ($μ= 7.18$ on a 1-10 scale), were consistent across institutions. Post-engagement confidence was associated with perceived improvement in conceptual understanding ($r_s = 0.37$) and the helpfulness of replicated practice ($r_s = 0.35$), but not with how often students used AI ($r_s = 0.02$) or with self-reported GPA ($r_s = 0.13$). Thematic analysis of open-ended responses showed that students valued AI primarily for conceptual clarification and structured problem solving (63.0\%), while their main concerns were AI accuracy (34.2\%) and the need for explanations that guide rather than simply provide answers (29.7\%). These findings suggest that how students engage with AI matters more than how often they use it, and that frameworks sequencing AI assistance with independent problem solving offer a practical, transferable approach for physics instruction.
title: Active Learning with Generative AI in Introductory Physics: A Multi-Institutional Study of the P-A.I.R. Framework

summary: Small students degrade on large reasoning models' (LRMs') long solutions, so recent work shortens them by interpolating an LRM with a short-answer model at ratio $λ$. We ask what student weights retain when this teacher stops thinking, comparing LoRA adapters of three students from three teacher pairs at each $λ$. In each pair, the adapters' update subspace shifts most where the teacher stops thinking and solutions shorten most, locating the change without attributing it. We identify a shared adapter subspace tied to thinking-like behavior (reflective markers, monologue format and long solutions). Shared by adapters before that point, it keeps about half (post hoc) while one pair's teacher halves its solutions but keeps its think tag, and largely empties after thinking stops. Removing it largely turns this behavior off for every pair, student and benchmark. Only in that pair and one other student does it leave clearly fewer markers than removing the update's top components; elsewhere, same-energy random directions often nearly match it. Grafted into a short-answer student at twice its weight, it turns early markers (a post hoc count) on, like the whole update, but the student rarely finishes. Our work identifies a weight subspace tied to distilled thinking-like behavior.
title: Where Do Distilled Students Store Thinking?

summary: Resumen La relación entre la tuberculosis, el bacilo de Calmette-Guérin (BCG) y las vacunas contra esta enfermedad constituye un objeto de estudio relevante, considerando que la BCG es la única vacuna disponible actualmente para prevenir la tuberculosis en humanos. Por ello, su perfeccionamiento y el desarrollo de nuevas vacunas representan estrategias fundamentales para el control de la enfermedad. El presente estudio busca contribuir a este campo de investigación desde la perspectiva de la métrica de patentes. Su objetivo es realizar un análisis métrico que permita describir la productividad de las patentes relacionadas con la tuberculosis, el bacilo de Calmette-Guérin y las vacunas contra esta enfermedad durante un periodo determinado. Para ello, se analizaron el comportamiento temporal y la distribución geográfica de la actividad patentadora en este ámbito, mediante técnicas y herramientas apropiadas para el análisis de documentos de patentes. La investigación sobre la tuberculosis, una enfermedad infecciosa y transmisible, ha recibido una atención considerable. Hasta hace relativamente poco tiempo, se consideraba principalmente un problema de salud de los países en desarrollo. Sin embargo, tras su reemergencia, la investigación sobre esta enfermedad ha adquirido una presencia destacada en los países desarrollados. No obstante, estos esfuerzos no se han correspondido proporcionalmente con la investigación orientada al desarrollo de una nueva generación de vacunas contra la tuberculosis, lo que también se refleja en la ausencia de nuevas patentes que respalden dichos avances. ABSTRACT The relationship between tuberculosis, Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), and tuberculosis vaccines constitutes a relevant field of study, given that BCG remains the only vaccine currently available for the prevention of tuberculosis in humans. Consequently, improving this vaccine and developing new alternatives are essential strategies for disease control. This study seeks to contribute to this research field from a patent-metrics perspective. Its objective is to conduct a metric analysis of patent productivity related to tuberculosis, Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, and tuberculosis vaccines over a defined period. To this end, the temporal evolution and geographical distribution of patenting activity in this field were examined using techniques and tools specifically suited to patent document analysis. Research on tuberculosis, an infectious and communicable disease, has attracted considerable attention. Until relatively recently, tuberculosis was regarded primarily as a public health problem affecting developing countries. However, following its re-emergence, research activity has increasingly involved developed countries. Nevertheless, these efforts have not been matched by a proportional increase in research aimed at developing a new generation of tuberculosis vaccines, a gap that is also reflected in the limited patent activity supporting such developments.
title: Tuberculosis, Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) and tuberculosis vaccines: a patent analysis

summary: A simulator-backed benchmark for cement pyroprocessing, released to make soft-sensor, fault-diagnosis, system-identification and control studies on cement thermal equipment comparable across research groups.The package contains (i) a calibrated one-dimensional mechanistic simulator of a 5000 t/d five-stage suspension preheater with an inline calciner, coupling effectiveness-NTU heat exchange, Leith-Licht grade efficiency, a duct-resistance pressure network and shrinking-core calcination kinetics, together with a reference PID-plus-interlock controller and a measurement-noise model; (ii) a scenario library of 400 Latin-hypercube steady states spanning the operating envelope, twenty 90-day closed-loop dynamic runs driven by block-bootstrap resampling of the historical operating distribution with thermal substitution rates from 0 to 60 percent, and 2700 labelled fault episodes covering fifteen parametrised modes; and (iii) four standardised benchmark tasks (parameter identification, soft sensing, fault detection and diagnosis, drift-aware operation) with fixed splits, metric implementations and reference baselines.</p><p>Code is licensed under MIT; data, documentation and figures under CC BY 4.0. Scores obtained on the library support fair relative comparison between algorithms under identical documented conditions and are not field-performance predictions. The companion manuscript is cited in the related identifiers.
tags: cement;preheater;calciner;alternative fuel;scenario library;benchmark;fault injection;system identification;soft sensor;process monitoring
title: preheater-scenario-library: an open scenario library of operating envelopes, alternative-fuel

summary: Progress Note No. 0 of the Law 15.506 series (Institut Atlantique Sud). It sets the baseline, as of 3 November 2026, against which the implementing acts of Brazil's national policy on critical and strategic minerals (Law 15.506 and Decree 13.118 of 16 September 2026) will be read: what is in force, what the texts settle, what remains open, what public trade statistics can verify, and four dated predictions, each with the observation that would prove it wrong.   The accompanying file IAS_Progress-note-00_data.csv contains every figure cited in section 4 (MDIC Comex Stat raw database, extraction of 3 November 2026, matching the official control totals).   Method: IAS Working Paper 2026/01 (10.5281/zenodo.22567731). Later numbers of the series are published as new versions of this record, on the day of the act they record.   Charter: publication on the same day for everyone; no funding from any measured entity; funders published every year; no review by a funder before publication; public, dated corrections.
title: Progress Note No. 0 — Law 15.506: baseline before the implementing decrees
Replication Data for: Cooperative governance and AWD compliance under salinity stress

summary: This dataset contains raw and processed data supporting the development and validation of phasor-based spectral flow cytometry (phSFC). This framework extends spectral phasor analysis, traditionally used in hyperspectral microscopy, to high-throughput flow cytometry, enabling model-free visualization and quantification of complex fluorescent signals. Archives all_data.zip: the complete dataset (all raw, pre-gated and technical benchmark files, for spectral flow cytometry and hyperspectral microscopy), organized as described below. source_data_fig_1.zip: Source Data for Figure 1. source_data_fig_2.zip: Source Data for Figure 2. source_data_extended_data_fig_1.zip: Source Data for Extended Data Figure 1. The three Source Data archives contain copies of the files from all_data.zip that are needed to reproduce the corresponding figure. Each one is organized in folders named after the figure panel they feed, so each figure can be reproduced without downloading the full dataset. Files used by more than one figure (for example, the MLV and BAL pre-gated files) are included in each archive that uses them. Dataset Contents The record is organized by experimental model, technical validation benchmarks, and acquisition modality: Multilamellar Vesicles (MLVs): Data of DOPC, DPPC, and Cholesterol mixtures labeled with LAURDAN. Used for cross-modal validation and establishing reference phasor coordinates for membrane order. Vero Cell Culture: Data from live cells treated with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) to induce cholesterol depletion. Includes an OLS Unmixed subfolder containing raw data unmixed via the ordinary least-squares algorithm. Ex Vivo Leukocytes: Data from a mouse model of lung inflammation (LPS-induced). Contains multi-color spectral flow cytometry data (LAURDAN + CD11c + CD45) from bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). Flow Rate Analysis: Whole blood cells stained with Hoechst and CD45-BV510, acquired across variable throughput regimes (Low, Medium, and Fast sample flow rates) to benchmark phasor coordinate stability. Gain Analysis: Unstained Vero cells acquired under systematic detector gain attenuation (-20%, -40%, -60%, and -80%) to evaluate robustness against signal dynamic range shifts. Data Organization & File Formats To ensure reproducibility and transparency, the files in all_data.zip are categorized as follows: Spectral Flow Cytometry (.fcs): Ungated Folder: Raw acquisition files directly exported from the Cytek Aurora. Pre-gated Folder: Files containing specific populations (e.g., singlets, LAURDAN+ events, or specific cell subsets) exported following the gating workflows described in the Methods. Technical Benchmarks: Dedicated folders for Flow rate analysis, Gain analysis, and OLS Unmixed files. Hyperspectral Microscopy (.lsm): Raw Data: Original hyperspectral stacks. Masks Folder: Binary masks (stored as image files) used to restrict analysis to specific regions of interest (ROIs), such as vesicle membranes or cellular boundaries. The Source Data archives contain only spectral flow cytometry files (.fcs), taken from the Pre-gated folders, the Flow rate analysis and Gain analysis folders, and, for Figure 2d, one file from the Ungated folder. Technical Specifications Spectral Flow Cytometry: Acquired on a Cytek Aurora (3-laser configuration). Spectral range analyzed: 428–812 nm (16 channels, Violet excitation). Hyperspectral Microscopy: Acquired on a Zeiss LSM 880 in Lambda Mode (63×/1.4 NA). Spectral range: 423–693 nm (28 channels, 10 nm spacing). Processing & Analysis: Initial gating and traditional unmixing performed in FlowJo / SpectroFlo. Downstream spectral phasor transformations, component calculations, and visualization performed using the PhasorPy library in Python.
title: Dataset for phSFC framework: Spectral Flow Cytometry and Hyperspectral Confocal Microscopy Files

summary: Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model. We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold. In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds. The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.
title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?

summary: Mainstream sequence-processing AI is temporally reactive: each update is driven by input and learned state transitions, rather than by an independently evolving internal temporal reference. Biological brains, by contrast, continuously generate rhythmic activity that structures perception, memory, and cognition, and this rhythmicity reaches all the way to behavior. We ask whether this difference is merely implementational or genuinely computational. Four lines of evidence suggest that endogenous temporal structure supports putative functions that input-driven architectures may not readily replicate: 1) phase-dependent routing of information, 2) delay-structured combinatorial representation, 3) cross-frequency multiplexing of items, and 4) oscillation-gated offline consolidation. A proof-of-concept delay-ablation test dissociates representational capacity from memory retrieval. In recurrent and spatial spiking networks with fixed synaptic weights and connectivity, shuffling delays preserves part of the capacity but substantially impairs the sequence retrieval. The relative contrast is more pronounced for spatial networks and longer propagations. Instantaneous transmission collapses capacity itself. We then outline a cross-frequency multiplexing scheme that combines item identity and serial order with alternative mechanisms for selective memory retrieval. Finally, we state one falsifiable hypothesis, conditions for matched-resource tests, and three research directions: the components already exist; the disciplined comparison does not.
title: Clocks all the way down: does sequence-processing AI need endogenous temporal structure?

summary: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.
title: What Remains in Sight? Autoregressive Video Decoding as Representation-Guided Context Rewriting

summary: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.
title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers

summary: Under temporal nonstationarity, model performance rankings reverse across training horizons due to heterogeneous sensitivities to memory. While existing literature addresses adaptive lookbacks, effective model complexity, and empirical forecast evaluation in isolation, no unified framework explains the structural mechanics driving these rank reversals. We bridge this gap by deriving a model-agnostic decomposition of out-of-sample $R^2$ into target alignment, miscalibrated aggressiveness, and predictive instability. Within this framework, we mathematically characterize complexity phase boundaries, establish closed-form optimal-memory equations for ridge regression under local drift, and extend these guarantees to complex model architectures via surrogate bounds. We validate these theoretical dynamics by benchmarking 14 linear, tree-based, and neural architectures across large-scale financial panels. In doing so, our framework demonstrates that empirical model rank reversals are driven by predictable surges in miscalibrated aggressiveness, providing a rigorous mechanistic diagnosis of generalization under temporal shift.
title: Decomposing Rank Reversals under Temporal Nonstationarity: Alignment, Aggressiveness, and Instability

summary: Under temporal nonstationarity, model performance rankings reverse across training horizons due to heterogeneous sensitivities to memory. While existing literature addresses adaptive lookbacks, effective model complexity, and empirical forecast evaluation in isolation, no unified framework explains the structural mechanics driving these rank reversals. We bridge this gap by deriving a model-agnostic decomposition of out-of-sample $R^2$ into target alignment, miscalibrated aggressiveness, and predictive instability. Within this framework, we mathematically characterize complexity phase boundaries, establish closed-form optimal-memory equations for ridge regression under local drift, and extend these guarantees to complex model architectures via surrogate bounds. We validate these theoretical dynamics by benchmarking 14 linear, tree-based, and neural architectures across large-scale financial panels. In doing so, our framework demonstrates that empirical model rank reversals are driven by predictable surges in miscalibrated aggressiveness, providing a rigorous mechanistic diagnosis of generalization under temporal shift.
title: Decomposing Rank Reversals under Temporal Nonstationarity: Alignment, Aggressiveness, and Instability

summary: Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However, new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data or reliable supervisory signals for further training. We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store what it learns: domain-specific skills and instructions on when to apply them, along with memories of past task experiences and reflections on what to improve. Recursa bootstraps the repository from domain materials and then refines it through recursive self-improvement. It uses parallel learners to execute tasks and synthesize local improvements, then validates and merges the improvements into the knowledge repository. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.
title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems

summary: To enable effective generalization in offline meta-RL, it is essential to accurately infer the underlying task through latent task representations, which provide a compact and transferable summary of task-specific characteristics for guiding policy generation. In this paper, we propose Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer (CoTA-DT), a DT-based offline meta-RL framework that learns task representations by jointly integrating four complementary components: (i) contrastive learning from offline trajectories, (ii) alignment with natural-language task descriptions, (iii) one-step supervision via a task-conditioned world model, and (iv) long-term supervision via a task-conditioned Q function. The learned task representations are used as conditioning signals for a DT-based policy, enabling task-aware meta-policy learning. To further support generalization in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, we design a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy that enables effective and reliable adaptation to unseen tasks. Notably, in CoTA-DT, the pretrained LLM serves as a shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning. This unified design facilitates parameter sharing, improving both efficiency and generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate that CoTA-DT consistently outperforms prior methods, particularly in challenging zero-shot generalization scenarios.
title: Decision Transformer with Task-Aware Representations for Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning

summary: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.
title: Controlling Action-Head Co-Adaptation to VLM Representation Anisotropy

summary: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (FastDEC) is an efficient variant of Density Peak Clustering (DPC) that achieves high clustering quality through dominance-based density estimation, but remains constrained by the computational cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) construction and dominance component (DC) processing. We present SymWarp-FastDEC, a GPU-accelerated implementation of FastDEC. At its core is SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry using upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. We also introduce WP-DC, a warp-parallel DC reduction algorithm designed for modern GPUs. Combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling, WP-DC eliminates DC reduction as a runtime bottleneck. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SymWarp-FastDEC produces clustering outputs identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. Compared with a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 for exact k-NN search, our approach achieves approximately 1.7x to 4.9x higher end-to-end performance, with the advantage generally increasing with dimensionality. Compared with the original single-threaded Python FastDEC implementation, speedups reach approximately 2.5 x 10^4 in a very high-dimensional case where its k-d-tree-based search degrades; this extreme result is not representative of typical acceleration.
title: Accelerating FastDEC Clustering Algorithm with GPUs

summary: A stored experience may answer one future question and offer little help with another. We measure this task-conditioned utility rather than assigning each memory a single importance score. A task-blind writer stores a memory without seeing the later task; a frozen reader then answers that task with and without the memory, using identical filler. A cost ledger records the resources used to form, store and expose the memory. On single-call factual-recall tasks built from LongMemEval-V2 web-agent memories, the same memory helps more when it contains information needed for the answer. Its mean paired reward gain on these answer-bearing task pairs exceeds that on matched-control pairs by $+0.33$ (95% interval $+0.21$ to $+0.46$). The tested task-blind summaries and structured records yield smaller gains than Raw, including at fixed total context; a budget sweep is consistent with retention of answer-bearing content contributing to the difference. The bearing--control contrast remains positive in a new session with randomized memory position and under a second reader, although individual memory--task labels change. Generic retrieval performs above chance but misses most screen-defined answer-bearing memories. The factual-recall gains do not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where even raw memories have no measurable effect. We provide a public, versioned Conditional Memory Utility Dataset of paired measurements and costs. The practical takeaway is to evaluate memory compression by the task utility it preserves alongside its costs. Task-conditioned measurements make this comparison possible; their stability must also be checked.
title: What Is This Memory Useful For? Measuring Task-Conditioned Utility in Long-Term Agent Memory

summary: Protein structure predictors reliably identify native conformations, but do not describe the continuum connecting unfolded ensembles to folded states. Here we present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework that generates C$α$ conformational ensembles at a specified folding fraction $Q$. FoldScape reconstructs three-dimensional chains through hierarchical, sliding-window regressions of one-dimensional inter-residue distances, followed by chain assembly and sampling with a rectified-flow decoder. It is trained on multi-scale coarse-grained folding trajectories and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. Across 20 human proteins (36-857 residues), at matched sample size, FoldScape covers about an order of magnitude more of the folding coordinate than seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles, robustly across proteins, order parameters and binning choices. AlphaFold 3 better anchors the immediate native vicinity, which FoldScape does not reach, making the approaches complementary. FoldScape reconstruction accuracy remains approximately constant along $Q$, from collapsed coil to near-native globule, rather than deteriorating away from the native state. A stride-one crop-and-superpose scheme extends inference to chains several times longer than a single chain-level forward pass. We also show that training trajectories resolve mechanical unfolding at residue resolution, that elongation-conditioned ensembles exhibit reproducible continuous observables across pulling velocities, and that partially unfolded chains form geometrically coherent segments. FoldScape thus combines broad coverage of folding stages with stable reconstruction accuracy, without per-protein simulation.
title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence

summary: We present an exact computational proof that the frozen QPLIB_2096 instance has global minimum 7,025,720. The solution and certification approach was explored and refined through ZiYor, a self-evolving AI system. The authors provide the mathematical account and exact validation reported here. The original formulation has 300 binary variables, 6,900 triangle inequalities, and 25 nonconvex quadratic constraints. A coefficient-level reconstruction identifies its variables with the unordered pairs of 25 items. The triangle inequalities encode partitions, while each quadratic constraint becomes a bound on the total weight of edges incident to one partition block. This yields a set-partitioning formulation over all capacity-feasible blocks, with a separate edge-cost graph determining the objective. Exact enumeration examines 245,505 subsets of sizes one through six and finds 14,981 feasible blocks. Every six-element subset is infeasible; nonnegative capacity weights exclude all larger blocks. An integer price vector satisfies the dual inequality for every feasible block and has sum 2,229,456. Subtracting this sum from the total objective edge cost 9,255,176 gives a lower bound of 7,025,720, attained by the supplied six-block partition. Fresh solver-free checks validate the candidate against both frozen model formats and verify the certificate. The result is an instance-specific optimality proof with an exact primal and dual witness; no cross-instance performance conclusion is drawn.
title: Exact Optimality Certification of QPLIB 2096 through Complete Set Partitioning

summary: Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality. In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.
title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking

summary: Non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging aims to sense objects outside the direct line of sight. While most previous work focuses on the canonical around-the-corner configuration, this work considers a more challenging occlusion-based NLOS setting in which targets are hidden by scene geometry. To avoid the challenge of collecting large real-world datasets, we have developed a photon-based Monte Carlo simulator to generate diverse synthetic training data and validate against experimental data. We trained an AI model to identify multi-bounce photon patterns associated with hidden targets. The model achieves an Average Precision (AP) of 0.91 on synthetic test data and, when transferred directly to 180 real measurements acquired with a TMF8829 SPAD flash LiDAR, achieves 86.67% accuracy and an AP of 0.95. These results show that simulated transient data can support hidden-target detection with a low-cost commercial sensor and provide an initial step toward more general occlusion-based NLOS sensing and, ultimately, hidden-scene reconstruction.
title: Simulation-Driven Approach for Occlusion-Based Non-Line-Of-Sight Detection Using a Low-Cost Flash LiDAR

summary: Prestress governs the stability, stiffness, and dynamic behavior of tensegrity structures, but it is not directly observable from sparse structural measurements, and it may decrease during service life. Under strong excitation, the cables may slacken and the dynamics become nonsmooth. Existing identification methods are limited to the taut regime, and physics-informed networks for tensegrities solve only the forward problem of predicting the response from known member parameters. This study formulates the inverse problem. Neural networks are trained on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, where the mass matrix is constant and the force densities enter linearly. The force densities, damping, and axial stiffness are trainable parameters, and the tension-only cable law is kept. A Fisher-information analysis shows, before inversion, which member parameters a record can determine. The method is tested on simulated planar tensegrity frames with up to five modules and a three-dimensional prism, and on measured records of a biomimetic leg and a full-scale tensegrity simplex. On the one-module frame, the identifiable force densities are recovered within 1.5% from noisy accelerations at half the free coordinates, on records with and without taut-slack transitions. Records with transitions determine members that taut records leave undetermined. On the five-module frame, a 16-cable two-span bridge, the median force-density error rises moderately, to 4.2%. On measured records, an identified spring stiffness is within 0.1% of its independently measured value on average, and the identified simplex prestress at 13 levels agrees with its cable force transducers to 2.9% root-mean-square.
title: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions

summary: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from $0.846$ under the original leaky evaluation to just $0.291$ under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.
title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation

summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is expected to observe gravitational-wave signals from massive black hole binaries, extreme mass ratio inspirals, and more. Despite the significant scientific potential, accurately extracting these signals from the data will only be possible if LISA's instrumental noise is understood: poor noise modelling will result in lost signals, biased parameter estimates, and incorrect astrophysical insights. Modelling LISA's instrumental noise is more challenging than its ground-based counterpart since the data is highly correlated, meaning that the noise covariance matrix can no longer be assumed diagonal in frequency and in the different data streams. In this work, we present an initial approach to perform non-parametric noise inference for LISA that requires no prior knowledge of the LISA observatory. By fitting the full noise covariance matrix with a combination of splines and inverse Lorentzians, we show that our model can estimate the power and cross spectral densities for LISA from 7 days of simulated noise-only data. We find that the median estimate from our non-parametric model whitens the data according to the expected unit normal distribution. We envision that our non-parametric model can be used as part of the global fit, as well as in combination with modelled approaches to identify, quantify, and constrain the frequency dependence of unknown noise artifacts.
title: Noisy pipelines II: Non-parametric Noise Inference for LISA

summary: Recently, we found a method to reconstruct the dilatation operator (sphere Hamiltonian) from a regulated conformal field theory groundstate. In this paper, we explore methods to construct the whole global conformal algebra, and test our construction using fuzzy sphere regularization. Starting from a groundstate of the same Hamiltonian, these methods perform better than constructions of the conformal generators based on a Hamiltonian density, are model-independent, require no additional tuning, and improve with system size. One purpose of reconstructing the conformal algebra is to identify conformal primary states, which we do with some success. We also find further evidence supporting the model of the short-distance corrections to the entanglement Hamiltonian proposed earlier and use it to make systematic improvements.
title: Reconstruction of the conformal algebra from a critical groundstate on the (fuzzy) sphere

summary: Mapping the three-dimensional distribution of dark matter is key to tracing the growth of cosmic structure. Two-dimensional weak lensing mass maps recover its projected distribution, but they blend structures at different distances along the line of sight. We reconstruct the three-dimensional matter distribution in the 0.54 deg$^2$ COSMOS-Web field using deep James Webb Space Telescope imaging, with an effective source density of 121 galaxies arcmin$^{-2}$ We combine a physical weak lensing forward model with a diffusion-based Bayesian generative prior learned from cosmological simulations, yielding a posterior distribution of the matter field across 20 lens planes to $z \simeq 2$, doubling the redshift reach of previous Hubble Space Telescope-based 3D reconstructions and approaching cosmic noon, an epoch of rapid galaxy growth. The reconstruction separates structures that overlap in projection and recovers non-Gaussian matter structure across a range of spatial scales, including over-densities associated with independently identified galaxy clusters that were not detected in earlier weak lensing maps. Posterior sampling quantifies the range of three-dimensional matter distributions allowed by the data, enabling a probabilistic visualization of the cosmic web while propagating uncertainties in its inferred structure. Null and simulation-based tests show that the recovered structures are supported by the lensing signal and are consistent with expectations from the fiducial $Λ$CDM cosmology. These results extend three-dimensional weak lensing mapping into the high-redshift, non-Gaussian regime and establish a route towards probabilistic mapping of the evolving cosmic web with current wide-field lensing surveys.
title: 3D dark matter map of the JWST COSMOS-Web field using diffusion-based generative priors

summary: Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN): mathematical revisions, corrected datasets, and reproducible computational resources This repository provides an integrated historical, mathematical, empirical, and computational resource for the Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN) framework. It brings together the foundational development of the model, revised property definitions and their algebraic consequences, corrected crown-network records, ecological reanalyses, editable network drawings, and software for reconstructing and analyzing existing or newly constructed WCHNs. The deposit is an independent scientific resource, not tied to a particular journal or manuscript. HISTORICAL FOUNDATION Four publications document the model's development: (1) Souza et al. (2011), the original network analysis of Cerrado crowns ( https://doi.org/10.1007/s11258-010-9797-7 ); (2) Prado et al. (2020), formalization of decomposition, topology, and four initial properties ( https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2020.110318 ); (3) Prado and Trovão (2023), expansion to eight properties and Caatinga–Cerrado comparisons ( https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2023.110345 ); and (4) Prado (2024), stochastic node-addition networks and size-matched comparisons ( https://doi.org/10.1007/s40626-024-00340-5 ). These references allow users to trace the original definitions and later revisions. MATHEMATICAL AND EMPIRICAL CONTENT The author-prepared document “Algebraic relationships and mathematical properties of the Woody Crown Hydraulic Network” explains the revised symmetry (SYM), complexity (COM), and vulnerability (VUL) definitions, algebraic dependencies, network-size effects, and reproducibility checks. In particular, revised VUL is exactly equal to normalized mean node depth in a rooted tree. The observed near-reciprocity between navigability (NAV) and VUL is a strong empirical association, not a second exact identity or independent hydraulic measurement. The deposit retains the original Cerrado and Caatinga source spreadsheets, recalculated property tables, comparisons, reduced principal component analyses (PCAs), and size-adjusted exploratory analyses. The previously deposited PCA outputs are preserved numerically; their interpretations should account for the revised mathematical meaning of VUL. The updated PCA technical note documents the analytical methods and limitations. CORRECTED CERRADO NETWORKS AND TOOLKIT A new workbook records corrections to 20 previously sampled Cerrado WCHNs (not additional independent observations). Six networks were reconstructed manually, including S. polyphyllum 1 as the manual feasibility pilot; fourteen were reconstructed semi-automatically, beginning with S. camporum 1 as the first test of the connector generator, followed by thirteen additional networks. In the semi-automatic workflow, the researcher marked the nodes, deterministic software proposed editable connectors and highlighted ambiguous nodes in red, and the researcher visually checked and corrected the complete graph against the original drawing beneath it. The WCHN toolkit v1.0.3 contains code, documentation, editable PowerPoint networks, intermediate files, tests, and a separate semi-automatic validation exercise using Miconia albicans 5, a network originally reconstructed manually. That exercise led to a verified terminal-connector decomposition correction without changing the network topology or any of its eight WCHN properties. The accompanying Practical Guide v1.0.3 provides step-by-step instructions for reconstructing, inspecting, validating, and analyzing WCHNs, including optional AI assistance under mandatory researcher supervision. REPRODUCIBILITY AND LIMITATIONS The accompanying README.md provides the complete file inventory, foundational references, directions for reusing the toolkit and statistical scripts, links among materials, and version history. These resources enable checking corrected topologies and calculations and exploring
title: Recalculated woody crown hydraulic network properties and reduced principal component analyses of Caatinga and Cerrado trees

The primary proposal tests operator-independent audit trail under a concealed challenge: swap a reference cartridge without notification. Measures: unassisted reconstruction yield [fraction]; separate witness: traceable calibration bias [nT]. Strong comparator: static archive with trained human curator. Failures remain reportable. summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning

summary: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.
title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation

summary: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers

We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers

summary: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.
title: Asynchronous Robot Policies

summary: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.
title: Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents

summary: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.
title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory

summary: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.
title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?

summary: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI

summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.
title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response

summary: We investigate the automated generation of executable robot reinforcement learning (RL) policies from natural-language task descriptions. Rather than using large language models (LLMs) as execution-time decision makers, we use them as designers that construct RL pipelines before deployment, including Markov decision process (MDP) formulation and simulator implementation. We identify a phase-wise structure in this problem: MDP formulation is dependency-structured and sequential, whereas simulator implementation becomes modular once the formulation is fixed. Based on this structure, we propose ARPG, a dependency-aware agentic framework that performs sequential MDP modeling, localized verification and correction, and simulator-structured implementation while externalizing intermediate artifacts. ARPG targets a key failure mode of automated policy generation: executable code may still yield non-learnable policies when state, action, reward, and termination artifacts are not semantically aligned. Experiments in Isaac Sim show that ARPG improves modeling correctness, environment executability, and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Additional demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL, and engineering-domain MDPs further suggest that the same modeling pipeline can be reused beyond the main benchmark suite.
title: LLMs as MDP Designers: A Dependency-Aware Agentic Framework for Automated Robot Policy Generation

summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.
title: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement

summary: Science is a process of useful models being proven wrong time and again, but despite its many flaws, it somehow works. Why is this? Paul Feyerabend argued that it works because people dare to hold and defend incompatible rival theories against the accepted one, since a theory's failures often lead to its abandonment in the presence of a more accurate or simpler alternative. He called this view theoretical pluralism. We introduce a theoretical and experimental model in which this can be examined. It compares communities of pluralist agents, which can hold rival theories side by side and maintain beliefs within and between those theories, with communities of monist agents, which can only incorporate what they hear or observe into a single model of their own. In a multi-agent variational inference setting, our experimental demonstrations illustrate how communities with rival theories can go through periods of uncertainty followed by a shift in the theories they hold true, how the information that is communicated between communities affects beliefs when those communities make different observations about the world, and how sharing support for theories and sharing beliefs within them contribute differently to collective belief dynamics.

summary: AI agents can make incorrect decisions or waste resources even when their tools and infrastructure work normally. Their nondeterministic behavior makes these problems difficult to reproduce and diagnose. We developed Signals to identify such problems from agentic traces and suggest concrete remediations. We built the method around a taxonomy of 45 problem types across eight families, with definitions and evidence requirements for each type. The method distinguishes realized failures, risk exposures, and inefficiencies, groups related findings into engineering issues called Signals, and assesses their severity from the supporting evidence. Each Signal includes actions a developer can take and checks for evaluating the change. Further executions can add evidence to an existing Signal or reveal a new problem. We evaluated the method on public agent executions and achieved 91.43% F1 when matching Signals to reference issues, about 18 percentage points higher than a one-pass LLM control that used the same model and taxonomy.
title: Signals: Continuous Diagnostics of AI Agents

summary: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system. Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.
title: Treating the Symptom, Missing the Cause: Anatomy of a Scientific Reasoning Failure

summary: Existing metalinguistic reasoning benchmarks require both inference of rules and their application, making failures hard to diagnose. We introduce typological feature induction (TFI) which targets the former step. Given sentences in an unnamed language paired with translations in a known pivot language, models must predict a typological feature of the unnamed language. From Grambank and multi-parallel corpora, we automatically build evaluation questions over 195 languages. We find that LLMs identify 59--80% of these languages from only 16 sentence pairs; and misaligning the translations barely affects their accuracy, suggesting reliance on prior knowledge of the language. Enciphering text to prevent recognition increases the corpus' utility, but mainly for features where target and pivot languages agree. On languages which models cannot identify, neither open model outperforms a majority-value baseline. Since induction from raw text aligns with field linguists' use-case, this work indicates the models tested are not yet ready for this role. TFI offers a scalable path to track progress in this direction.
title: Typological Feature Induction as a Benchmark for Inductive Metalinguistic Reasoning

summary: On a public agent leaderboard, a general-purpose agent trails a scaffold built for an airline customer-service benchmark by 13 points on the tasks that touch its database, and a reader could conclude that generality costs accuracy. The gap comes from the grader. The general agent often ends its conversations in a way that never triggers grading, so only about half of its episodes were scored and the rest were stored as failures. Grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the pooled gap, without rerunning any agent. We audit two carefully maintained public leaderboards, HAL and tau2-bench, from their published artifacts alone and find three more instrument errors. A cost column counts nested model calls twice, unevenly across rows. Archived trajectories record grader-written actions as agent actions. Re-grading saved trajectories under a newer evaluator is itself a new measurement: a correct and announced fix reorders a leaderboard, and a mode check that misreads four files collapses their scores by 59 to 82 points while printing no error. Each produced a plausible number, and the HAL maintainers confirmed their three within five weeks. Together the cases show that the infrastructure of agent evaluation, meaning the code that grades, logs, replays and versions an evaluation, is part of the measurement and fails silently, so scores and orderings can move with no visible sign. These failure modes follow from how agent evaluation pipelines are built, and those pipelines change as fast as the agents they measure, so we expect more of them elsewhere. We propose cheap checks that expose the instrument: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of every recorded action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.
title: Silent Instrument Errors Reorder Agent Leaderboards

summary: Result files behind the tables and figures of the article "USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching" and its supplementary material: JSON result records with provenance blocks, run logs, CSV episode tables, trajectory and simulated-frame arrays, the acoustic window file and seven CT label caches derived from the TotalSegmentator dataset. MANIFEST.tsv maps each file to the printed tables and figures it feeds, and SHA256SUMS lists the digest of every file. Local paths, user and host names and the names of private folders and repositories were replaced, as listed in SANITIZATION.md. Wording of the pre-specified plans that the records quoted and change-history notes were withheld, and codes of process-record entries and post hoc items, dated process notes and words of the development process were removed (SANITIZATION.md lists each rule with its counts); the mixed-model row labels, status strings and citations take the form the article prints. CROSSWALK.tsv gives the original and the public sha256 and md5 of each changed file. The files are licensed under CC BY 4.0, except the eight files that hold content derived from the AMOS 2022 CTs, which are shared under CC BY-SA 4.0 (listed in README.md).

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. The isolated Kalman filter (IsoKF) of Jung, Luft and Weiss (Autonomous Robots, 2025) lets the nodes of a robot or sensor network share an estimation task cheaply: only the nodes involved in a measurement update, and their correlations with everyone else are rescaled by a correction factor. Its authors conjectured that for any completely observable and controllable system the covariance it reports converges to a finite, unique, stable steady state. Result: the conjecture is false. A three-node system with pair-sum observations x1+x2, x2+x3, x3+x1 and dynamics A = 3I is observable from one epoch and controllable, every local block the filter uses stays positive definite, yet the reported marginal variances satisfy m_k ≥ (5/4)(9/5)^k − 1/4, while the centralised Kalman filter keeps every variance at most 3/4. A Perron-root comparison extends divergence to every connected non-bipartite pair-sum graph when a^2 is large enough; extra attenuation or deletion of cross-covariances does not help. Schur-stable dynamics always give bounded marginals (proved). Computer-assisted proofs (outward-rounded interval arithmetic) show that for a^2 in (1, 1.38] large priors diverge at rate a^(2k), entry certified from 10^12 I at eight values down to a^2 = 1 + 10^-8, and that at a^2 = 21/20 the prior I converges while 10^12 I diverges: there is no globally attracting steady covariance. Also: exact classification of participant overlaps (|U ∩ V| ≤ 1) that keep every local block positive definite, and a bounded regime for anchored relative measurements. Scope: in high-precision numerical tests the actual estimation error stays bounded; the failure is gross pessimism of the reported covariance, not divergence of the estimate. The counterexample uses pair-sum measurements, not plain differences. Nothing is proved for a^2 in (1.38, 2+√5); uniqueness for stable dynamics remains open. The ikf_lib software was inspected but not run; no software failure is claimed. Version 0.2.0 (correction). Version 0.1.0 compared this work with Luft, Schubert, Roumeliotis and Burgard (2018, IJRR, doi:10.1177/0278364918760698) at abstract level only. This version compares it with the full text: Luft et al. introduce the correction factor (their eq. 26) and a scaled variant (eq. 28), and prove that two-robot blocks stay positive definite (Proposition 1, now credited at Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 5.3); they make no claim about boundedness or convergence of the covariance and give no divergence example. The two citing works are now also compared in full text. No theorem, proof, certificate, computation or numerical finding changed. Archive: LaTeX manuscript and PDF, bibliography with registry records, exact rational verifiers, interval certificates C1–C3, numerical scripts and their outputs (normal and python -O), figures, CI and SHA-256 manifest. Assurance: internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); certificates are computer-assisted, not formal proofs. Creator: Anonymous.
