summary: Saigon300 is a semi-synthetic benchmark for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (VRPTW) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Version 1.0.0 archives 56 instances with 300 customers and one depot each: C1 (9), C2 (8), R1 (12), R2 (11), RC1 (8), and RC2 (8). The package contains eight shared asymmetric OSRM distance/duration matrices, instance files, BIH verification and OR-Tools code, figures, and recorded experimental outputs. Matrix units are metres and seconds; the routing profile is car. Source metadata reports an OpenStreetMap snapshot dated 2026-05-26. This deposit is an unchanged snapshot of public repository commit 555ac7d2eb9d2af402bdb23f9633e3af435d8ab4: https://github.com/ltlong-SGU/Saigon300-VRPTW . ZIP integrity and node IDs 0..300 for all 56 instance files have been checked. This is not a new solver experiment or full independent replication. Authors: Le Tan Long and Phan Tan Quoc (Saigon University); Do Phan Thuan (Ho Chi Minh City University of Industry and Trade), as stated in the source metadata. Original source licences are retained: CC BY 4.0 for the dataset; source metadata separately declares MIT for code. Upstream rights remain applicable to OpenStreetMap/OSRM-derived components; OpenStreetMap attribution: https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright . This dataset deposit is separate from the accepted Saigon300 camera-ready paper, which is not included.

summary: Abstract Water balance penalties may improve numerical closure while reallocating error among unobserved ‎fluxes. We investigate this compensation and the limits of selecting a penalty for annual flood ‎prediction. Forty-five trained synthetic LSTMs isolate forcing, exchange, and initialization ‎disturbances. Thirty-five matched regional models and five accounting references use 89 quality-quality-‎screened CAMELS-AUS catchments, partitioned into 54 for development, 15 for selector validation, ‎and 20 for confirmation. Under 40% precipitation underestimation, fixed and bounded penalties ‎reduce estimated evapotranspiration below 1% of generating truth in all eight held-out synthetic ‎catchments. A historically selected rule lowers confirmation-normalized annual-maximum error ‎from 2.29 to 2.21, a 3.54% point reduction. The original conditional interval barely excludes zero, ‎and river-region sign randomization gives p = 0.0625. A post hoc 100,000-draw analysis retains a ‎near-zero upper endpoint, with numerical sub-batches still reaching or crossing zero. Direct paired ‎comparisons with simpler alternatives all span zero; the selector does not establish added predictive ‎value. Its seven active catchments occupy only five regions. Recovery of the original final archive ‎verifies the selection lock, completed fit records, and hashes of all 40 real/reference prediction files. ‎These findings support a controlled latent-compensation mechanism and a reproducible limitation ‎of selective regularization, while leaving real-catchment process attribution and robust predictive ‎superiority unresolved. ‎ Keywords: rainfall-runoff modeling; water balance; annual flood maxima; model misspecification; ‎spatial transfer; uncertainty
title: Ayad-Kathim-Hussein/Prof.-Dr.-Ayad-K.-H.-Alkhafaji: Why selective mass penalties do not reliably improve annual flood maxima: An 89-‎catchment diagnostic with recovered provenance

summary: Fractal Geometry and the Verifiability of Electronic Election Results: Limits of Identification and a Multiscale Framework for Analyzing Tabulation This record contains an integrated research article (preprint; not peer reviewed) that asks a deliberately narrow question: under what conditions can fractal and multiscale methods applied to the published tabulation of a two-candidate election yield useful statistical evidence of irregularity, and under what conditions can no such method identify the origin of the data? The paper is addressed equally to those who read smoothness in a tabulation curve as a certificate of integrity and to those who read any irregularity as proof of manipulation; it argues that both readings mistake arithmetic and model specification for evidence. The analysis separates five stages of the electoral chain (voter choice, machine record, transmission, tabulation, publication) and three research questions that are routinely conflated: whether the order in which precincts are reported is atypical, whether precinct-level results are atypical relative to an explicit reference model, and whether published results agree with independently preserved records. Three elementary propositions formalize what tabulation data can and cannot show. The cumulative vote share is mechanically damped as the count grows, so late smoothness is a property of weighted averaging rather than a sign of control. Two scenarios that induce the same distribution over the observable data cannot be separated by any test confined to those data, with discriminating power bounded by their total variation distance. And a class of proportional vote transfers leaves every increment-based statistic (first differences, centered CUSUM, zero-mean wavelet contrasts) unchanged while shifting the cumulative margin by 2δN_k. A fully synthetic experiment models 256 precincts in 16 regions with correlated regional preferences and geographically dependent reporting times, and compares four two-sided detectors (level test, centered CUSUM, multiscale scan and Haar contrast over windows of 4 to 128 precincts), each calibrated separately on 2,000 null elections and evaluated on 1,500 independent elections per scenario. Under the correct null, alert rates lie between 4.1% and 5.7%. With a 4% transfer concentrated in a block of 51 precincts, the Haar contrast alerts in 94.0% of replicates (Wilson 95% interval 92.7%–95.1%); with a diffuse 0.8% transfer across all 256 precincts, moving approximately the same number of votes (608 versus 612 on average), it alerts in 4.5%, indistinguishable from the null. A legitimate regional preference shift omitted from the reference model produces Haar alerts in 57.7% of elections in which no vote was transferred, and a deliberately homogeneous reference that ignores geography drives three of the four detectors to 100% false alerts. Sensitivity depends on the shape of the alteration and on the specification of the reference model, not on the volume of votes moved. The limits of these findings are stated explicitly. The reference model is an oracle known to the simulator; all data are synthetic; the experiment was not preregistered; detection delay and localization accuracy were not systematically evaluated; no actual election is analyzed, and nothing in the paper certifies or refutes the integrity of any election. A p-value is not a probability of fraud, and the absence of an alert cannot certify the absence of manipulation. The paper closes with a protocol for future application to real tabulation records, covering data provenance and chronology, preregistration, a global multiscale statistic with Monte Carlo calibration, nonfractal comparators at equal false-alert rates, adversarial and benign alternatives, and robustness checks, and situates the discussion within software independence and the cast-as-intended, recorded-as-cast and tallied-as-recorded framework of election verifiability. summary: This archive contains the Python code, raw numerical results and figure-generation scripts accompanying the paper "An Alternated Inertial Method for Bilevel Split Variational Inequalities Beyond Monotonicity and Lipschitz Continuity" by N. T. T. Thuy and P. T. Hieu (submitted to Optimization, Taylor & Francis, 2026). The paper studies the bilevel split variational inequality problem with multiple output sets (BSVIP-MOS) governed by non-monotone, possibly non-Lipschitz operators, and proposes AISE-VS, an alternated inertial subgradient-extragradient method with a look-ahead self-adaptive stepsize, a split correction and a viscosity step, together with an Armijo line-search variant (AISE-VS-LS) that dispenses with the stepsize conditions. The archive reproduces every table and figure of the paper: - numerical certification of the assumptions (Table 1); - Experiment 1: a certified non-quasimonotone benchmark with skew-type operators, 20 starting points (Table 2, Fig. 1); - Experiment 2: a Hölder (non-Lipschitz) benchmark, self-adaptive rule versus line search, up to 2×10^5 iterations (Table 3, Fig. 2); - Experiment 3: a trade-network instance built from BACI-VI-Bench (year 2022 and a study over 2017–2024) with an independently certified reference solution (Table 4, Fig. 3); - long-run convergence (Fig. 4) and a look-ahead ablation (Fig. 5). The package contains the source code (src/), the raw results behind all tables and figures (results/), the figures (figures/), a README.md that maps each table and figure to the command that regenerates it, run_quick.sh (smoke test) and run_all.sh (full reproduction). Seeds are fixed (global seed 2024). Requirements: Python 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib. The BACI-VI-Bench dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20607238), derived from CEPII-BACI, is NOT redistributed here; it must be downloaded separately to rerun Experiment 3 (see README). Experiments 1 and 2 are fully synthetic. Version 1.0.1. This version adds the scripts (verification/, run by run_verification.sh) and logs (results/verification/) of the additional checks reported in the revised manuscript. The source code in src/ and all tables and figures are unchanged from version 1.0.0. The checks are: (i) an independent recomputation of the reference solution x† for 2017–2024 with an interior-point solver (CVXPY/Clarabel), compared with the stored x†; (ii) the marginal residual of the stored x†; (iii) an a-posteriori check that every point at which the operators are evaluated stays in the region where the extended operator coincides with the original one; and  (iv) the number of times the restart criterion is examined and the number of times it is activated in Experiments 1–3, including two runs of 10^5 iterations. The logs of one complete run are summarised in results/verification/SUMMARY.md; the version history is in CHANGELOG.md.  Check (i) additionally requires cvxpy (requirements-verification.txt); the other checks need only the packages of requirements.txt.
title: AISE-VS for bilevel split variational inequalities with multiple output sets: code and raw results

The archive reproduces every table and figure of the paper: - numerical certification of the assumptions (Table 1); - Experiment 1: a certified non-quasimonotone benchmark with skew-type operators, 20 starting points (Table 2, Fig. 1); - Experiment 2: a Hölder (non-Lipschitz) benchmark, self-adaptive rule versus line search, up to 2×10^5 iterations (Table 3, Fig. 2); - Experiment 3: a trade-network instance built from BACI-VI-Bench (year 2022 and a study over 2017–2024) with an independently certified reference solution (Table 4, Fig. 3); - long-run convergence (Fig. 4) and a look-ahead ablation (Fig. 5). The package contains the source code (src/), the raw results behind all tables and figures (results/), the figures (figures/), a README.md that maps each table and figure to the command that regenerates it, run_quick.sh (smoke test) and run_all.sh (full reproduction). Seeds are fixed (global seed 2024). Requirements: Python 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib. The BACI-VI-Bench dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20607238), derived from CEPII-BACI, is NOT redistributed here; it must be downloaded separately to rerun Experiment 3 (see README). Experiments 1 and 2 are fully synthetic. Version 1.0.1. This version adds the scripts (verification/, run by run_verification.sh) and logs (results/verification/) of the additional checks reported in the revised manuscript. The source code in src/ and all tables and figures are unchanged from version 1.0.0. The checks are: (i) an independent recomputation of the reference solution x† for 2017–2024 with an interior-point solver (CVXPY/Clarabel), compared with the stored x†; (ii) the marginal residual of the stored x†; (iii) an a-posteriori check that every point at which the operators are evaluated stays in the region where the extended operator coincides with the original one; and  (iv) the number of times the restart criterion is examined and the number of times it is activated in Experiments 1–3, including two runs of 10^5 iterations. The logs of one complete run are summarised in results/verification/SUMMARY.md; the version history is in CHANGELOG.md.  Check (i) additionally requires cvxpy (requirements-verification.txt); the other checks need only the packages of requirements.txt.
title: AISE-VS for bilevel split variational inequalities with multiple output sets: code and raw results

summary: Abstract   Objective : In a previous study, the author used a Cox proportional hazards regression model to analyze the relationships between emergency transport data for heatstroke cases in Tokyo in 2025, meteorological factors, and urban aerosols, thereby identifying factors that alter the risk of heatstroke in an urban environment. While the analysis suggested a positive correlation between PM2.5 concentrations and the risk of heatstroke, this association was not statistically significant. The present study reports the results of an analysis that integrates data from 2023, 2024, and 2025. Method : Analysis was performed using a Cox proportional hazards regression model in which ambient temperature was incorporated as a parameter of the baseline hazard function . Result and Discussion : The results of the Cox proportional hazards regression analysis identified atmospheric pressure and relative humidity as positive predictors. Furthermore, an increase in PM2.5 levels was found to be statistically significantly associated with an elevated risk of heatstroke. Conversely, duration of sunshine, PM10 levels, and the cumulative number of days since June 1st were identified as negative predictors. PM2.5 contains numerous substances derived from combustion, which generate free radicals that are harmful to the human cardiopulmonary system. Consequently, it is thought that PM2.5 may increase the risk of heatstroke. In the present study, which integrated data from 2023, 2024, and 2025, PM2.5 concentration was identified as a statistically significant positive modifying factor. It should be noted, however, that while this study demonstrates an association, it does not establish a causal relationship.   Conclusion: Further research was conducted on the relationship between PM2.5 and the risk of heatstroke, utilizing a larger number of cases. PM2.5 showed a positive correlation with the risk of heatstroke, and this association was statistically significant.

summary: IberCloud-L is a dataset of 1,094 Landsat patches annotated for cloud and cloud shadow segmentation in four classes. It covers Landsat 5, 7, 8 and 9 imagery over the Iberian Peninsula, including Cantabrian, Mediterranean and southern coastal regions, an inland region and a mountainous region in the Pyrenees, with contrasting cloud regimes. The images are Landsat Collection 2 top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance downloaded via Google Earth Engine. Annotations were produced in two stages. A model trained on CloudSEN12 generated initial masks, which an expert annotator then reviewed and corrected manually. Landsat 7 scenes affected by the Scan Line Corrector failure (after May 2003) were excluded. This dataset accompanies the article “NIMBUS: A multisensor cloud segmentation model for Sentinel-2 and Landsat coastal monitoring using RGB imagery”. Files train.zip val.zip test.zip Format Bands 1–3: RGB Band 4: GT mask (0 = clear sky, 1 = thick cloud, 2 = thin cloud, 3 = cloud shadow)
title: IberCloud-L

summary: What are the capacity limits of a bounded observer’s epistemic activity, and what constructions attain those limits? This technical and philosophical companion connects preservation, acquisition and discovery, construction, certification, adoption, continuation and revision, with resource accounting, self-application and coverage throughout. The full connected capacity characterization remains OPEN. Interim technical revision r7t, 4 November 2026. This corrected successor improves the reader’s guide, lifecycle explanation, prior-work comparisons and model-to-system discussion. It preserves the published finite-Fourier orbit-separating construction with its explicit nonzero-reference condition, arithmetic-cost model and conditioning limits. Orientation is an explanatory atlas, not a proof premise. Exact results, assumptions and review evidence govern mathematical claims. The revision qualifies empirical-verification and identifiability statements by their evidence models; separates expected, probabilistic and worst-case guarantees; and distinguishes imported mathematics from unresolved transfer obligations. Historical cases and dated internal AI-agent trials illustrate the lens without establishing universal performance or research novelty. It separates native builder controls from generated-application behavior, passing local checks from authorized outcomes, and prospective tests from completed observations. Review is internal and AI-assisted, not external peer review or whole-program mathematical acceptance. Earlier versions and dated evidence cutoffs are preserved. This is an explanatory and corrective edition, not a claim that the full research program is complete. The manuscript retains its review-candidate designation. This record contains the manuscript, not a standalone proof-reproduction package.

summary: Proposals document accompanying the talk "Digital therapeutics: state of the art in Italy" (SIFO 2026 National Congress, Rome, 6 November 2026). It is a proposals paper, kept separate from the Supplementary Information of the talk, which contains the data and analyses. Each paragraph is tagged as Data, Analysis or Proposal, so that sourced facts, the author's inferences and the author's opinions can be told apart. The starting point is the "efficacy without use" problem: digital therapeutics (DTx) that work in controlled settings are abandoned early in real life. Trial dropout ranges from about 19% to 48%, real-world abandonment reaches a median of 70% within 100 days, and human contact is the best-documented protective factor, although only as an association. The paper notes that most usage data concern health apps in general, not DTx as defined by ISO/TR 11147:2023, and that we found no post-marketing usage data for DTx. The bill S. 1918, as approved by the Italian Chamber of Deputies on 27 May 2026, defines digital therapies and their assessment, but in our reading it does not mention prescription or dispensation. The step between prescription and intake is therefore undefined. We propose three distinct activities with three actors: prescription (prescriber), dispensation (a health mediator distinct from the prescriber) and intake (patient). We distinguish software and procedural "digital excipients", to be described in HTA dossiers and assessed on use endpoints, separately from the clinical endpoint of the active function. Health mediation comprises five acts: verify, explain, activate, control, and vigilance, delivered at three levels of intensity proportional to risk. We propose the term "dispensazione", with an explicit definition, and discuss its legal risks. As mediator we propose a specialised DTx pharmacist in the pharmaceutical services of the local health authorities, working remote-first from regional or inter-ASL hubs, with in-person dispensation when needed and with other professionals as co-mediators. An illustrative sizing, built on German activation data, suggests that a few dozen full-time pharmacists would suffice in the first years. Evidence for the model is limited: a Danish routine-care programme with psychologist support shows that human mediation is feasible at scale, but not that it improves outcomes. We propose a comparative pilot with retention at 12 weeks as primary endpoint, and state what result would lead to revising or withdrawing the proposal. Conflicts of interest and the use of an AI model (Claude, Anthropic) for analysis and drafting are declared in the document. The Italian version is published on the website of the Associazione TendenzeSaluteSanità.
title: Analysis and Proposal for the Dispensation of Digital Therapeutics in Italy

summary: Source, programs and Lean 4 certificate of the paper Yang–Mills Mass Gap Follows from One Cube, by Deep Bhattacharjee, Ushashi Bhattacharya, James Montgomery Lockwood and Tristan Romanov (Hexagon preprint 2610.00341). The gauge of four-dimensional lattice Yang–Mills theory is fixed on a period-two field of straight lines that meets every plaquette in exactly one link. At fixed lattice spacing this gives a unique free-boundary state, reflection positivity, exponential clustering and an explicit transfer-matrix gap: for SU(2) up to beta_W = 0.348 through plaquette blocks with constants proved by hand, and for SU(3) up to beta_W = 0.52 through plaquette blocks with constants proved by hand, and for every compact simple group G when N|beta| < 2 kappa_G/29, with kappa_G the least Ricci curvature. A Dobrushin–Shlosman condition on one cube of fixed physical size, uniform along the continuum tuning, gives a mass gap in physical units in every continuum limit, also for observables smoothed by the gradient flow; the paper proves what that cube estimate needs and which Osterwalder–Schrader properties a limit of the flowed fields has. Towards the estimate it labels the blocks of Balaban's averages, proves that the weight of bad islands factorises through kernels on the good layers between them with cross-ratios exponentially small in the widths of the layers, gives the explicit coupling past which bad islands and their clusters are rarer than their entropy, and controls one step of the block map on the large fields and on the calm small fields. It also reduces the cube estimate to an averaged condition, proves that this condition descends to block variables and climbs one scale under a split inequality, proves that inequality at strong coupling and on each finite torus, reduces the condition at the coarsest scale to Dobrushin bounds on the single-link coefficients of the laws of the block variables, which one step of the block map contracts and which gauge covariance excludes at weak coupling, and states the conditional chain for every compact simple group. Lean 4 (Mathlib) checks the combinatorics of the line field and the block gauge, the finite arithmetic of the perturbation propositions and the chain of rational bounds of the SU(2) blocks; the ball-arithmetic programs (python-flint), which no proof uses, are included. The averaged covariance of the labels, the effective action across all scales and a nontrivial continuum limit are not proved; the Clay Millennium problem is open. The archive also keeps the sources of two earlier papers of the project in tex/ and strong-coupling/prd/.
title: Yang–Mills Mass Gap Follows from One Cube

summary: This replication package accompanies the paper “Code-to-Prompt-to-Code: An Empirical Study of Prompt Recovery, Adaptation, and Structural Drift.” It contains everything needed to reproduce the study’s results. A Jupyter notebook reproduces the main tables, the statistical tests, and the RQ1 and RQ2 plots. The analysis/ folder contains scripts for the additional analyses (effect of the repair loop, prompt-level measures, change coverage of adapted prompts with bootstrap confidence intervals, a data-leakage check based on git blame , and repository statistics) and for the final versions of the RQ2 figures. Two further scripts recompute the CodeSage similarity scores. The data/ folder contains the 200 sampled real-world Python functions, 8,400 prompt-recovery records (7 information levels, 2 models, 3 repetitions), 2,400 prompt-adaptation records (400 modifications across 6 modification types, 2 prompt-adapting models, 3 repetitions), and precomputed CodeSage similarity scores for both research questions. The figures/ folder holds the generated plots. The README maps each table and figure in the paper to the notebook cell or script that produces it.
title: Replication Package -- Code-to-Prompt-to-Code: An Empirical Study of Prompt Recovery, Adaptation, and Structural Drift

summary: This repository contains the replication package for the paper "What Changes When Generative Artificial Intelligence Enters Project Management? Insights from Software Project Managers", accepted at the XXV Brazilian Symposium on Software Quality (SBQS 2026) . The package includes consolidated qualitative data, the codebook, and category analysis supporting the study of 20 software project managers. All participant-related information was anonymized or sanitized prior to disclosure. The interview materials and qualitative coding artifacts are in Portuguese, the language of data collection.
title: What Changes When Generative Artificial Intelligence Enters Project Management? Insights from Software Project Managers

summary: This study presents the results of portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) analysis of a pale grey-bluish ceramic brush washer. Two measurements were obtained from the vessel: one from the side wall and one from the glazed base. The analytical results demonstrate an exceptionally high degree of compositional consistency between both measurement locations. Major and trace element concentrations are virtually identical, indicating that the vessel is covered by a single homogeneous glaze and shows no evidence of secondary glazing, restoration, or later surface modification. The glaze is characterized by elevated silica and calcium concentrations, a strong predominance of lime over alkali fluxes, extremely low titanium content, negligible lead concentrations, and the complete absence of artificial coloring agents. Comparison with published analytical studies of Southern Song Guan kilns from Jiaotanxiao, Laohudong, and Wansongling demonstrates close correspondence in major technological parameters, including high-calcium glaze chemistry, iron-based coloration, low titanium values, and lead-free high-temperature firing technology. The analytical data define a coherent high-fired lime glaze system colored exclusively by iron and closely aligned with the archaeometric characteristics of Southern Song Guan ware. Keywords: Guan ware, Southern Song Dynasty, brush washer, celadon, XRF analysis, archaeometry, lime glaze, Chinese ceramics, high-fired glaze technology. 1. Introduction Guan ware (官窑) occupies a distinguished position among the imperial ceramic productions of the Southern Song Dynasty. One of the defining technological characteristics of Southern Song Guan ceramics is the use of high-fired lime-rich glazes producing subtle grey-blue, grey-green, and jade-like surface tones. These visual effects were achieved through carefully controlled glaze compositions and reducing firing atmospheres rather than through the addition of artificial pigments. Archaeometric investigations conducted on kiln materials from Jiaotanxiao, Laohudong, and Wansongling have established a characteristic technological profile for Guan glazes, including elevated calcium concentrations, low titanium content, iron-controlled coloration, and the absence of lead-based flux systems. The present study examines the glaze chemistry of a pale grey-bluish brush washer and compares the analytical results with published archaeometric data from Southern Song Guan kiln sites. 2. Description of the Object The investigated object is a glazed ceramic brush washer. Visual examination reveals: a uniform monochrome glaze; pale grey-bluish coloration; absence of painted decoration; absence of localized artificial color effects; soft vitreous surface luster; visually homogeneous glaze coverage across the entire vessel. The glaze extends continuously over both the body and the base of the vessel. The analytical target images demonstrate excellent contact between the instrument window and the glaze surface, resulting in high-quality measurements. 3. Materials and Methods The analysis was conducted using a Geochem (3-Beam) Extra portable X-ray fluorescence spectrometer. Measurement conditions: acquisition time: 30 seconds; non-destructive in situ analysis; Geochem analytical mode. Two analytical locations were examined: ID 1 – Side Wall Glazed side surface of the vessel. ID 2 – Base Glazed lower surface of the vessel. The lightweight-element index (LE) ranged between approximately 45% and 46%, indicating excellent analytical conditions and high confidence in the elemental results. 4. XRF Results Table 1. summary: Nonlinear root-finding, analytic signal extrapolation, and Marchenko inverse scattering share a common mathematical bottleneck: the inversion of ill-posed linear or linearized operators that suffer from spectral clustering, numerical instability, and spurious pole proliferation in unconstrained continuous spaces. Projecting these systems onto the maximal class-number-one Heegner modular curve establishes a unique factorization domain that eliminates fractional holonomy phase slips, preventing branch-cut bifurcations and suppressing spurious pole-zero doublets. Truncating the singular modulus expansion at its principal term provides an analytical starting anchor that strictly satisfies Smale point-estimate convergence criteria, placing the system directly within the quadratic attraction basin and reaching machine precision in a single iteration. In analytic continuation, the modular coordinate under the maximal discriminant is suppressed well below double-precision machine epsilon, truncating out-of-band noise and bypassing the Runge phenomenon without empirical regularization parameters. For high-dimensional networks and discretized scattering kernels, operator preconditioning via Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak Ramanujan graph Laplacians enforces a uniform spectral gap derived from the Deligne bound on Hecke operators. This holds the condition number on the invariant zero-mean subspace to a small, constant bound, ensuring that both the Newton Jacobian update and the Marchenko integral equation converge in very few Krylov iterations regardless of network scale.
title: Arithmetic Operator Inversion: Resolving Nonlinear Root-Finding, Analytic Extrapolation, and Inverse Scattering via Heegner Modular Uniformization and Ramanujan Preconditioning

summary: Audited research compendium supporting the evaluation of Big Five league representation as a candidate squad-composition performance indicator for FIFA World Cup knockout progression from 1998 to 2026. The release contains 1,584 first-knockout starting-eleven records nested within 144 team-tournaments across eight men’s World Cups and 48 national teams. The analytical framework evaluates three linked properties: discrimination between levels of format-harmonised knockout progression; incremental information beyond pre-tournament World Football Elo; and transportability of any increment to World Cup editions and national teams excluded from model estimation. The 1998–2010 historical extension preserves the frozen exposure, outcome and model definitions established for 2014–2026. Historical starter status derives from the Fjelstul World Cup Database and was cross-checked against RSSSF match details. Club affiliation and top-division status were adjudicated using tournament squad records and season-specific domestic-league reference files. The 2014–2026 subset retains the completed provenance audit, including 505 re-checked starter records, 13 starter-name corrections, 45 club-affiliation checks and seven Big Five reclassifications. Analyses include tournament-adjusted ordinal and cut-point models, AICc comparison with Akaike weights, 5,000 national-team cluster-bootstrap samples with bias-corrected and accelerated intervals, leave-one-edition-out validation, leave-one-national-team-out validation, a strict 2026 temporal and tournament-format holdout, and a predictive cluster bootstrap that refits both competing models within every fold and resample. Additional checks address collinearity, edition adjustment and dependence through within-edition permutation testing and an edition-level block bootstrap. Big Five representation was associated with deeper knockout progression before adjustment for Elo, but this association attenuated after adjustment. Model comparisons and held-out evaluations did not establish a stable, transportable increment beyond prior team strength. These findings concern the predictive information provided by current league representation; they do not distinguish the mechanisms through which players enter elite leagues or develop within them. Version 5.2.0 updates presentation and documentation only. Figure 1 presents the relationship between Big Five representation and Elo alongside the four primary ordinal-model estimates. Figure 2 displays the held-out difference in ignorance score between the joint Big Five + Elo model and Elo alone for each World Cup edition, together with the equal-edition mean and its 95% BCa interval. The former supplementary interval figure was removed; its underlying estimates remain available in the deposited machine-readable results. No data, frozen definition, model specification, inferential estimate, predictive score, random seed or substantive conclusion changed from v5.1.0. The estimand is knockout progression conditional on qualification for the knockout stage. These observational data do not identify a causal effect of Big Five employment, estimate the long-term developmental return to elite-league exposure or address group-stage qualification. The compendium includes analytical data, provenance records, analysis code, machine-readable results and publication-ready figures. The derivative dataset is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, with attribution to the Fjelstul World Cup Database.
title: Big Five representation, Elo and FIFA World Cup knockout progression, 1998–2026: audited data and reproducibility materials

summary: EB04119, Golden Gate-compatible lentiviral barcoding vector with mScarlet dropout cassette (10,917 bp). EB04119 is a derivative of pEGZ2 (REF1,2) domesticated for Golden Gate cloning. An internal BsmBI site in the hygromycin cassette was removed by a synonymous substitution (GTC→GTT). A bacterial mScarlet dropout cassette flanked by two outward-facing BsmBI sites was inserted between the WPRE and the bGH polyA signal. The BsmBI sites produce the EMMA position-17 fusion sites GCTC and CGGT (REF 3). summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.

summary: Open-Source Moon: A Technical Framework for Intelligent Development of Extraterrestrial Bodies Based on Sensor Dispersal and Golden Consensus Abstract: The exploration and development of the Moon and other celestial bodies currently depend heavily on State-led, integrated space missions that are costly, slow, and difficult for the public to join. To address this situation, this paper proposes “Open-Source Moon”, a technical framework that applies the open-source philosophy to the intelligent development of extraterrestrial bodies. The framework treats the Moon as a large developer platform that all of humankind can program collectively. Following the progressive principle of “information first, from the outside in, from sensing to action”, it transforms the Moon layer by layer into a “smart planet” that can be programmed as a whole, and it organizes global participation through open-source protocols and the contribution-securing mechanism of “Golden Consensus”: massive numbers of low-cost, standardized micro sensors are first dispersed over the lunar surface to form a distributed sensing network whose nodes are beacons and hotspots; delay-tolerant networking (DTN) and a predictive compensation mechanism then overcome the one-way communication delay of about 1.28 s; and a small-machine cooperation ecosystem, LEGO-style combination of medium-sized machines, and finally unmanned factories and lunar computing carry the staged evolution from sensors to a “smart planet”. Based on the self-similar allocation principle and the Schelling focal point, which secure and incentivize decentralized contributions, a “Golden Consensus” system founded on the golden ratio ( φ ≈ 1.618) is proposed: explorers receive 61.8% of the development-rights return (of which a further 2.8% is set aside as a “common allocation” for public facilities), and 38.2% is designated as socially shared. A model with 880 000 cornerstone nodes is set up, in which a distributed ledger establishes ownership of contributions and keeps tamper-proof records. Verifiable engineering models of network coverage, link budget, energy budget, and delay compensation are established, and the compatibility of this approach with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, as well as the general applicability of extending it to other celestial bodies such as Mercury and Mars, is demonstrated. This study provides a feasible technical route and governance framework for public participation in the development of extraterrestrial bodies. Keywords: Lunar Landing; Human Lunar Landing ; Open-Source Moon; sensor network; smart planet; Golden Consensus; delay-tolerant networking; lunar development; citizen science; Outer Space Treaty; Human Spaceflight 1. Introduction 1.1. Background and Motivation For more than half a century, the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies has taken the form mainly of large, integrated, State-led missions. After Apollo 17 in 1972, crewed spaceflight remained confined to near-Earth orbit for a long time, until Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby (without landing) in April 2026 [1]. On 22 February 2024, the Odysseus lander of Intuitive Machines achieved the first soft landing on the Moon by a commercial spacecraft [2], marking the beginning of the era of commercial lunar landings. However, the development and launch cost of a single mission is still on the order of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of US dollars, and most of the failure risk is concentrated in the powered-descent and landing phases. From the soft landing of Chang’e-3 in 2013 to June 2025, there were 14 soft-landing attempts on the lunar surface worldwide (Table 4): six full successes, three partial successes (in which the attitude or mission capability was impaired after landing), and five failures. According to public reports retrieved for this study, no new lunar landing attempt had occurred

summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.
title: MELITE — Multi-Model Supervised Learning Evaluator

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.

The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule

summary: Replication package of the paper on SpecDetect4ML, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. SpecDetect4ML detects ML code smells in Python ML pipeline code. Each smell is written as a short rule in a declarative DSL, and the rules run on a code property graph (CPG) that links syntax, control flow, data flow, imports, aliases and wrappers across the files of a project.  Requirements: Python 3.11 or newer, packages pinned in requirements.txt. Docker only for the web app. License: the source code of the tool and the scripts is under the MIT license (see LICENSE).
title: SpecDetect4ML: replication package

summary: The calibration and test probabilities of every run of a tabular classification benchmark, released so that prediction sets and their metrics can be recomputed without refitting a model. A conformal set is a function of four arrays: the class probabilities and labels on a calibration split, and the same on a test split. This deposit is those arrays, together with the software that reads them. The benchmark comprises 218 classification datasets and 22 models from four families, among them 13 tabular foundation models, each evaluated with the same ten seeds. Of the 218, 178 are real datasets and 40 are a synthetic block generated for this benchmark; three of the real ones are Bayesian-network resamplings of small classical datasets and are much larger than their seeds; of those, only one has its own seed in the collection, so that pair is not independent of itself while a rank test treats datasets as independent. Dataset size does not indicate provenance: the largest datasets in the collection are real. Coverage is not uniform and the per-model dataset count is reported for every cell. Eleven datasets carry more than ten classes, and the in-context models measured on them cannot enter them: one refuses and names the limit, another builds a ten-output head and fails inside a kernel. That is a capability limit observed on the models that were run rather than a property claimed of the family, and it is not missing work. One foundation model is measured on the original datasets only. Anything computed across models should be computed on a complete submatrix: the datasets on which every model being compared has all ten seeds. The calibration rows are held out of fitting, of tuning, of early stopping and of the in-context data, and each cell records which rows they were. The code that does it is included, with the line of each step documented. Probabilities are float64 and are not rounded: a prediction set is a comparison against a threshold, and a point sitting on that threshold moves if the value it is compared to is shortened. The data are released under CC BY 4.0. The software included in the source archive is released under the MIT licence, as stated by the LICENSE file it contains. The datasets themselves are not redistributed: each cell carries the row indices into its source dataset, and the synthetic datasets regenerate from their seeds with an included script. Model weights are not redistributed; every checkpoint is named in the model table. Version 1.2.0 adds the runs completed after version 1.1.0 and changes or removes nothing in it. Three new shards (cells-011 to cells-013, 2.02 GB) hold 311 further cells; index.parquet now lists all 46,182 cells and manifest_1016.parquet is their manifest. The files prefixed blocks_1016__ recompute the two blocks outside the main comparison on the completed runs, with the pipeline that produced the article's tables: the large-dataset block on 49 datasets and 21 models (42 in version 1.1.0) and the many-class block on 11 datasets and 7 models (5 in version 1.1.0). The main block of 113 real datasets and 22 models is unchanged. CHANGELOG.md lists what is added and the pairs that are still missing, with the reason for each.
title: TabSets: calibration and test probabilities for set-valued evaluation of tabular classifiers

summary: Replication data for: Cho, F. H. T., Rhodes, J. R., Maron, M., Lunney, D., Iftekhar, M. S., McIlwee, A., & Williams, B. A. (forthcoming).  Leakage effects of establishing protected areas in multi-use forests . This dataset contains the pre-computed data files needed to reproduce all figures and summary tables in the paper. The study estimates the causal effect of New South Wales (NSW) state forest revocations on deforestation in adjacent areas using a Before–After Control–Impact (BACI) design with propensity-score matching. Two leakage channels are estimated: (1) leakage to private land within 10 km of a revoked state forest, and (2) leakage to neighbouring state forests within 10 km. Contents: processed_data_for_plotting.RData  — all model estimates, Average Marginal Effects (AME), matched pair summaries, and spatial objects required to reproduce Figures 1–6 (103 MB) state_forests_revoked_update.gpkg  — NSW state forest polygons with revocation year and woody vegetation attributes focal_sf_year.gpkg  — focal state forest polygons aggregated by revocation year nsw_grid_points.parquet  — NSW 10 km regular grid cell centroids (712,714 cells; 1.2 GB) matching_data/parquet/  — pixel-level covariate and deforestation panel for all NSW grid cells, split across 1,000 Parquet files The R code for full replication is available at Github . To reproduce all figures, download the data files, place them in the  data/  subdirectory of the code repository, and run  scripts/05_replicate_figures.R with R ≥ 4.2.
title: Replication data: Leakage effects of establishing protected areas in multi-use forests in NSW, Australia

summary: Dataset description This dataset provides gap-filled daily, high-resolution binary snow cover maps for 12 eddy-covariance stations within the FLUXNET, ICOS, and i-Box networks distributed across the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps. The maps were generated to characterize surface snow conditions within the source areas of eddy-covariance measurements for the updated analysis of Scheidt et al. (2026). The dataset was specifically used to determine whether the area enclosed by a station’s 80% flux-footprint contour was snow covered and to calculate the snow-cover fraction (SCF) within that footprint. Footprint-scale SCF can be calculated from the maps as the proportion of valid pixels within the footprint classified as snow covered. The data cover the following eddy-covariance sites for the hydrological years (1 st October - 30 th September) from 2013/14 to 2023/24: Alp Weissenstein (CH-Aws), Switzerland Col du Lautaret (FR-CLt), France Früebüel (CH-Fru), Switzerland Monte Bondone (IT-MBo), Italy Mazia Pasture (IT-MtP), Italy Neustift (AT-Neu), Austria Nivolet (IT-NiG), Italy Torgnon (IT-Tor), Italy The i-Box observational network in the Inn Valley, Austria, comprising the Eggen (CS-SF1), Kolsass (CS-VF0), Hochhäuser (CS-NF27), and Weerberg (CS-NF10) stations For each station outside the i-Box network, the NetCDF files cover a 15 km × 15 km square centered on the station. Because the four i-Box stations are located close to one another, they are represented by a common 20 km × 20 km domain centered on the station cluster. The maps have a spatial resolution of 50 m and are provided in the WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N coordinate reference system (EPSG:32632). Files are organized by site and hydrological year. The binary snow cover condition variable represents daily snow-cover conditions, while the reconstruction_method variable distinguishes pixels obtained from high-resolution satellite observations from pixels reconstructed by the gap-filling procedure. High-resolution snow cover fraction maps were derived from Sentinel-2 MSI and Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 OLI imagery using SnowFLAKES ( Snow extent from applying a Flexible Learning Algorithm using KErnel-based Spectral unmixing ) at a resolution of 50m. SnowFLAKES is an unsupervised, image-adaptive snow-mapping approach developed for mountainous terrain and challenging observation conditions, including topographic shadows and variable illumination. The processing follows the approach described by Barella et al. (2022). Daily, spatially complete maps were generated by combining the available high-resolution snow observations with daily, lower-resolution MODIS SCF from the MOD10A1 product (Hall and Riggs, 2021). Gap filling and spatial downscaling were performed using an implementation adapted from the hierarchical multiresolution data-fusion method proposed by Premier et al. (2021). The approach uses spatial patterns learned from available optical observations to reconstruct snow-cover conditions on days without usable high-resolution satellite imagery. The resulting product represents daily binary snow presence at high spatial resolution. Raw Sentinel-2, Landsat, and MODIS imagery, eddy-covariance measurements, and flux footprint polygons are not included in this archive. The archive also includes an interactive Python viewer for the daily *_SC_GAM.nc snow-cover products. It can display snow-cover classes and reconstruction provenance over time, with station locations shown for context. Setup instructions and examples are provided in the README. NetCDF structure and value conventions For each site and hydrological year a NetCDF product is provided. Files ending in _SC_GAM.nc contain the 50 m high-resolution product. The main variable,  binary_snow_cover_condition (time, y, x) , has units of percent and represents binary snow presence: 0 denotes snow-free ground and 100 denotes snow-covered ground. summary: Microbiome Repo — data package v1.29.0 (2026-11-02) One catalog, two tiers, all ages. The catalog tables ( catalog_* ) are the curated tier: human-associated microbial communities sequenced by shotgun DNA or RNA sequencing, from every body site and at every age — 5,053 projects, 810,820 samples, 4,789,110 sample × field values — with body site, age at collection, sex, BMI, country, health condition (controlled vocabulary), antibiotic exposure, subject and timepoint recovered from archive attributes (R1), supplementary tables (R2), paper full text (R3) and abstracts (R4); every value carries a verbatim evidence quote (≤ 12 words), a labelled source, a route and a confidence. Each run is labelled DNA or RNA ( catalog_runs.nucleic_acid ), each sample says which data sets it has ( has_dna , has_rna ), and each project carries the nucleic acid of its data sets ( catalog_studies.nucleic_acid ). Coverage over all catalog samples: age 24%, sex 29%, country 89%, health condition 43%, antibiotic exposure 16%. The registry tables ( registry_* ) list every screened public study in ENA/SRA/DDBJ with a human-associated metagenome signal — 64,369 studies — with archive-only classification (host, UBERON-anchored body sites, life stages, assay, access) and the harvested BioSample tier (637,397 BioSamples with normalised site / age / sex / country). Start here. catalog_studies.parquet (one row per project: body sites, DNA / RNA, papers, methods and setting read from the paper, per-field coverage, age-category and health-condition mix, curated depth) → catalog_sample_metadata_wide.parquet (one row per sample: every field with __route / __confidence , body_site_code , age_category + basis, has_dna / has_rna ) → catalog_sample_determinations.parquet (the evidence behind every value) and catalog_runs.parquet (every run). registry_studies.parquet is the registry; registry_runs_v1.29.0.parquet (every screened run) ships as a GitHub Release asset. Infant extension. The 370 infant gut projects carry a deeper infant-field curation (delivery mode, feeding mode, preterm status, gestational age, birth weight, maternal antibiotics, probiotics, HMO supplementation, NEC). Those rows are present in the catalog_* tables ( curated_source = infant_catalog ; infant_scope = true selects them: 66,355 samples) and the deep tables ( sample_metadata_wide , sample_determinations , study_metadata_wide , cohorts , universe_studies_all , sandpiper_* , …) are in the package as well. summary: Validation dataset of the H5MD biophysics module, a metadata schema that stores the topology, force field, MD parameters, selection groups and observables of a molecular dynamics simulation together with its trajectory in one H5MD (HDF5) file. It accompanies the paper A Hierarchical Metadata Schema for Self-Contained Molecular Dynamics Trajectory Archives . validation_systems.zip contains the GROMACS inputs of the 58 chemical systems used in the paper's technical validation, reduced to what grompp needs: topology, force field, coordinates or run input, index groups and MD parameters. The systems range from 711 to 1,066,628 particles, cover AMBER, CHARMM, GROMOS, OPLS-AA and MARTINI force fields, and come in six groups by origin: self_generated (8): built with GROMACS from PDB entries bena (10): sessions of the Bena dataset ( 10.5281/zenodo.17632513 ) jcp_benchmark (6): GROMACS benchmark systems ( 10.5281/zenodo.3893789 ) hexabc (8): hexABC nucleic-acid and protein–nucleic-acid deposits from MDposit memprotmd (6): MemProtMD membrane proteins, atomistic and coarse-grained misato (20): MISATO protein–ligand complexes ( 10.5281/zenodo.7711953 ) Run under 23 simulation protocols, these inputs give the 379 reference files of the validation. The files can be regenerated with the validation scripts ( github.com/miemiemmmm/h5md-biophysics-validation ) and the GROMACS implementation published with the paper. Each group's MANIFEST.md credits its source and states the changes made; provenance/ holds the scripts that selected and prepared the systems. Four of the reference files are included as examples, each a short trajectory with the full metadata. They also serve as test data for the validator in gitlab.com/gromacs/h5md-biophysics : hexabc_a001u2_rna_protein__nvt-vrescale.h5md bench_villin__tcoupl-multigroup.h5md bench_villin__sd-langevin.h5md bench_villin__selection-noncontiguous.h5md

summary: Open-Source Moon: A Technical Framework for Intelligent Development of Extraterrestrial Bodies Based on Sensor Dispersal and Golden Consensus Abstract: The exploration and development of the Moon and other celestial bodies currently depend heavily on State-led, integrated space missions that are costly, slow, and difficult for the public to join. To address this situation, this paper proposes “Open-Source Moon”, a technical framework that applies the open-source philosophy to the intelligent development of extraterrestrial bodies. The framework treats the Moon as a large developer platform that all of humankind can program collectively. Following the progressive principle of “information first, from the outside in, from sensing to action”, it transforms the Moon layer by layer into a “smart planet” that can be programmed as a whole, and it organizes global participation through open-source protocols and the contribution-securing mechanism of “Golden Consensus”: massive numbers of low-cost, standardized micro sensors are first dispersed over the lunar surface to form a distributed sensing network whose nodes are beacons and hotspots; delay-tolerant networking (DTN) and a predictive compensation mechanism then overcome the one-way communication delay of about 1.28 s; and a small-machine cooperation ecosystem, LEGO-style combination of medium-sized machines, and finally unmanned factories and lunar computing carry the staged evolution from sensors to a “smart planet”. Based on the self-similar allocation principle and the Schelling focal point, which secure and incentivize decentralized contributions, a “Golden Consensus” system founded on the golden ratio ( φ ≈ 1.618) is proposed: explorers receive 61.8% of the development-rights return (of which a further 2.8% is set aside as a “common allocation” for public facilities), and 38.2% is designated as socially shared. A model with 880 000 cornerstone nodes is set up, in which a distributed ledger establishes ownership of contributions and keeps tamper-proof records. Verifiable engineering models of network coverage, link budget, energy budget, and delay compensation are established, and the compatibility of this approach with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, as well as the general applicability of extending it to other celestial bodies such as Mercury and Mars, is demonstrated. This study provides a feasible technical route and governance framework for public participation in the development of extraterrestrial bodies. Keywords: Lunar Landing; Human Lunar Landing ; Open-Source Moon; sensor network; smart planet; Golden Consensus; delay-tolerant networking; lunar development; citizen science; Outer Space Treaty; Human Spaceflight 1. Introduction 1.1. Background and Motivation For more than half a century, the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies has taken the form mainly of large, integrated, State-led missions. After Apollo 17 in 1972, crewed spaceflight remained confined to near-Earth orbit for a long time, until Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby (without landing) in April 2026 [1]. On 22 February 2024, the Odysseus lander of Intuitive Machines achieved the first soft landing on the Moon by a commercial spacecraft [2], marking the beginning of the era of commercial lunar landings. However, the development and launch cost of a single mission is still on the order of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of US dollars, and most of the failure risk is concentrated in the powered-descent and landing phases. From the soft landing of Chang’e-3 in 2013 to June 2025, there were 14 soft-landing attempts on the lunar surface worldwide (Table 4): six full successes, three partial successes (in which the attitude or mission capability was impaired after landing), and five failures. summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.
title: MELITE — Multi-Model Supervised Learning Evaluator

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule

summary: 本資料集整理58,269筆臺灣公共圖書館來源觀測,參照年涵蓋1991–2026,逐筆保留官方URL、原件雜湊、頁表及儲存格定位、原始值、期間、單位、母體與來源版本。v0.9.2新增2004年圖書館年鑑統計章三表的完整公共館相關子群,含16個實體格與24筆來源觀測。提供同內容的CSV、JSONL與SQLite及完整ZIP,供資料檢索、來源對照與保留原統計口徑的研究。不同出版版本、地域層級與年/月口徑並存,並非連續一致的全國縣市年度面板,不能整表加總為館數;人工抽樣核讀與雙校尚未完成。 This dataset compiles 58,269 source observations of Taiwan public-library statistics with reference years spanning 1991–2026. Each observation retains an official URL, original-file hash, page/table/cell locator, raw value, period, unit, population and source version. Version 0.9.2 adds the complete selected public-library subsets from three tables reporting 2004 statistics: 16 physical cells and 24 source observations. Equivalent CSV, JSONL and SQLite representations and a complete ZIP support discovery, source comparison and research that preserves statistical definitions. Publication versions, geographic levels and annual/monthly definitions coexist. The data are not a complete harmonized national county-year panel and must not be summed wholesale as library counts. Human sample reading and double collation remain incomplete.

summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.
title: BasisSimulator.jl: Open-source polychromatic CT simulation with a GPU-portable reconstruction stack

summary: The stability of the 861-node toroidal vorton lattice is established by five mutually reinforcing principles that eliminate arbitrary cutoffs and prevent turbulent mode decay: Solenoidal Dipole Dynamics: Three-dimensional vorton dipoles maintain exact incompressibility off their singular cores without artificial smoothing. Reconnection events introduce singular inviscid dissipation, providing an irreversible non-Hamiltonian drain that prevents high-frequency turbulent blow-ups. Toroidal Regularization: Compactification onto a flat two-torus eliminates boundary losses and forces a zero Euler characteristic. This guarantees an unfrustrated, globally defect-free six-fold coordination while mapping infinite Biot–Savart dipole sums into an exact Weierstrass elliptic function. Heegner Arithmetic Firewall: The lattice modulus is locked to the terminal class-number-one imaginary quadratic field with discriminant negative 163. Because no unramified abelian extensions exist, continuous shear deformations are forbidden by an arithmetic energy barrier. Johnson Manifold Spectral Gap: The 861 nodes map isomorphically to the Johnson graph J(42, 2), producing an exact integer Laplacian Fiedler gap of 42 with a 41-fold degeneracy. This multiplicity mirrors Euler's maximal prime-generating constant, creating a spectral mass barrier that suppresses low-frequency wave excitations. Dedekind Casimir Tension: Partitioning the 861 nodes across a 72-fold modular gear symmetry leaves a structural defect of negative one twenty-fourth, exactly matching the modular weight of the Dedekind eta function. This generates an intrinsic topological tension that stabilizes inter-vorton spacing against both expansion and collapse.
title: Topological and Arithmetic Rigidity of the 861-Node Vorton Lattice on the Two-Torus

summary: This release brings spatially varying particulate media to Eradiate: aerosol and cloud fields can now vary per voxel, with particle properties interpolated over particle size distribution parameters (new ParticleMSComponent ) or other state variables such as relative humidity (new ParticleStateComponent ). To support this, the aerosol data format is generalized to the Prt family of particle radiative property formats, and a new Ppr format describes particle profiles. In CKD mode, the sample count set by Measure.spp is now distributed across spectral loop iterations according to their contribution to the final result, and variances use the unbiased estimator. The kernel is upgraded to v0.6.0 (based on Mitsuba v3.9.1), which adds Python 3.14 support and drops Python 3.9 and macOS x64 support. The gecko and komodo monochromatic absorption databases are updated to version 2. Testing infrastructure and the development environment are also substantially reworked. Most renamed components, fields and functions remain available with a deprecation warning until v2.0.0. Deprecation warnings are now displayed by default. The following changes may require action: Use Python 3.10 or later. On Intel Macs, stay on v1.2.x. Download the updated absorption databases: eradiate data install gecko and/or eradiate data install komodo . In CKD mode, expect different noise levels at a given spp : per-g-point and per-bin sample counts are no longer equal. spp must now be at least spp_min (default: 2) per g-point, or a ValueError is raised. To restore the v1.2 behaviour, set spp_allocation="uniform" on the measure, or sample_allocation = "uniform" in the configuration file. Variances are now unbiased and NaN where fewer than 2 samples were taken. Regression thresholds based on variance may need adjustment. Replace ParticleLayer with ParticleOTComponent (the Python name is removed; the "particle_layer" dictionary type is still accepted), and HeterogeneousAtmosphere(particle_layers=...) with particle_components=... . Replace aer_core_v2 datasets and helpers with their prt_core_v1 counterparts, and load_aerosol_libradtran() with libradtran_to_prt . AbstractHeterogeneousAtmosphere.eval_radprops output now has (x_cell, y_cell, z_layer) dimensions; select x_cell=0, y_cell=0 (or squeeze() ) to recover 1D profiles. Replace eradiate.test_tools imports with eradiate.testing , and the --update-references pytest flag with --force-regen . Code calling {func} .mi_render directly must unpack (bitmap, spp) pairs. Test suites that turn warnings into errors will now fail on Eradiate deprecation warnings: these are now FutureWarning s. » Detailed change log «

summary: This record contains the Python code and the reference outputs for the manuscript *How much can a bonus–malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating* by Wei Zhu (University of Groningen).   The code treats a bonus–malus system as a finite-state estimator of a policyholder's claim propensity, evaluated by Norberg's credibility criterion. It computes the share of the variance of the claim propensity explained by no-claim discounts, −1/+m scales and hidden-counter scales as the number of classes grows; benchmarks for any rule with a given number of memory states (optimisation over tilted binomial and multinomial laws, exhaustive and heuristic search over deterministic machines, the van Trees lower bound); the evaluation of fourteen historical bonus–malus scales in the long run, at finite policy ages and with one premium scale for all ages; out-of-sample tests and a segmented-tariff analysis on a public French motor panel (1999–2007); and checks against the published tables of Norberg (1976) and Borgan, Hoem and Norberg (1981).   README.md maps every table and result of the paper to the script that produces it. The French motor data (CASdatasets, fremotor2/3/4freq9907b) are public and are not included; data/README.md lists the files and their SHA-256 checksums. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, mpmath, rdata and xarray.   Version 1.1.0 accompanies the version of the manuscript submitted to the Annals of Actuarial Science: flat layout (code/, results/), three scripts added for the revised manuscript (brier_translation.py, design_levers.py, det_exhaustive_reducible.py), a replication script run_all.py, and a README mapped to the current numbering of tables, sections and propositions. The computations of the scripts in version 1.0.0 are unchanged.

summary: This package reproduces all tables and figures of the article “Completing Ecosystem Knowledge Graphs: Few-Shot Learning with Calibrated Rules and the Governance of Innovative Start-ups”. The article builds LUCE-KG, an ontology-rich knowledge graph of 15,493 Italian innovative start-ups and SMEs and 25,982 persons. It proposes CRML, a few-shot learner whose predictions are explained by rules with empirical-Bayes calibrated confidences, and tests it on four graphs (FB15k-237, CoDEx-M, NELL-One and LUCE-KG). It then analyses 11,764 firm-years with panel estimators, clustering and explained machine-learning models. Contents code/ : the full pipeline, from graph construction through few-shot completion, baselines (MetaR, TransE, AnyBURL, LLM re-ranking), econometrics, clustering and machine learning, to the build of the manuscript; config/ : few-shot splits, fold assignments, selected hyperparameters and the LUCE-KG ontology; results/ : aggregated results from which every table is built; data_open/ : open-data extracts of the Italian register of innovative start-ups and SMEs (July 2026); README.md with the order of execution, and requirements.txt with software versions. Data not included. Officer and financial records from AIDA (Bureau van Dijk) are licensed and contain personal data, so they are not redistributed. Licensed users can rebuild every input with the scripts provided. The public benchmarks are available from their original sources. Environment. CPU only (2 cores, 8 GB RAM), Python 3.13; the full pipeline takes about 40 CPU-hours. Funding. Project “LUtech Campus Ecosystem—LUCE” (Project Code 22ROJB5), Puglia Region, Program Agreement (Contratto di Programma).

summary: Unlike prostate cancer, where PSA anchors screening, colorectal cancer has no circulating protein with comparable discriUnlike prostate cancer, where PSA anchors screening, colorectal cancer has no circulating protein with comparable discrimination, and CEA is used for monitoring rather than detection. Whether the circulating proteins that precede a colorectal cancer diagnosis are the same as those that precede death from colorectal cancer has not been examined across the plasma proteome with time-to-event methods. Methods.In 52{,}752 participants of the UK Biobank Olink proteomics subcohort without colorectal cancer at baseline, we screened 2{,}920 proteins against incident colorectal cancer (cancer registry, ICD-10 C18 to C20; 699 events) and death from colorectal cancer (underlying cause C18 to C20; 230 deaths) over a median follow-up of 13.2 and 15.3 years. Each protein was residualized on age and sex and ranked by Harrell's concordance ($C^*$)\footnote{$C^*$ denotes Harrell's concordance statistic for censored time-to-event data: the probability that, of two participants whose order of events is known, the one with the earlier event has the higher score.}. Endpoint-specific Cox panels (Detection, Lethality), a reference model of age, sex and the leading shared protein, stability-selected full-proteome models, a four-gate discovery against CEACAM5 (CEA) and 25 clinical covariates, and a cross-cancer test against prostate and lung cancer models were evaluated by nested cross-validation. The screen was repeated with a flexible age-by-sex adjustment. Findings. No protein dominated either endpoint, and none reached $C^* = 0.60$. Seven of the ten leading proteins were shared between the two endpoints. Two of the leading proteins, RLN1 (first for mortality, $C^* = 0.590$) and RLN2, ranked high only because a linear age adjustment did not follow their steep decline with age in women; with a flexible adjustment they fell out of the leading proteins and carried no weight beside age and sex. In the flexible screen, six of the ten leading proteins were shared (REG4, CRYBB2, KRT19, TFF2, POF1B, GDF15). Age and sex alone reached nested $C^* = 0.666$ for incidence and 0.671 for mortality. The Detection panel reached 0.672 and 0.690, the Lethality panel 0.679 and 0.685. The Lethality panel did not predict death better than the Detection panel (difference $-0.005$, 95\% CI $-0.023$ to $+0.014$), and on incidence it was slightly ahead ($+0.007$). Over age and sex, the panels gained between $+0.005$ and $+0.019$; only the Lethality panel on incidence was significant ($+0.013$, $+0.004$ to $+0.022$). CEACAM5 alone reached 0.553 and 0.590, and age, sex and CEACAM5 0.670 and 0.682. Full-proteome models were below the panels (0.653 and 0.660); the mortality model kept three stable proteins, and none in three of five training folds. The panels and the reference model were calibrated in the large on both endpoints (observed to expected 0.961 to 0.985). nterpretation. The circulating proteins that rank highest years before a colorectal cancer diagnosis also rank highest before death from it, and a panel selected for diagnosis predicts death as well as a panel selected for death. Unlike prostate cancer, colorectal cancer shows largely shared leading proteins for the two endpoints; as in prostate cancer, no lethality-specific model survived nested validation. The proteomic models discriminate modestly and add little to age and sex. A linear age adjustment can promote proteins with sex-specific age patterns to the top of a residualized screen; such screens should be checked with a flexible adjustment and against Cox models with age and sex. The panels are provided with full coefficients for external validation.

The package contains the PLEDGE implementation (LG-ABE on BLS12-381, threshold key-share services, FHIR Consent compiler, Hyperledger Fabric chaincode and gateway), re-implementations of three baseline systems, the attack suite, the Tamarin models, all benchmark scripts and the raw results reported in the paper.

summary: What are the capacity limits of a bounded observer’s epistemic activity, and what constructions attain those limits? This technical and philosophical companion connects preservation, acquisition and discovery, construction, certification, adoption, continuation and revision, with resource accounting, self-application and coverage throughout. The full connected capacity characterization remains OPEN. Interim technical revision r7t, 4 November 2026. This corrected successor improves the reader’s guide, lifecycle explanation, prior-work comparisons and model-to-system discussion. It preserves the published finite-Fourier orbit-separating construction with its explicit nonzero-reference condition, arithmetic-cost model and conditioning limits. Orientation is an explanatory atlas, not a proof premise. Exact results, assumptions and review evidence govern mathematical claims. The revision qualifies empirical-verification and identifiability statements by their evidence models; separates expected, probabilistic and worst-case guarantees; and distinguishes imported mathematics from unresolved transfer obligations. Historical cases and dated internal AI-agent trials illustrate the lens without establishing universal performance or research novelty. It separates native builder controls from generated-application behavior, passing local checks from authorized outcomes, and prospective tests from completed observations. Review is internal and AI-assisted, not external peer review or whole-program mathematical acceptance. Earlier versions and dated evidence cutoffs are preserved. This is an explanatory and corrective edition, not a claim that the full research program is complete. The manuscript retains its review-candidate designation. This record contains the manuscript, not a standalone proof-reproduction package.
title: The Missing Distinction: The Connected Capacity of a Bounded Observer
