summary: Audited research compendium supporting the evaluation of Big Five league representation as a candidate squad-composition performance indicator for FIFA World Cup knockout progression from 1998 to 2026. The release contains 1,584 first-knockout starting-eleven records nested within 144 team-tournaments across eight men’s World Cups and 48 national teams. The analytical framework evaluates three linked properties: discrimination between levels of format-harmonised knockout progression; incremental information beyond pre-tournament World Football Elo; and transportability of any increment to World Cup editions and national teams excluded from model estimation. The 1998–2010 historical extension preserves the frozen exposure, outcome and model definitions established for 2014–2026. Historical starter status derives from the Fjelstul World Cup Database and was cross-checked against RSSSF match details. Club affiliation and top-division status were adjudicated using tournament squad records and season-specific domestic-league reference files. The 2014–2026 subset retains the completed provenance audit, including 505 re-checked starter records, 13 starter-name corrections, 45 club-affiliation checks and seven Big Five reclassifications. Analyses include tournament-adjusted ordinal and cut-point models, AICc comparison with Akaike weights, 5,000 national-team cluster-bootstrap samples with bias-corrected and accelerated intervals, leave-one-edition-out validation, leave-one-national-team-out validation, a strict 2026 temporal and tournament-format holdout, and a predictive cluster bootstrap that refits both competing models within every fold and resample. Additional checks address collinearity, edition adjustment and dependence through within-edition permutation testing and an edition-level block bootstrap. Big Five representation was associated with deeper knockout progression before adjustment for Elo, but this association attenuated after adjustment. Model comparisons and held-out evaluations did not establish a stable, transportable increment beyond prior team strength. These findings concern the predictive information provided by current league representation; they do not distinguish the mechanisms through which players enter elite leagues or develop within them. Version 5.2.0 updates presentation and documentation only. Figure 1 presents the relationship between Big Five representation and Elo alongside the four primary ordinal-model estimates. Figure 2 displays the held-out difference in ignorance score between the joint Big Five + Elo model and Elo alone for each World Cup edition, together with the equal-edition mean and its 95% BCa interval. The former supplementary interval figure was removed; its underlying estimates remain available in the deposited machine-readable results. No data, frozen definition, model specification, inferential estimate, predictive score, random seed or substantive conclusion changed from v5.1.0. The estimand is knockout progression conditional on qualification for the knockout stage. These observational data do not identify a causal effect of Big Five employment, estimate the long-term developmental return to elite-league exposure or address group-stage qualification. The compendium includes analytical data, provenance records, analysis code, machine-readable results and publication-ready figures. The derivative dataset is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, with attribution to the Fjelstul World Cup Database.
title: Big Five representation, Elo and FIFA World Cup knockout progression, 1998–2026: audited data and reproducibility materials

summary: EB04119, Golden Gate-compatible lentiviral barcoding vector with mScarlet dropout cassette (10,917 bp). EB04119 is a derivative of pEGZ2 (REF1,2) domesticated for Golden Gate cloning. An internal BsmBI site in the hygromycin cassette was removed by a synonymous substitution (GTC→GTT). A bacterial mScarlet dropout cassette flanked by two outward-facing BsmBI sites was inserted between the WPRE and the bGH polyA signal. The BsmBI sites produce the EMMA position-17 fusion sites GCTC and CGGT (REF 3). The vector was then reassembled from five PCR fragments by Golden Gate with PaqCI to add a sequencing-primer binding site; the final vector contains no PaqCI sites. The final construct was sequence-verified. This record contains the vector with the dropout cassette. Barcodes are inserted by a second Golden Gate reaction with BsmBI and annealed oligonucleotides, which replaces the cassette (transformants with the barcode are white, those with the cassette red). The barcode (42 nt) has seven blocks of three random nucleotides alternating with constant sequences (21 random positions; theoretical diversity 4.4 × 10¹²). The barcoded product is 9,951 bp.  EB04120, sequence-verified barcoded lentiviral vector derived from EB04119 (9,951 bp). EB04120 is an example of a final barcoded vector produced from EB04119 (this record) by Golden Gate cloning with BsmBI and annealed barcoded oligonucleotides, which replaces the mScarlet dropout cassette with a 42 nt barcode insert. The insert lies between the WPRE (positions 1181–1769) and the bGH polyA signal (from position 1834), flanked by the EMMA position-17 overhangs GCTC (1784–1787) and CGGT (1830–1833), both given 5′→3′ on the top strand. The barcode (positions 1788–1829, top strand: AGTCAGTGAGTTCGTACTATGCTCTTCAGGTATGACTAAGAG) is one clone from the semi-random barcode design: seven blocks of three random nucleotides alternating with seven constant trinucleotides (21 random positions; theoretical diversity 4.4 × 10¹²). In this file the barcode is on the reverse strand, so its constants (CTC, GTC, CCT, GAG, AGT, AAC, CTG) read as their reverse complements. The sequence contains no BsmBI or PaqCI sites. The whole plasmid was sequence-verified . Used in"Barcoded-Plasmid DNA library construction for recording cell lineage tracing enabled by a Scalable and modular Biofoundry-based Automated Robotic Pipeline" as an example of a library member. EB01447, earlier-generation lentiviral barcoding vector (9,925 bp). This sequence was used for the manual plasmid extractions in "Barcoded-Plasmid DNA library construction for recording cell lineage tracing enabled by a Scalable and modular Biofoundry-based Automated Robotic Pipeline" as a comparison arm for the automated extraction. It is a barcoded derivative of a domesticated, Golden Gate-compatible version of pEGZ2 ((REF1,2) and contains no BsmBI or PaqCI sites. The vector was verified by sequencing. The 42 nt barcode region has the same design as in EB04119: seven random NNN blocks alternating with constant sequences (21 random positions). Here the barcode lies downstream of EGFP and upstream of the WPRE, whereas in the EB04119-derived barcoded vectors (9,951 bp) it lies between the WPRE and the bGH polyA signal.    1.Wojtowicz, E. et al. Panhematopoietic RNA barcoding enables kinetic measurements of nucleate and anucleate lineages and the activation of myeloid clones following acute platelet depletion.  Genome Biology 24 (06/27/2023). https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-023-02976-z 2.Belderbos, M. title: Golden Gate compatible plasmid for lineage tracing in mammalian systems

summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.
title: MELITE — Multi-Model Supervised Learning Evaluator

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule

Each observation retains an official URL, original-file hash, page/table/cell locator, raw value, period, unit, population and source version. Version 0.9.2 adds the complete selected public-library subsets from three tables reporting 2004 statistics: 16 physical cells and 24 source observations. Equivalent CSV, JSONL and SQLite representations and a complete ZIP support discovery, source comparison and research that preserves statistical definitions. Publication versions, geographic levels and annual/monthly definitions coexist. The data are not a complete harmonized national county-year panel and must not be summed wholesale as library counts. Human sample reading and double collation remain incomplete.
title: 臺灣公共圖書館跨年度統計 / Taiwan Public Library Statistics

summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.
title: BasisSimulator.jl: Open-source polychromatic CT simulation with a GPU-portable reconstruction stack

summary: The stability of the 861-node toroidal vorton lattice is established by five mutually reinforcing principles that eliminate arbitrary cutoffs and prevent turbulent mode decay: Solenoidal Dipole Dynamics: Three-dimensional vorton dipoles maintain exact incompressibility off their singular cores without artificial smoothing. Reconnection events introduce singular inviscid dissipation, providing an irreversible non-Hamiltonian drain that prevents high-frequency turbulent blow-ups. Toroidal Regularization: Compactification onto a flat two-torus eliminates boundary losses and forces a zero Euler characteristic. This guarantees an unfrustrated, globally defect-free six-fold coordination while mapping infinite Biot–Savart dipole sums into an exact Weierstrass elliptic function. Heegner Arithmetic Firewall: The lattice modulus is locked to the terminal class-number-one imaginary quadratic field with discriminant negative 163. Because no unramified abelian extensions exist, continuous shear deformations are forbidden by an arithmetic energy barrier. Johnson Manifold Spectral Gap: The 861 nodes map isomorphically to the Johnson graph J(42, 2), producing an exact integer Laplacian Fiedler gap of 42 with a 41-fold degeneracy. This multiplicity mirrors Euler's maximal prime-generating constant, creating a spectral mass barrier that suppresses low-frequency wave excitations. Dedekind Casimir Tension: Partitioning the 861 nodes across a 72-fold modular gear symmetry leaves a structural defect of negative one twenty-fourth, exactly matching the modular weight of the Dedekind eta function. This generates an intrinsic topological tension that stabilizes inter-vorton spacing against both expansion and collapse.
title: Topological and Arithmetic Rigidity of the 861-Node Vorton Lattice on the Two-Torus

summary: Flow matching models have emerged as a dominant paradigm for generative posterior sampling in imaging inverse problems. Existing solvers follow two distinct lines of work: trajectory-space methods, which refine sampling dynamics from random initial noise, and source-space methods, which optimize the initial noise itself. While most prior work treats these as independent design choices, we show that they are inherently coupled. We derive a unified stability bound that links initialization proximity and cumulative sampling stochasticity through a multiplicative envelope, complemented by two empirical observations. First, we identify a sufficiency regime in which a moderately optimized proximal source initialization is enough to attain the performance plateau, rendering exhaustive source-space optimization unnecessary. Second, this initial advantage is fragile: it is eroded by excessive stochasticity accumulation during guided sampling, necessitating a mechanism that bounds the cumulative noise injection. These findings motivate FLINT, a two-stage framework that operationalizes this coupling. FLINT establishes a high-fidelity starting point via a manifold-constrained proximal objective in only a few iterations, then performs guided sampling under a bounded stochasticity schedule that helps prevent erasure of the initialization advantage. Across diverse inverse problems, FLINT delivers state of the art perceptual quality and competitive distortion metrics while maintaining superior computational efficiency.
title: FLINT: Coupling Proximal Initialization and Bounded Stochasticity for Flow-Matching Inverse Problems

summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.

summary: This record contains the reproducibility materials for a reanalysis of published bearing-capacitance measurements. No new experimental measurements were collected. The materials support controlled comparisons of capacitance-side and force-output calibration using one or two target labels, including specimen-held-out source fits, cross-condition tests, capacitance-free controls, calibration-choice sensitivity and numerical checks. Complete adverse, null and non-evaluable results are retained. Supplementary_cross_conditions.zip is the canonical cross-condition mean-capacitance analysis. It includes screening records, protocols and amendments, forward-response caches, predictions, diagnostics and cached replay scripts. The archive includes 1868 operationally qualified flag-0/1 mean records, of which 1213 are flag 0, from six types and 18 archive specimen identifiers. These are not 18 independent ceramic specimens. B2 remains three mixed-bearing specimens, with two primary physical source folds evaluable. Supplementary_reference.zip preserves the earlier six-type fixed-reference scalar benchmark. Supplementary_waveforms.zip preserves the original B2 waveform benchmark and conceptual-image provenance. These benchmarks share physical specimens with the new analysis and do not constitute independent experiments. Supplementary_methods.pdf describes their methods, results, counterexamples and boundaries. Original experimental data: https://doi.org/10.48328/tudatalib-1685 . summary: Supporting research data for “Reliable Spatiotemporal Generalization for Snow Water Equivalent Forecasting” (ReST). This dataset contains processed daily inputs, observation masks and SWE targets for 399 active stations from SNOTEL, CanSWE, CDEC and NorSWE; 590,988 forecast windows and seven training/validation splits; fixed station priors; archived publication result tables and numerical source data for Figures 2–6; and ReST prediction/observation pairs for 31 Alaska stations across three random seeds (735,300 rows). The package supports primary-dataset model training/evaluation and numerical reanalysis of the supplied results and figures. It includes English and Chinese documentation, variable definitions, provenance, component-specific data rights, validation records and SHA-256 checksums. Figure numbering follows the accompanying manuscript version used to assemble this package. The complete ReST implementation and Temporal pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/team-tgq/ReST/releases/tag/v1.0.1 . Comparative and ablation result values are included as supporting data; their model implementations and checkpoints are not distributed. Original observations and derived components retain the applicable provider terms described in DATA_RIGHTS.md. Please cite the original data providers and versions, the ReST manuscript, and this data record. For data questions or requests concerning additional research materials, contact 202512070422@std.uestc.edu.cn .

summary: The dataset, the full pipeline (corpus selection, extractive grounding with Gemini, LLM paraphrase augmentation, balancing, cross-validation folds), the training code for the five encoders in the STL and MTL settings, every prediction of every trained model, and the evaluation and statistics code. It is a re-implementation of the study, built from the paper, the undergraduate thesis it is based on and the source spreadsheet. The tables of the paper are the results of the original runs. The re-implementation reproduces the CT-Introduction results and the main conclusion (MTL does not significantly outperform STL in any task); it gives lower CT-Conclusion and CT-Abstract scores and higher CT-Planning scores (Reproducibility paragraph, Section 6 of the paper). Details in `REPRODUCTION.md`.  Version 1.1 (artifact review): adds the Provenance section to REPRODUCTION.md, a summary of the execution scenarios to the README, and SHA256SUMS. Code, data and results are unchanged from version 1.0. The original training implementation and generated data files of the study were not preserved. This package is an independent re-implementation; REPRODUCTION.md (section Provenance) states what is original, what is reconstructed and how differences affect comparability.

summary: This Zenodo record is the supplemental material for the manuscript "Probing Coherent Noise with Stabilizer Codes: Identifiability, Ambiguity, and Decoder Priors" (Long Huang, Sichuan Normal University), and it documents a three-qubit fixed-frequency transmon experiment together with the prepare–encode–expose–decode–recover–tomograph protocol, the seven stabilizer-code channels measured at idle times T ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2} µs, and the analysis needed to reconstruct process tensors, deconvolve state-preparation-and-measurement error, test linearity, monitor drift across interleaved blocks, and apply the acceptance criteria reported in the supplement. The archive contains circuit definitions, PTM reconstruction and calibration scripts, processed data such as fitted angles and per-block drift monitors, and documentation of the hardware parameters, twelve-settings-per-channel scheme, and shot budget, so that the identifiability, ambiguity, and decoder-prior claims of the paper can be independently reproduced; the code is released under the MIT license and the data and documentation under CC-BY-4.0.

The archive contains circuit definitions, PTM reconstruction and calibration scripts, processed data such as fitted angles and per-block drift monitors, and documentation of the hardware parameters, twelve-settings-per-channel scheme, and shot budget, so that the identifiability, ambiguity, and decoder-prior claims of the paper can be independently reproduced; the code is released under the MIT license and the data and documentation under CC-BY-4.0.

summary: Supplementary material and reproducibility package for the article Probing Coherent Noise with Stabilizer Codes: Identifiability, Ambiguity, and Decoder Priors . The supplement analyses the null result of a recent repetition-code experiment (arXiv:2606.07377), in which the logical fidelity of d = 3 and d = 5 bit-flip repetition codes was found to be indistinguishable under coherent and stochastic error injection, contrary to the circuit-level simulation of that work. It establishes three results, each independently checkable: The average gate infidelity of a coherent rotation is exactly invariant under randomization of its rotation axis by a drifting frame phase, so no fidelity-based comparison can detect such randomization at all. For a bit-flip repetition code read out in the computational basis, an X-type coherent injection and a stochastic injection of equal single-site average fidelity give logical error probabilities that agree to machine precision (3×10 −15 ), for d = 3 and d = 5, R = 10 rounds, with and without syndrome misreports. The gap reported in the experiment therefore cannot originate in coherent accumulation on the data qubits. The coherent–stochastic gap obeys [1 + (N−1)ρ]/N with ρ = <cos Δφ> = exp(−σ φ 2 ). The frame-phase spread required for the drift hypothesis to apply (σ φ ≳ 1.5 rad) lies a factor 30 outside the parameter domain of the generator model and an order of magnitude outside the small-angle domain in which the leading-order polarization expansion is formulated. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is δ i , with |δ i | ≤ 0.05 rad), the ε 2 /ε 4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is delta_i, with |delta_i| <= 0.05 rad), the eps^2/eps^4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The supplement closes with a channel-level ratio, coh(R_code)/coh(R_ref), that would settle the question with data of the size already recorded. Contents. supplementary_material.pdf (9 pp., 5 figures, 2 tables) and its LaTeX source; five 400 dpi figures; Python code (numpy / scipy / matplotlib) that regenerates every figure and every quoted number from a single entry point; all generated data files in JSON; README with the model assumptions, the limitations, and the relation to the two source papers. Code is released under the MIT licence; text, figures and data under CC BY 4.0.

summary: Graphs play an increasingly important role in large language model (LLM) systems, supporting structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, and memory. As these systems evolve toward the agentic era, graphs also organize execution dependencies and multi-agent communication, linking intermediate observations and retained information to subsequent decisions. However, understanding their contribution requires distinguishing the function of each graph operation, the component responsible for its computation, and the subsequent use of its output. This survey introduces an operation-level role--locus taxonomy for reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. We compare how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery. These comparisons distinguish improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance while retaining the conditions under which results were reported. We then organize benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework. Finally, we identify open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery. The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages.

summary: Decision models choose among predefined options in tasks such as routing and action selection. In multi-agent collaboration, a decision determines how members divide work, exchange resources, and act in parallel. We introduce TandemBench, a benchmark of 1,200 questions in multi-agent cooking scenarios where coordination choices affect goal completion. Models receive complete global information and candidate team plans, with reference answers established through execution and exact search. Models select an optimal team plan and, in paired variants that retain or remove it, judge whether better arrangements exist beyond the supplied options. We evaluate 40 native decision models and compare them with 10 general-purpose language models. The best native decision model achieves 62.50% decision accuracy. Native decision models remain close to chance in optimality verification. Paired tests reveal that some report better alternatives regardless of whether an optimal plan is already present. These findings show that team-plan decision accuracy alone can conceal systematic errors in judging whether the supplied options contain an optimal arrangement. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/lililibaohang/TandemBench.
title: TandemBench: Benchmarking Decision Models for Multi-Agent Collaboration

summary: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. summary: Repeated mobile GUI tests can reuse routes, locators, and recovery strategies from earlier executions. However, a route that worked in one workflow or app version may be irrelevant or misleading in another. We study how an LLM-based tester can retain useful experience while withholding entries contradicted by current observations. We present a maintenance contract for AdaptiTest in which reusable experience has an explicit applicability scope, trace provenance, and a lifecycle for confirmation, revalidation, and withdrawal. The contract reserves persistence for a Reflector role and treats recalled experience as advice. The archived implementation does not establish end-to-end enforcement of every specified mechanism. The design changes retrieved context, not model weights. The evaluation uses read-only Android workflows and archived internal comparisons. A six-task, three-repeat ready subset reports 18/18 completed runs with memory versus 3/18 without it, but a grounded single-agent control also solves the earlier hard-task slice. A separate cross-session probe is excluded from efficacy conclusions because of confounded route schedules and unvalidated state labels. We examine 13 selected real-update hazard records across nine subjects, distinguishing stale-locator observations from policy-based withholding and offline retrieval diagnostics. The latter do not measure live-device failures or actions saved. These events are UI changes, not confirmed regression bugs. The evidence supports a bounded design and case study; it does not establish general efficacy, superiority over independent GUI-agent systems, or unrestricted exploration.

summary: We present a method for efficient simulation of error propagation and decoding in universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits under stochastic Pauli noise, requiring only that the circuit has a high fault distance and that all logical non-Clifford operations are implemented by physical T, CS and CCZ gates. This is achieved using modified Pauli frame-based error tracking in which the frame contains no logical information. Decoding success is identified by verifying that the Pauli frame is still logically trivial after decoding. Using the results of Ref. [1] and the observation that the distribution of non-logical measurement outcomes in the circuit is independent of the logical state, we show that we can accurately sample all detector outcomes. Our approach can also simulate circuits containing adaptive operations conditioned on logical measurements, provided these measurements have a known outcome distribution. This applies to the majority of adaptive operations such as state teleportation and preparation by measurement. Our method only detects decoding failures and so is consistent with complexity-theoretic expectations as it cannot be used to sample from the noiseless outcome distribution of the logical circuit.
title: Efficiently tracking errors and outcomes in universal quantum circuits

summary: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.

summary: LLM-based coding agents are primarily evaluated by their solve rates. However, this metric does not reveal how difficult the solved tasks are or account for differences intask difficulty across benchmarks. Determining the difficulty of individual tasks by repeatedly running multiple agents is costly, while a predicted difficulty score alone provides limited guidance on what support an agent needs. To address these challenges, we propose DARE (Difficulty Analysis for Repair Enhancement), which integrates repair-task difficulty measurement, prediction, feature-group contribution analysis, and task-specific repair support. We define continuous task difficulty as the observed failure rate across multiple coding agents. The DARE difficulty model predicts this difficulty using 151 static features extracted from benchmark artifacts. The framework also analyzes the contributions of seven Repair-Task Feature Groups to identify the characteristics most salient to each task and uses this information to select task-specific agent support. We evaluate DARE on four benchmark partitions comprising 2,594 tasks. The difficulty model's aligned predictions achieve Spearman's $ρ$ = .476-.621 on held-out partitions, and the most salient Feature Groups vary across tasks and benchmarks. Furthermore, coding-agent experiments show improved repair success when support is matched to each task's salient Feature Group. These findings demonstrate that difficulty prediction and interpretation can lead to practical improvements in automated program repair (APR), while also providing a basis for difficulty-stratified agent evaluation, cross-benchmark comparisons, and identifying areas of repair capability that warrant further improvement.

summary: In this paper, we study the graph shotgun assembly problem in the labeled lattice model, as introduced by Mossel and Ross (2019). We start with a $d$-dimensional lattice of length $n$, where the color of each vertex is sampled i.i.d. from a distribution $π$. Then, we ask whether it is possible to reconstruct the coloring of the lattice given the coloring of each subgrid of length $k$. While previous work by Ding and Liu (2023) and Demidovich, Panichkin, and Zhukovskii (2023) identified the reconstruction threshold when $π$ is uniform, we examine the non-uniform case. This paper establishes a sufficient condition for the impossibility of reconstruction for $d \geq 2$ using information-theoretic arguments. Our negative result matches the known threshold in the uniform case.

summary: This record contains the code, a simulated benchmark dataset, and the result files for a study on detecting cyberattacks that are masked by AI data-center load transients in inverter-rich distribution grids. The manuscript itself is not included. Benchmark. The IEEE 33-bus distribution feeder is driven by 61 measured GPU power traces: 10 large-language-model training runs and 51 inference runs, recorded on A100, H100, H200 and L40S GPUs at 0.1 s. These traces form the load of an AI data center at bus 7, rated at 15–30% of feeder load. A photovoltaic inverter at bus 17 follows the IEEE 1547-2018 Category B volt-var curve. Nine channels are recorded at 10 Hz: three bus voltages, feeder-head P and Q, data-center P and Q, and inverter P and Q. The dataset holds 1,000 labeled scenarios of 120 s each. Of these, 598 contain one of seven attack types (bias, scaling, ramp, pulse, replay, coordinated mimic, and control-loop), and 220 of the attacks are hidden inside data-center load transients. Every sample is labeled for attack and for load transient. Code. The Python code covers: a linearized DistFlow model and an exact AC backward/forward-sweep power flow; data-center load generation from the GPU traces; attack injection and 10 Hz scenario simulation; physics-residual features learned from historical measurements, without feeder impedances; the RIME optimizer and a CNN-LSTM-attention detector (PR-Net); gradient-boosting, random-forest, MLP and logistic-regression baselines; window-level and event-level evaluation with scenario-bootstrap confidence intervals. Results. The result files contain the numbers behind all tables and figures: comparisons of detectors trained with and without load-transient awareness and physics residuals; ablations, computational cost, and an equal-budget comparison of RIME, random search and an untuned default; robustness tests under seven conditions, including exact AC power flow, unseen workload shapes, and changes in noise, photovoltaic share, data-center size and inverter location; a replay-attack consistency check; trained Stage-1 network weights. Third-party data. The GPU power traces come from the public LLM Power Trace Explorer repository (commit 9c25218). Because that repository has no license file, the raw traces are not redistributed here; scripts/prepare_gpu_traces.py rebuilds them from the public source. The included benchmark contains only simulated feeder signals driven by normalized, scaled versions of those load shapes.
title: Physics-Residual Detection of Cyberattacks Masked by AI Data-Center Load Transients in Inverter-Rich Distribution Grids

summary: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.

summary: Oscillatory power components in AI data-center demand can produce large frequency deviations when they coincide with vulnerable grid modes. Mode-aware hybrid energy storage systems (HESSs) can selectively suppress these components, but their effectiveness degrades when the grid mode changes while the control target remains fixed. This paper proposes a closed-loop grid-mode-adaptive HESS control framework that integrates measurement-based modal identification with mode-selective control. A sliding-window N4SID estimator identifies the local grid dynamics from grid-side power and frequency measurements, and the resulting natural-frequency estimate is used to retune the modal suppression branch assigned to the supercapacitor. The framework is evaluated under a grid-mode shift from 0.50 to 1.35Hz while maintaining equal physical damping and approximately equal load excitation at both frequencies. Compared with the fixed-target controller, the adaptive method reduces the post-change grid-side modal power component from 8.78 to 2.02MW, corresponding to a 76.94% reduction, and substantially lowers the resulting frequency deviation.

summary: Personalized retrieval-augmented generation requires extracting and applying user preferences from extended interaction histories. This task is challenging because preference evidence is scattered across past conversations and remains bound to specific temporal and situational contexts. Consequently, isolated fragments rarely provide complete support for a response, while preferences expressed under different conditions are easily conflated. To address these limitations, we propose Weaver, a framework that incrementally weaves memory-conditioned retrieval trajectories with compositional preference reasoning for personalized responses. Weaver operates on a Dual-Layer Retrieval and Reasoning Graph that couples an upper Intent Dependency Graph with a lower Memory-Conditioned Retrieval Trajectory Graph. Dependency Information Gap Tracking represents the information needed to answer the current request and its prerequisite dependencies in the upper graph. Memory-Conditioned Incremental Retrieval uses established premises and clues from retrieved conversations to locate missing evidence, recording the resulting retrieval trajectories in the lower graph. Scope-Aware Compositional Reasoning jointly interprets the accumulated evidence to determine which preferences apply to the request. It identifies complementary and alternative support and distinguishes conflicting claims within the same temporal and situational context. These conclusions iteratively update task premises and remaining information gaps, guiding subsequent retrieval to establish a coherent contextual basis for the final response. Experiments on personalized RAG benchmarks, particularly PersonaMem, demonstrate that Weaver outperforms leading baselines in both evidence completeness and answer quality.

summary: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.

summary: In transactional databases, achieving active-active replication among geo-distributed replicas is challenging due to the high coordination cost in ensuring the serializability of concurrent cross-node transactions. Deterministic concurrency control (DCC) has emerged as a promising alternative: it establishes a global order for a batch of transactions before execution and thereby amortizes this coordination cost across the batch. To better understand the performance characteristics of DCC, we conduct a theoretical analysis of traditional two-phase locking and optimistic concurrency control to account for geo-replication and introduce a model for DCC. We compare the three paradigms and identify the conditions under which DCC is advantageous. Guided by the insights from this analysis, we then present Quirinus, a DCC-based geo-replicated database that optimizes transaction execution through speculative execution, transaction reordering, integration of conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), and fast-path commit. Even without these optimizations, Quirinus achieves up to 6.2x the TPC-C throughput of Tiga under our configuration.

To better understand the performance characteristics of DCC, we conduct a theoretical analysis of traditional two-phase locking and optimistic concurrency control to account for geo-replication and introduce a model for DCC. We compare the three paradigms and identify the conditions under which DCC is advantageous. Guided by the insights from this analysis, we then present Quirinus, a DCC-based geo-replicated database that optimizes transaction execution through speculative execution, transaction reordering, integration of conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), and fast-path commit. Even without these optimizations, Quirinus achieves up to 6.2x the TPC-C throughput of Tiga under our configuration.
title: Optimizing Geo-replicated Deterministic Databases

summary: Confidence estimates guide human review in LLM-built knowledge graphs, but better error prediction can yield little improvement in an audit. We study this gap through repairability, selection headroom and label validity. Modelling non-adaptive auditing as budgeted covering, we characterise the minimal decision-relevant error statistics and bound the regret of scalar-preserving first-order planning by a structural mass $Δ^{\mathrm{cl}}$. We simulate ideal repair against benchmark-aligned labels for five extraction configurations and two cross-document graphs on Re-DocRED, followed by frozen confirmation on test and replication on 500 hash-selected training documents. On the held-out cross-document graphs, an error-rate $\times$ fan-out queue leaves 3.98-4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint model with the same actions. By comparison, opening shared actions for that joint planner reduces residual errors by 0.89-1.43 points relative to its own fact-only plans, in point estimates. Equivalence between joint and independent-block models remains inconclusive. Generic LLM verification improves three of four model-budget configurations on each held-out set. LLM adjudication identifies possible benchmark omissions.
title: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge-Graph Audit?

summary: Temporal-difference (TD) learning underlies many prediction and control algorithms, but can diverge when combined with off-policy learning, bootstrapping, and function approximation. TD with Regularized Corrections (TDRC) is theoretically sound and practically simple, but existing convergence theory covers only the one-step case under i.i.d. sampling, while the Huber Bellman-error formulation has not been extended to TDRC or eligibility traces. In this work, we establish convergence of constrained TDRC($λ$) with diminishing stepsizes and non-i.i.d. off-policy data, for state-dependent and history-dependent $λ$-parameters. We also propose TDRC($λ$)-Huber, which preserves the TDRC($λ$) fixed point while reducing sensitivity to large Bellman errors. For both algorithms, we apply an ODE-based weak-convergence method from stochastic approximation theory. For the nonlinear mean dynamics of TDRC($λ$)-Huber, we give an integral small-gain condition that guarantees uniqueness and global asymptotic stability of the target equilibrium. We then establish convergence of the constrained algorithm, derive computable sufficient conditions for convergence, and identify a regularization-based convergence mechanism shared by linear TDRC($λ$) and TDRC($λ$)-Huber. When the mean TD matrix is positive stable, both constrained algorithms converge under sufficiently strong regularization without requiring positive definiteness.
title: On Convergence of Gradient Temporal-Difference Learning with Regularized Corrections and Eligibility Traces

summary: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert--Schmidt asymmetry (\(\AHS\)), which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit \(S\)-wave \(p+{}^3\mathrm{He}\) two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from \textit{ab initio} many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, \(\AHS\)-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.
title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization

summary: Periodic driving enables ultrafast control of electronic structures in solids through the formation of photon-dressed Floquet-Bloch states. However, the measured photoemission spectra are influenced not only by these states but also by their interference with Volkov-dressed outgoing photoelectrons. Here, we demonstrate that Floquet-Volkov interference can generate spin-polarized photoemission in a collinear antiferromagnetic Dirac model without spin-orbit coupling (SOC). An in-plane linearly polarized pump preserves $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry, leaving the Floquet quasienergies spin degenerate. Under near-resonant driving, photon-dressed conduction and valence bands hybridize, producing spin-dependent relative phases that are converted into unequal spin-resolved photoemission intensities through interference between pathways reaching the same Volkov-dressed final state. We analytically identify this interference mechanism and verify it using nonequilibrium Green-function calculations under periodic driving and finite pump-probe pulses. We further demonstrate that rotating the probe polarization can suppress or reverse the spin polarization without modifying the Floquet bands. Our findings establish Floquet-Volkov interference as a route to spin-selective photoemission in driven antiferromagnets without Floquet spin splitting or SOC.
title: Floquet-Volkov spin polarization in spin-degenerate Antiferromagnets

summary: As Generation Z becomes the dominant demographic cohort entering the global labor force, organizational human resource practices face an unprecedented paradigm shift regarding work-life balance and employee retention. This critical review systematically synthesizes recent empirical and theoretical literature (2021–2026) examining the nexus between work-life balance dimensions—including flexible hybrid schedules, digital boundary management, autonomous schedule crafting, and mental health support—and job satisfaction among Gen Z employees. Applying PRISMA 2020 protocol, 16 benchmark studies were critically evaluated. Meta-synthesis indicates that work-life integration significantly enhances job satisfaction and organizational loyalty, primarily mediated by perceived autonomy, reduced burnout, and work-family enrichment. However, hyper-connectivity and blurriness in digital work boundaries introduce novel stressors. The review constructs a structural structural equation modeling (SEM) path framework and formulates a multi-level organizational alignment matrix to optimize Gen Z work-life integration.

summary: Flexible work arrangements (FWAs), encompassing temporal flexibility (flexitime, compressed workweeks) and spatial flexibility (hybrid work, telecommuting), have evolved from fringe employee perks into strategic imperatives for modern workforce governance. This critical review synthesizes empirical evidence from 16 benchmark studies published between 2021 and 2026 to examine the structural mechanisms linking FWAs with employee engagement and organizational citizenship behavior (OCB). Applying Social Exchange Theory, Job Demands-Resources Theory, and Self-Determination Theory, this study identifies psychological autonomy, perceived organizational support, and work-life harmony as primary mediating drivers that amplify both vigor and dedication (engagement) and extra-role behaviors (OCB-Individual and OCB-Organization). However, the review uncovers critical boundary conditions, demonstrating that unmanaged spatial flexibility risks boundary blurring, isolation, and professional erosion if uncoupled from supportive leadership and clear boundary management norms. The paper delivers a multi-level conceptual framework, methodologically evaluates current structural equation modeling (SEM) findings, and outlines actionable strategic HR directives to optimize FWA implementation.
tags: Employee Engagement, Flexible Work Arrangements, Hybrid Work, Organizational Citizenship Behavior, Social Exchange Theory
title: THE EFFECTS OF FLEXIBLE WORK ARRANGEMENTS ON EMPLOYEE ENGAGEMENT AND ORGANIZATIONAL CITIZENSHIP BEHAVIOR: A REVIEW

summary: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.
title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application

summary: The memory of production agents is increasingly becoming a bottleneck and is built almost exclusively from text: key points are extracted from out-of-limit context and retrieved into context at query time. Therefore, every new query incurs an additional cost that grows with the accumulated history. Weight memory is a complementary alternative that internalizes knowledge into model parameters and answers with no context at all, and has recently proven effective in self-evolving agents for internalizing skills and behaviors. However, its application in episodic and semantic memory, such as user-specific facts, remains comparatively unexplored, and a gap remains between earlier attempts at weight memory and text-based systems regarding recall performance. We study how to make weight memory competitive as a long-term factual store by applying on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). It trains a context-free student from a teacher, which is the same model conditioned on the user's memory, together with a verify-then-regenerate router that lets weight and text memory each cover the queries they handle best. On the HaluMem benchmark, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query. We further conduct an extensive study that characterizes the behavior of weight memory and analyzes how different training recipes affect its performance. As agent harnesses move toward persistent, multi-session deployments, these results position weight memory as a practical, low-cost component of agent memory and provide insights into feasible training and evaluation protocols for combining it with retrieval.

summary: Self-supervised world models are often said to organize their latents around physical quantities. We test this on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow in three pre-registered studies, each tested once on held-out data. In Study 1, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained to predict the flow fails the pre-registered criteria for organizing its latent around fluid quantities better than an untrained network of the same architecture (not supported); a JEPA trained on non-physical linear dynamics and a static invariance model that never sees time do as well or better. In Study 2, plain autoencoders that render the field make enstrophy prominent in their slowest unsupervised latent directions (best r 0.80-0.86 vs 0.38 untrained; fresh seeds, sealed data). Adding VICReg lowers this prominence in every comparison, though not by the pre-registered margin for vorticity, while raising the autoencoders' linear decodability (partially supported). In Study 3, we build steerable directions ("dials") by routing: the decoder gets overall scale only through a small conditioning code, while its other pathway carries a degraded copy of spectral shape. summary: Existing generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement $\mathbf{y}_0$ is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, the image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint flow and show that they are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image given the current joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond selecting the number of inference steps and achieves substantially shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.

summary: Reconstruction of three-dimensional vascular structures from a limited number of X-ray projections is a severely underdetermined and ill-conditioned inverse problem. This work presents a unified matrix-free computational framework for evaluating iterative numerical methods for sparse-view cone-beam tomography. Forward and backprojection are implemented from ray-voxel intersection lengths computed with the Amanatides-Woo traversal algorithm, avoiding explicit construction of the large sparse system matrix. We systematically compare ART, SART, SIRT, gradient descent (GD), and Krylov subspace methods, including Conjugate Gradient, LSQR, and GMRES. The common matrix-free operators and geometry are used for all methods, allowing consistent comparisons under matched conditions. Particular emphasis is placed on gradient scaling using scalar step sizes, Jacobi preconditioning, and diagonal Hessian majorization, together with L1, Tikhonov, and total variation regularization. Numerical experiments use five three-dimensional coronary vessel models reconstructed from ten simulated X-ray projections under noise and scattering conditions, and are extended to real X-ray projections of a static thin-vessel phantom. Performance is evaluated in terms of convergence, computational cost, volumetric overlap, contrast-to-noise ratio, vessel diameter and centerline errors, and projection consistency at an unseen viewing angle. The results show that total-variation-regularized gradient descent with diagonal majorization provides the best overall reconstruction performance within the investigated computational budgets. By contrast, the tested Krylov implementations achieve limited geometric recovery despite higher computational cost. These findings emphasize the importance of appropriate gradient scaling and regularization for stable and computationally efficient sparse-view tomographic reconstruction.

summary: Audited research compendium supporting the evaluation of Big Five league representation as a candidate squad-composition performance indicator for FIFA World Cup knockout progression from 1998 to 2026. The release contains 1,584 first-knockout starting-eleven records nested within 144 team-tournaments across eight men’s World Cups and 48 national teams. The analytical framework evaluates three linked properties: discrimination between levels of format-harmonised knockout progression; incremental information beyond pre-tournament World Football Elo; and transportability of any increment to World Cup editions and national teams excluded from model estimation. The 1998–2010 historical extension preserves the frozen exposure, outcome and model definitions established for 2014–2026. Historical starter status derives from the Fjelstul World Cup Database and was cross-checked against RSSSF match details. Club affiliation and top-division status were adjudicated using tournament squad records and season-specific domestic-league reference files. The 2014–2026 subset retains the completed provenance audit, including 505 re-checked starter records, 13 starter-name corrections, 45 club-affiliation checks and seven Big Five reclassifications. Analyses include tournament-adjusted ordinal and cut-point models, AICc comparison with Akaike weights, 5,000 national-team cluster-bootstrap samples with bias-corrected and accelerated intervals, leave-one-edition-out validation, leave-one-national-team-out validation, a strict 2026 temporal and tournament-format holdout, and a predictive cluster bootstrap that refits both competing models within every fold and resample. Additional checks address collinearity, edition adjustment and dependence through within-edition permutation testing and an edition-level block bootstrap. Big Five representation was associated with deeper knockout progression before adjustment for Elo, but this association attenuated after adjustment. Model comparisons and held-out evaluations did not establish a stable, transportable increment beyond prior team strength. These findings concern the predictive information provided by current league representation; they do not distinguish the mechanisms through which players enter elite leagues or develop within them. Version 5.2.0 updates presentation and documentation only. Figure 1 presents the relationship between Big Five representation and Elo alongside the four primary ordinal-model estimates. Figure 2 displays the held-out difference in ignorance score between the joint Big Five + Elo model and Elo alone for each World Cup edition, together with the equal-edition mean and its 95% BCa interval. The former supplementary interval figure was removed; its underlying estimates remain available in the deposited machine-readable results. No data, frozen definition, model specification, inferential estimate, predictive score, random seed or substantive conclusion changed from v5.1.0. The estimand is knockout progression conditional on qualification for the knockout stage. These observational data do not identify a causal effect of Big Five employment, estimate the long-term developmental return to elite-league exposure or address group-stage qualification. The compendium includes analytical data, provenance records, analysis code, machine-readable results and publication-ready figures. The derivative dataset is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, with attribution to the Fjelstul World Cup Database.
title: Big Five representation, Elo and FIFA World Cup knockout progression, 1998–2026: audited data and reproducibility materials

summary: 本資料集整理58,269筆臺灣公共圖書館來源觀測,參照年涵蓋1991–2026,逐筆保留官方URL、原件雜湊、頁表及儲存格定位、原始值、期間、單位、母體與來源版本。v0.9.2新增2004年圖書館年鑑統計章三表的完整公共館相關子群,含16個實體格與24筆來源觀測。提供同內容的CSV、JSONL與SQLite及完整ZIP,供資料檢索、來源對照與保留原統計口徑的研究。不同出版版本、地域層級與年/月口徑並存,並非連續一致的全國縣市年度面板,不能整表加總為館數;人工抽樣核讀與雙校尚未完成。 This dataset compiles 58,269 source observations of Taiwan public-library statistics with reference years spanning 1991–2026. Each observation retains an official URL, original-file hash, page/table/cell locator, raw value, period, unit, population and source version. Version 0.9.2 adds the complete selected public-library subsets from three tables reporting 2004 statistics: 16 physical cells and 24 source observations. Equivalent CSV, JSONL and SQLite representations and a complete ZIP support discovery, source comparison and research that preserves statistical definitions. Publication versions, geographic levels and annual/monthly definitions coexist. The data are not a complete harmonized national county-year panel and must not be summed wholesale as library counts. Human sample reading and double collation remain incomplete.
title: 臺灣公共圖書館跨年度統計 / Taiwan Public Library Statistics

summary: This record contains the Python code and the reference outputs for the manuscript *How much can a bonus–malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating* by Wei Zhu (University of Groningen).   The code treats a bonus–malus system as a finite-state estimator of a policyholder's claim propensity, evaluated by Norberg's credibility criterion. It computes the share of the variance of the claim propensity explained by no-claim discounts, −1/+m scales and hidden-counter scales as the number of classes grows; benchmarks for any rule with a given number of memory states (optimisation over tilted binomial and multinomial laws, exhaustive and heuristic search over deterministic machines, the van Trees lower bound); the evaluation of fourteen historical bonus–malus scales in the long run, at finite policy ages and with one premium scale for all ages; out-of-sample tests and a segmented-tariff analysis on a public French motor panel (1999–2007); and checks against the published tables of Norberg (1976) and Borgan, Hoem and Norberg (1981).   README.md maps every table and result of the paper to the script that produces it. The French motor data (CASdatasets, fremotor2/3/4freq9907b) are public and are not included; data/README.md lists the files and their SHA-256 checksums. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, mpmath, rdata and xarray.   Version 1.1.0 accompanies the version of the manuscript submitted to the Annals of Actuarial Science: flat layout (code/, results/), three scripts added for the revised manuscript (brier_translation.py, design_levers.py, det_exhaustive_reducible.py), a replication script run_all.py, and a README mapped to the current numbering of tables, sections and propositions. The computations of the scripts in version 1.0.0 are unchanged.
title: Code for: How much can a bonus-malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating

summary: Flow matching models have emerged as a dominant paradigm for generative posterior sampling in imaging inverse problems. Existing solvers follow two distinct lines of work: trajectory-space methods, which refine sampling dynamics from random initial noise, and source-space methods, which optimize the initial noise itself. While most prior work treats these as independent design choices, we show that they are inherently coupled. We derive a unified stability bound that links initialization proximity and cumulative sampling stochasticity through a multiplicative envelope, complemented by two empirical observations. First, we identify a sufficiency regime in which a moderately optimized proximal source initialization is enough to attain the performance plateau, rendering exhaustive source-space optimization unnecessary. Second, this initial advantage is fragile: it is eroded by excessive stochasticity accumulation during guided sampling, necessitating a mechanism that bounds the cumulative noise injection. These findings motivate FLINT, a two-stage framework that operationalizes this coupling. FLINT establishes a high-fidelity starting point via a manifold-constrained proximal objective in only a few iterations, then performs guided sampling under a bounded stochasticity schedule that helps prevent erasure of the initialization advantage. Across diverse inverse problems, FLINT delivers state of the art perceptual quality and competitive distortion metrics while maintaining superior computational efficiency.
title: FLINT: Coupling Proximal Initialization and Bounded Stochasticity for Flow-Matching Inverse Problems

summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials

On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials

summary: Supplementary material and reproducibility package for the article Probing Coherent Noise with Stabilizer Codes: Identifiability, Ambiguity, and Decoder Priors . The supplement analyses the null result of a recent repetition-code experiment (arXiv:2606.07377), in which the logical fidelity of d = 3 and d = 5 bit-flip repetition codes was found to be indistinguishable under coherent and stochastic error injection, contrary to the circuit-level simulation of that work. It establishes three results, each independently checkable: The average gate infidelity of a coherent rotation is exactly invariant under randomization of its rotation axis by a drifting frame phase, so no fidelity-based comparison can detect such randomization at all. For a bit-flip repetition code read out in the computational basis, an X-type coherent injection and a stochastic injection of equal single-site average fidelity give logical error probabilities that agree to machine precision (3×10 −15 ), for d = 3 and d = 5, R = 10 rounds, with and without syndrome misreports. The gap reported in the experiment therefore cannot originate in coherent accumulation on the data qubits. The coherent–stochastic gap obeys [1 + (N−1)ρ]/N with ρ = <cos Δφ> = exp(−σ φ 2 ). The frame-phase spread required for the drift hypothesis to apply (σ φ ≳ 1.5 rad) lies a factor 30 outside the parameter domain of the generator model and an order of magnitude outside the small-angle domain in which the leading-order polarization expansion is formulated. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is δ i , with |δ i | ≤ 0.05 rad), the ε 2 /ε 4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is delta_i, with |delta_i| <= 0.05 rad), the eps^2/eps^4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The supplement closes with a channel-level ratio, coh(R_code)/coh(R_ref), that would settle the question with data of the size already recorded. Contents. supplementary_material.pdf (9 pp., 5 figures, 2 tables) and its LaTeX source; five 400 dpi figures; Python code (numpy / scipy / matplotlib) that regenerates every figure and every quoted number from a single entry point; all generated data files in JSON; README with the model assumptions, the limitations, and the relation to the two source papers. Code is released under the MIT licence; text, figures and data under CC BY 4.0.
